lead: Both readings ask what makes a teacher of God’s word trustworthy. Paul describes his own ministry: no cunning, no tampering with the word, no preaching of himself, only the open statement of the truth, because the light that shines in the face of Christ is not his to dim or to own. In Matthew, Jesus speaks to teachers who have made access to God harder rather than easier, and whose cleverness over oaths has lost sight of the God in whose name they are sworn. In the last days of the season of the Apostles, the Church hears what the sending of the apostles was for: that others might see the light, and that no one be kept from it.

r.h: The light shines in the face of Christ
set: Second Corinthians is the most personal of Paul’s letters. He writes after a time of sharp tension with the Corinthian community, in which some had questioned his authority and his sincerity. In 2:14 to 3:18 he has defended his ministry as a ministry of the new covenant, of the Spirit and not of the letter, and has compared it with the veil that lay over Moses’ face (3:12–18). Chapter 4 begins with a quiet conclusion: because this ministry is a mercy from God, he does not lose heart.

The verses are also a kind of examination of conscience for anyone who preaches. Paul lists what he has put aside (hidden shame, cunning, the falsifying of God’s word) and what he does instead (the open statement of the truth). Then comes one of the most luminous sentences in his letters: the God who said at creation “Let light shine out of darkness” has shone in our hearts.
str: v. 1: because the ministry is God’s mercy, we do not lose heart.
v. 2: what we have renounced (hidden shame, cunning, falsifying God’s word) and what we do: state the truth openly.
vv. 3–4: if the gospel is veiled, it is so to those who are perishing, whose minds the “god of this world” has blinded.
v. 5: we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for his sake.
v. 6: the God of the first creation has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ.
kw: The ordinary word for waiting at table and for any service done for others. Paul uses it for his whole apostolic work: he is not a ruler of the Corinthians but a servant given to them by God’s mercy.
The Greek word behind our “icon”. Christ is the image of God (v. 4): in him the invisible God can be seen. The same thought stands behind Colossians 1:15 and Hebrews 1:3.
A rare word in the New Testament, found in verses 4 and 6. It means the shining out of light, not only light that is there. It is God who makes it shine, in creation and in the heart.
vv: Therefore, since it is by God’s mercy that we are engaged in this ministry, we do not lose heart.

Paul has just spoken of the glory of the new covenant (3:7–18). The ministry is a gift, so he does not rest on his own strength. The same phrase, “we do not lose heart”, returns in 4:16, after he has listed his sufferings.
we refuse to practice cunning or to falsify God’s word
The Greek verb for “falsify” was used of traders who watered down wine or diluted goods. A preacher who adapts the word of God to please his hearers does something like this.
the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers

This is a title for Satan, the great adversary, who has real but limited power (compare John 12:31). Paul is not teaching two gods: the Catholic faith holds one God, creator of all, and the Tempter is a creature. Blindness here is a darkening that the Gospel can lift, not a sentence on any person, and Paul himself was once blind in this way.
we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’ sake

“Lord” is the earliest Christian confession (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11). Paul uses the word “slaves” of himself as a minister of the Church, which turns the proud claims of the Corinthian teachers upside down.
in the face of Jesus Christ

Moses’ face shone with a fading glory that he covered with a veil (3:13). Now the glory of God is seen, without a veil, in a human face: that of Jesus Christ. The vision on the road to Damascus, which Paul remembers here, lies behind the verse.
ch: The Church sees in this passage the pattern of all preaching. The Second Vatican Council begins its constitution on the Church with the same image: Christ is the light of the nations, and the Council wishes to brighten all people with the light of Christ shining on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1). The Church is not the source of the light, but the face in which it shows. The Catechism teaches that the Church does not speak of herself but hands on what she has received from the Lord (CCC 76–78 on the handing on of the faith, in substance), which is exactly what Paul means by “we do not proclaim ourselves”.

r.h: Woe to you who lock people out
set: Matthew 23 is the last of the five great discourses of Jesus, delivered in the Temple in the final days before his Passion. It is addressed “to the crowds and to his disciples” (23:1) and begins with a statement that is easy to forget: the scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat, so do what they teach, but do not follow what they do (23:2–3). The seven woes that follow (counted without the disputed verse 14) are the speech of a prophet inside his own people, like those of Amos or Jeremiah. They are not a verdict on Pharisees as such, still less on the Jewish people.

The Church has to hear these words with care. In the Gospel they warn every religious leader, the apostles included, that teaching can become a barrier. Many Pharisees of the time were sincere and devout, and the early Church includes Pharisees who came to faith (Acts 15:5; Philippians 3:5). The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be blamed on all Jews then living, nor on Jews today (Nostra Aetate 4).
str: v. 13: first woe: you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces, neither entering yourselves nor letting others in.
v. 15: second woe: zeal to make a convert, who then becomes a worse “child of hell” than the teachers.
vv. 16–22: third woe: the teaching on oaths. Swearing by the sanctuary or altar was treated as not binding, but by the gold or the gift as binding. Jesus answers that every such oath reaches God.

¶ Verse 14 does not appear in the text of the NRSV, because it is missing in the best manuscripts; many copies added it from Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47, with the words about devouring widows’ houses. The verse numbering therefore jumps from 13 to 15.
kw: In Greek the word first meant an actor on stage, one who plays a part. In the Gospel it describes a person whose religious role covers over a heart that has not been changed.
A prophetic cry that is also a lament. The same cry opens several of the prophets’ oracles, for example Isaiah 5:8–24. It expresses grief over those who go wrong and a warning to turn back.
An oath calls God as witness to the truth of what is said. Jesus does not abolish oaths here; he rejects the idea that some formulae bind and others do not.
vv: you lock people out of the kingdom of heaven. For you do not go in yourselves, and when others are going in, you stop them.

The key image is in Luke 11:52: the teachers have taken away the key of knowledge. A good teacher opens a door; a bad one stands in the doorway. Jesus does not say the teachers had no learning but that they used it as a barrier.
you cross sea and land to make a single convert, and you make the new convert twice as much a child of hell as yourselves

The first century had many Jewish teachers who welcomed Gentile converts. Jesus is not blaming the mission itself but the harm done when a convert is taught zeal without mercy, and copies the faults of the teacher. The word “hell” is Gehenna (see Matthew 18:9).
Whoever swears by the sanctuary is bound by nothing, but whoever swears by the gold of the sanctuary is bound by the oath.

The teachers had worked out a system for which oaths were binding and which were not. The result was that people could swear and escape. Jesus sees that such a system trains the conscience to look for loopholes.
whoever swears by the altar, swears by it and by everything on it

Jesus’ answer is plain: the altar sanctifies the gift, and the sanctuary is the dwelling of God, so every oath ends in God. In the Sermon on the Mount he asks that the disciple’s “Yes” simply be “Yes” (5:37).
whoever swears by heaven, swears by the throne of God and by the one who is seated upon it.
The last step in the argument takes the oath to its end. No formula is empty, because God is present to everything that is said in his name.
ch: The Church applies these woes first to herself. The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ words on oaths show that every oath involves a reference to God, whose presence and truth are to be honoured in all speech (CCC 2150–2155, in substance). St John Chrysostom, preaching on Matthew 23, reads the woes as a call to those entrusted with teaching, who are above all to be careful that their own life agrees with their words (in substance, Homilies on Matthew 72–73). The Church’s teaching on the Jewish people, from Nostra Aetate 4 onwards, reminds us that the Gospel’s sharp words belong to a family quarrel in Israel and give no ground for contempt.

qa: Who is “the god of this world” in 2 Corinthians 4:4, and is Paul saying that there are two gods?

No. The Church believes in one God, creator of all things. Paul uses a bold phrase for Satan, the tempter, who has real influence over human minds that turn from God but is only a creature and has no power that God does not permit. The phrase appears in the setting of Paul’s own call: he too once lived in darkness, and the light of Christ opened his eyes. So the verse is a warning about the blindness that sin can cause, and a promise that the Gospel is stronger.
study: Paul says, “we do not proclaim ourselves”. In my own speaking about the faith, at home, in the parish or at work, where do I speak more about myself than about Christ?
Are there words that I use in a way that lets me escape what I have promised? What would it mean for my “Yes” to be simply “Yes”?

lead: The four readings of this day speak of God who provides, calls and holds fast. In Isaiah the Lord turns the desert into a garden for the poor who have nothing but their thirst. In Acts Paul, preaching at Antioch of Pisidia, tells Israel’s story from the exodus to David as the road that leads to the Saviour, Jesus. In Romans, Paul sings of a love from which nothing can separate us, and in Matthew Jesus sends out his messengers and tells them what following him will cost and what it will gain. On the day when the Church remembers the seventy disciples whom Jesus sent before him (Luke 10:1), these readings ask what it means to be sent, and what is promised to those who receive the sent. The notes below take the Isaiah, Romans and Matthew readings.

r.h: I will open rivers on the bare heights
set: These verses belong to the part of Isaiah (chapters 40 to 55) that many scholars date to the time of the Babylonian exile, and that Catholic tradition has always read as part of the one book of Isaiah. The exiles feel forgotten; the Lord answers through the prophet that he is about to act, as at the Exodus, leading his people home. In 41:8–16 God has just told Israel, “You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off”. Our passage turns that comfort into a picture: water in the desert and trees in the wasteland.
str: v. 17: the poor and needy seek water, find none; the Lord will answer and will not forsake them.
vv. 18–19: rivers, fountains and pools in the wilderness; trees planted together in the desert.
v. 20: the purpose: that all may see and know that the Lord’s hand has done this.
kw: A pair of words used in the Psalms for those who have no resources but God. In Isaiah they stand for the whole exiled people, but the phrase has always been read more widely, of every person who knows his need.
The same verb is used in Isaiah 49:14 (“the Lord has forsaken me”), where the answer is again that God does not forget. Here the promise is stated as a promise from the Lord’s own mouth.
A verb used in the Old Testament only with God as the subject. The new rivers in the desert are a work of creation, not a lucky change in the weather.
vv: When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the Lord will answer them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them.

The thirst is real, a picture drawn from the desert road between Babylon and Judah, but it also stands for a deeper need. The answer is a person: “I the Lord”. The promise is not first of water but of presence.
I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys

Rivers on bare heights is a startling picture, for water runs down to the valleys and not along the hilltops. God does not only supply what is lacking; he makes the dry places themselves a source of life.
so that all may see and know, all may consider and understand, that the hand of the Lord has done this

Four verbs for knowing pile up. The purpose of the miracle is that people come to know the Lord who has acted. The same thought runs through the Gospel of John, where the signs are given so that people may believe.
ch: From the Church’s earliest days, the water that flows in the wilderness has been read as a sign of the Spirit and of baptism. Jesus speaks of “rivers of living water” in John 7:37–39, and the Catechism teaches that the prophets’ promises of water find their fulfilment in the Spirit poured out in Christ (CCC 694, in substance). Many Christian readers have seen in the trees of many kinds planted together (verse 19) a picture of the Church, gathering people from every nation under the one Lord.

r.h: Who will separate us from the love of Christ?
set: This is the climax of the first great section of Romans (chapters 1 to 8). Paul has shown that all, Jew and Gentile, need the grace of God, that justification comes through faith in Christ, and that the Holy Spirit gives the baptised the life of sons and daughters of God (8:14–17). He has also said that creation itself groans in hope (8:19–23). Now he gathers it all into a statement of confidence: God works through everything, even through suffering, for the good of those who love him.

Verses 29–30 are sometimes read as a chain, as if God sorted people ahead of time. Paul is writing a song of assurance to Christians who are being pressed, not a lecture on who is saved and who is lost. The Church reads them in that spirit.
str: v. 28: all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose.
vv. 29–30: God’s plan in five steps: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified.
vv. 31–34: four questions (who is against us, who will bring a charge, who is to condemn), and one answer: God, who gave his Son, and Christ, who died, was raised and intercedes.
vv. 35–37: tribulations cannot separate us from Christ’s love; we are more than conquerors.
vv. 38–39: a list of powers that cannot separate us from the love of God in Christ.
kw: The verb has the sense of working with others. Some ancient manuscripts add “God” as the subject (“God works all things together for good”), and the Malayalam Catholic Bible follows that reading. Either way the thought is of an active providence, not a blind fate.
Literally “marked out beforehand”. Paul’s goal is stated at once: to be conformed to the image of the Son. Predestination in the Church’s teaching is a plan for glory, not a doom for anyone.
One word in Greek: “we over-conquer”. Paul does not say that suffering is absent or pleasant, only that the victory is already won through the one who loved us.
vv: We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose.

The verse is not a claim that everything that happens is good. It says that God can bring good out of everything, even evil, for those who love him. The “good” is explained in the next verse: being made like the Son.
If God is for us, who is against us?
Paul does not deny that there are enemies. He says that no opponent counts when God has taken our side. The proof follows at once: God gave up his own Son for us all (verse 32).
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
The victory is “through him who loved us”, so it belongs to Christ and is shared with us. The martyrs have been the most faithful readers of this verse.
nor height, nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord

The list reaches everything in the universe. “Love” here is God’s own love, which is the beginning of the whole chapter, as of the whole creation. Only we ourselves can turn away from it, which is why Paul’s letters also contain warnings.
ch: The Church hears in this chapter the whole Gospel of hope. The Catechism quotes Romans 8:28–30 in its teaching on how God’s grace calls us to a share in the divine life (CCC 2012), and teaches that God predestines no one to hell; that comes only from a person’s own turning away from God (CCC 1037, in substance). The Roman liturgy uses verses 31–39 for the Mass of martyrs, and many Christians in every age have taken them as their strength in trial.

r.h: The cost and the reward of following Jesus
set: These verses end the Mission Discourse (Matthew 10), in which Jesus sends the twelve out to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (10:5–6) and tells them what to expect: hostility, trials, and the care of the Father who counts every sparrow (10:16–31). In 10:32–36 Jesus has said that following him may divide a family. Today’s verses finish the discourse with three steps: what Jesus asks (loving him above all and carrying the cross), what he promises (the one who loses life for his sake finds it), and what he gives to those who welcome his messengers.
str: vv. 37–38: love for Jesus above family; the cross.
v. 39: to find one’s life is to lose it, and to lose it for his sake is to find it.
vv. 40–42: welcome of the messengers is welcome of Jesus and of the Father; the reward of the prophet, the righteous, and the one who gives a cup of water.
kw: Literally “weighing as much as”. A person is worthy of Jesus when Jesus is given the weight that belongs to him. It is not a matter of merit earned but of the order of love.
Matthew uses this word of the disciple’s way before the cross of Jesus has been lifted. The hearers would have known it as the Roman means of execution. Jesus speaks plainly of the cost.
A word that means pay or wage, but used here for a gift from God that exceeds any deserving. Even a cup of water, given in the name of a disciple, has its reward.
vv: whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me
Jesus first mentions the cross here, long before the Passion. The Gospel was written after the Passion, and its readers understood: the disciple takes up what Jesus himself will carry.
Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
The Greek word for life, psychē, means the whole self. The paradox is the heart of the Gospel: a life held on to for its own sake is lost, a life given for Christ is found, and not only after death.
whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple … truly I tell you, none of these will lose their reward
The “little ones” are the humble disciples whom the world overlooks. The smallest kindness done to them is done to Christ (compare Matthew 25:40), and it is never lost.
ch: The Church has always taken the first verses as the foundation of the vocation to follow Christ in a special way. The Catechism, speaking of the duties of children and parents, teaches that family ties, though precious, are not absolute, and that parents must respect and encourage the vocation of their children (CCC 2232, in substance). Verse 42 is one of the passages on which the Church bases the works of mercy (CCC 2447, in substance), and the cup of cold water has become a lasting image for the smallest gift done with love.

qa: Does Jesus really ask us to love our family less?

No. In the language of the Gospel, to “love more” than another is to give first place to Jesus, without removing the love owed to parents and children, which God himself commands in the Fourth Commandment. Jesus says this to people for whom following him may bring a break with a family that opposes the faith, and to every disciple who must remember that God comes first. Christian love for family is not lessened when God is first; it is purified and strengthened.
rite: The seventy disciples named in Luke 10:1 are remembered today. The Church of the East counts among them Addai (Thaddaeus), the traditional apostle of Edessa and of Mesopotamia, whom Eusebius of Caesarea in his Church History calls one of the seventy. The ancient Anaphora of Addai and Mari, which the Syro-Malabar Church prays in the Holy Qurbana, carries the names of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, and so links every Qurbana on our altars with this early sending.
study: Jesus says, “those who lose their life for my sake will find it”. What is one thing I am holding on to that I could place in his hands this week?
Who are the “little ones” in my parish or neighbourhood to whom I could give a cup of cold water in Jesus’ name?

lead: On the Dukhrana of Mar Thoma, the Church’s great memorial of the apostle of the East, the four readings of the feast build one picture: a house, a road and a confession. Genesis opens with God planting a garden in the east and setting the man in it to till and keep it. Proverbs shows a father leading his child along the way of wisdom, a path that grows brighter until full day. In Ephesians, Paul says that the Gentiles are no longer strangers but citizens and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. And in John, Thomas, who has asked for proof, receives it, and finds in it more than he asked: “My Lord and my God!”

Together they say what the Church believes about the apostles: they are not the source of the faith but the foundation on which Christ builds, and the road they open leads to the Lord whom they confess. The Thomas Christians of India have always remembered their own apostle in just this way, as the one through whom the light came to them.

The day also has the readings of the Seventh Saturday of the Apostles, 1 Corinthians 7:8–16 (Paul on peace in marriage and in families where one partner is not a believer) and Matthew 19:1–12 (Jesus on marriage and on celibacy for the kingdom). The notes below follow the Dukhrana readings.

r.h: God plants a garden in Eden, in the east
set: Genesis 2:4b to 3:24 is the second account of creation, told in a different style from the seven days of chapter 1, and many scholars attribute it to an older source than the first. Here God forms the man from the dust (2:7), then plants a garden, and sets the man in it. The story is told with the simple pictures of ancient storytelling (God as gardener, trees, rivers), and its purpose is to say who God is, who the human being is, and what the first relationship was meant to be.

The verses read today are the planting of the garden and the first commandment. They come before the creation of the woman (2:18–24) and before the sin (chapter 3). Nothing here has gone wrong yet. It is a picture of what God intended: a home, work, a river of life, and one limit, which makes the gift a relationship and not only a possession.
str: v. 8: God plants a garden in Eden, in the east, and puts the man there.
v. 9: trees good for sight and food; in the middle, the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
vv. 10–14: the river that goes out of Eden and divides into four: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, Euphrates.
v. 15: the man is put in the garden to till it and keep it.
vv. 16–17: the one commandment: eat of every tree except one; to eat of it is death.
kw: “Eden” is often connected with a word for delight. In the Greek Old Testament the garden is called paradeisos, a Persian word for an enclosed park, and this is the word that came into Christian use for the place of God’s presence (see Luke 23:43).

The two verbs of verse 15. The first means to work, and also to serve; the second means to guard. The same pair is used elsewhere for the priests’ service in the sanctuary (Numbers 3:7–8), which is why many readers see the garden as the first sanctuary, and the human being as given a calling, not only a job.

In Proverbs wisdom is called “a tree of life” to those who hold her (3:18). The tree stands for life that comes only from God. At the end of the Bible it appears again, by the river of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 22:2).
vv: And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, in the east; and there he put the man whom he had formed.

God is shown as one who plants, who makes a place for his creature before asking anything of him. “In the east” is said from the writer’s side: Eden lies towards the sunrise. For the Churches of the Syriac East the word has its own warmth.
A river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides and becomes four branches.

The river of life flows out from God’s garden into the whole world. Pishon and Gihon cannot now be identified, while the Tigris and the Euphrates are known. The point is that life, from its source in Eden, reaches all lands. Some Fathers saw in the four rivers a figure of the four Gospels and, more widely, of the grace that flows from the Church.
The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it.

The man is not placed in the garden to be idle. Work, in the first picture, is part of the gift: a share in God’s own care for the world. Pope Francis, in Laudato Si’ 67, explains that “till” means to cultivate and “keep” means to protect and preserve.
You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat

The commandment begins with an enormous permission: every tree but one. The single limit shows that the man is a creature who receives life, and does not make it. The tree is not a trap: it marks the difference between God, who decides what is good and evil, and the human being who must trust him.
ch: The Church reads the garden as a picture of the friendship with God for which we were made. The Catechism teaches that the first man was created good and placed in friendship with his Creator, and that in this state of original justice he was to “till and keep” the garden (CCC 374–379, in substance). The Fathers of the East gave the garden a special love. St Ephrem’s Hymns on Paradise describe it as a place of light, fragrance and fruit, which the Church on earth already foreshadows, and which Christ has opened again (in substance). Many Fathers saw in the river of Eden a first sign of the water of baptism, and in the tree of life a figure of the cross and of the Eucharist.

r.h: Keep hold of instruction, for she is your life
set: Proverbs chapters 1 to 9 form a long introduction to the book, made of speeches in which a father (or teacher) speaks to his “child” and urges him to follow wisdom and to avoid folly. Today’s passage is one of these speeches. It is not a set of rules but an appeal, full of the language of the road: walking, running, stumbling, turning aside.

Wisdom in this book is more than clever advice. It is the way of living that fits the world as God made it, and in the later books of the Old Testament it comes to be spoken of almost as a person at God’s side (Proverbs 8; Wisdom 7–9). The New Testament sees that wisdom fulfilled in Christ.
str: vv. 10–13: the teacher’s promise: long life, a path that is clear, and a command: keep hold of instruction, for she is your life.
vv. 14–17: the other road: the way of the wicked, who cannot sleep unless they have done wrong, and whose food and drink is violence.
v. 18: the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day.
kw: The commonest word for the road in the Old Testament, and also for a manner of life. “The two ways”, of life and of death, is a theme found throughout the Bible, and the first Christians called themselves “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
The teaching that shapes a person, sometimes with correction. It is not only knowledge but formation, which is why the teacher asks the child to “keep hold” of it as of life itself.
A shining that increases. The verse uses it of the sunrise which grows till noon. The righteous life is a road on which the light grows, not a single flash.
vv: When you walk, your step will not be hampered; and if you run, you will not stumble.
The teacher’s promise is not that the road is level but that the walker will not be caught. Those who walk in wisdom, even in difficulty, are not thrown.
Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life.

Instruction is spoken of as a person (“her”) and as life itself. The Hebrew word for “life” is in the plural, hinting at fullness of life. Whoever holds on to wisdom holds on to what makes a human being truly alive.
For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.

Bread and wine are the daily food and the festive drink. Here wickedness and violence have become the very food of those who follow them: they live on it. The verse warns that evil, once chosen, becomes a habit that feeds itself.
But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day.

This is the hopeful end of the passage. The life lived in the way of God does not remain in the half-light but grows towards noon. The image fits the history of Israel as well as the life of every believer, and the Church has seen in it the light of Christ.
ch: The Church hears in the “way” of Proverbs a call that Christ fulfils: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), spoken in answer to a question from Thomas, “how can we know the way?” (14:5). Because of this, the early Christians called their faith the Way, and the Thomas Christians of India long spoke of their faith as Mar Thoma Margam, the Way of Thomas. The Church also reads Proverbs as a school of everyday holiness, in which the teacher’s patience is the pattern of the patience of parents and priests with those who are growing in faith, and she sees in Wisdom a first sketch of Christ, whom Paul calls “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

r.h: The household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles
set: The letter to the Ephesians speaks of the Church as the one body of Christ in which Jews and Gentiles are made one. Many scholars hold that Paul himself wrote it, while others think it was written by a close follower in his tradition; the Church receives it as Scripture either way. In 2:11–18 the writer has described how Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile, and made peace through the cross. Our verses draw the conclusion with the pictures of a city, a household and a building.

Three images follow one another. First comes citizenship in a city (“citizens with the saints”), then family (“members of the household of God”), then a temple (“a holy temple in the Lord”). The movement is from stranger to citizen, from citizen to child of the house, and from the house to a sacred building.
str: v. 19: no longer strangers and aliens, but citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.
v. 20: built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus as cornerstone.
v. 21: in him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
v. 22: in him you are also built together into a dwelling place for God.
kw: People who lived in a city without the rights of citizens. Gentiles were once in this position in relation to the covenant. Now the status has changed completely: they belong.
The stone at the corner (or at the head) of a building, on which the lines of the walls depend. Christ is the stone by which all the rest is aligned. Compare Psalm 118:22 and 1 Peter 2:6–7.
One verb, with two prefixes: “built” and “together, as a dwelling”. The word suggests that each stone is placed in relation to the others. No one is built into the Church alone.
vv: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God

The change is from outsiders to insiders. The Gentile Christians of Ephesus had no ancestral claim to the promises. Paul says that, in Christ, they belong. The “saints” are God’s holy people, Israel, to whom the Gentiles are now joined (compare Romans 11:17–18).
built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone

Christ is the cornerstone; the apostles and prophets are the foundation laid on him. The prophets here may be Old Testament prophets or those of the New Testament Church (see 3:5); both readings are held. The Church takes “apostolic” from this verse, as an essential mark.
In him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord
A building that grows is a strange thing, and Paul does it on purpose. The Church is built, and it is alive. Each new believer is a stone added to the temple, and the whole is “in the Lord”.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is God’s building, resting on the foundation of the apostles, with Christ the cornerstone (Lumen Gentium 6, in substance), and the Catechism declares that the Church is apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, in three ways: she was built on their witness, she keeps their teaching through their successors, and she is taught and led by them until Christ returns (CCC 857, in substance). In the Creed of the Syro-Malabar Church we say that the Church is “one, holy, catholic and apostolic”. For the Thomas Christians the word apostolic has a particular sweetness: they believe their faith was planted by an apostle of the Lord himself.

r.h: My Lord and my God
set: These verses are the last appearance of the risen Lord in the main part of John, and they lead straight to the Gospel’s first ending (20:30–31). Chapter 21 will add an epilogue. On the evening of Easter the risen Jesus has come to the disciples behind locked doors, shown them his hands and his side, and breathed on them the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins (20:19–23). Thomas was not with them.

Thomas appears twice before in John: ready to die with Jesus (11:16), asking the way (14:5), and now here. The name Thomas means “twin” (Aramaic te’oma, Greek didymos), as John says. Who his twin was, the Gospel does not say.
str: v. 24: Thomas, called the Twin, one of the twelve, was not with them when Jesus came.
v. 25: the others say, “We have seen the Lord”; he demands to see and touch before he will believe.
v. 26: a week later, Jesus comes again, though the doors are shut, and says, “Peace be with you”.
v. 27: Jesus offers Thomas what he asked: “Put your finger here... Do not doubt but believe”.
v. 28: Thomas’s confession: “My Lord and my God!”
v. 29: Jesus: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe”.
kw: A Greek word, translating the Aramaic. John uses it as a second name for Thomas (11:16; 20:24; 21:2). Tradition has often wondered whom he was twin to; the Gospel is silent.

Jesus’ words in verse 27 are literally “do not become unbelieving, but believing”. The two adjectives are one word with and without a negative. Jesus does not condemn Thomas but calls him to move from one to the other.
ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou

Thomas’s words in Greek use the definite article for each title, as is done for God himself in the Greek Old Testament (for example Psalm 35:23, “my God and my Lord”). The confession gives Jesus the names of God.
vv: Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.

Thomas does not ask for more than the others had been given. In verse 20 Jesus showed the others his hands and side. What he wants is to know that the risen Lord is the same as the crucified one, with the wounds still marked on him.
Although the doors were shut, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”

The week-later appearance happens on the Sunday, the eighth day. The Church has always seen in this the origin of the gathering for the Eucharist on the Lord’s Day. The same greeting of peace, the same Lord, the same doors shut: but now Thomas is inside.
Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.
Jesus repeats Thomas’s own words back to him. He knew the conditions Thomas had set, though he was not there. The text does not say that Thomas touched. It says that he believed.
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”

This is the highest confession of faith in the Gospels. It comes at the end of a book that began, “the Word was God” (1:1). The one who doubted most gives the clearest witness, and that is why Thomas is the patron of faith that grows through struggle.
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.
Here Jesus looks beyond Thomas to every later believer, to us, who believe through the witness of the apostles. This is the last beatitude of the Gospel, spoken for the readers of the book.
ch: The Church treats Thomas with great love. The Catechism says that even before the risen Lord the disciples were slow to believe and uses Thomas as an example (CCC 643–644, in substance), and teaches that in “My Lord and my God” the title “Lord” takes on the sense of adoration (CCC 448, in substance). St Augustine says that Thomas saw and touched the man, and confessed the God whom he neither saw nor touched (in substance, Tractates on John 121). St Gregory the Great says that the doubt of Thomas helped our faith more than the quick belief of the other disciples, because his touching leaves no room for doubt in us (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 26). Pope Benedict XVI, in his general audience of 27 September 2006, spoke of Thomas’s confession as the faith of the whole Church, and mentioned the tradition that he carried the Gospel to India (in substance).

qa: Did St Thomas really come to India?

The Church holds this as an ancient and honoured tradition. There is no document from the first century that settles the matter, but the Thomas Christians of Kerala have passed down the memory of his arrival, according to tradition at Muziris on the Malabar coast in the year 52, and of the churches he founded, and the memory is very old and very firm. In the early third century the Acts of Thomas, probably written in Syriac, perhaps at Edessa, tells of his mission to India. That book has many legendary elements, but it shows that Christians then believed Thomas went east. Popes have spoken of it with respect, and Pope Benedict XVI mentioned the tradition in 2006. When speaking of the details, the Church uses the phrase “according to tradition”, and this is the honest way to say it.
Is Thomas rightly called “doubting Thomas”?

The name is not fair to him. Thomas was loyal: he was ready to die with Jesus (John 11:16). He asked questions that we all ask (14:5). In John 20 he does not refuse to believe; he wants to meet the risen Lord for himself, as the others had. Jesus does not scold him but gives him what he asked for, and Thomas answers with the plainest declaration of Jesus’ divinity in the Gospels. The Church honours him as a man whose honest questioning led to a deeper faith.
Why does a reading from Genesis about a garden belong to the feast of an apostle?

The garden of Eden is where the story of salvation begins, with the human being at home with God. The apostles are sent to bring people back to that home. At the end of the Bible the tree of life and the river appear again (Revelation 22). So the reading sets the apostle’s work in its widest frame: to open the way back to the garden, through Christ, to people in every land, including the East, which Genesis names first.
rite: The Syriac word Dukhrana means remembrance, and the Dukhrana of Mar Thoma on 3 July is the principal feast of the apostle in the Syro-Malabar Church. According to tradition, on this day his relics were brought from India to Edessa, in the early third century. Tradition also keeps 21 December as the day of his martyrdom at Mylapore. The Church remembers him as “our father in faith”. According to tradition he founded seven communities on the Malabar coast, at Kodungallur, Palayoor, Kottakkavu (Paravur), Kokkamangalam, Niranam, Nilackal and Kollam. Other Churches that trace their origin to him also keep his memory, and the day is a gift to share. Every Holy Qurbana of the Syro-Malabar Church is also a thanksgiving for the faith that came by the apostle’s hand.
study: Thomas asked for what he needed in order to believe and was not rejected. What honest question about faith am I afraid to bring to the Lord?
“Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” Who passed the faith on to me, and how can I pass it on to someone else?
Ephesians says we are built together as a dwelling place for God. Which “stones” in my parish or family do I find hard to fit beside, and how might Christ the cornerstone align us?
Proverbs says the path of the righteous grows brighter. Where in my life do I see the light increasing, and where am I still in the half-light?

lead: On the first Sunday of Kaitha, the summer season, the Church keeps the feast of the Twelve Apostles, and the four readings ask what it means to belong to a people that God has gathered and sent. In the First Book of Kings, Elijah takes twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel, and builds the Lord’s altar again; when the fire falls, the people cry, “The Lord indeed is God”. In Acts, signs and wonders are done through the apostles, the sick are carried into the streets, the high priest’s party seizes them, and an angel opens the prison and sends them back to the temple to tell “the whole message about this life”. In First Corinthians, Paul begs a divided community to be united, for Christ is not divided. And in Luke, Jesus teaches at a dinner the way of the kingdom: take the lowest place, and invite those who cannot repay.

The twelve stones and the Twelve Apostles are not an accident of numbers. God builds a people around a new foundation, and the people are marked by unity, by humility and by an open table. The feast asks us to look at the Church as she is in this world, a people sent, often divided, always dependent on the Lord, and still the place where his signs are seen.

r.h: Elijah builds an altar of twelve stones
set: Elijah appears in the reign of King Ahab and his wife Jezebel, who have promoted the worship of Baal, the Canaanite storm god, in Israel. There has been a long drought, and the question on Mount Carmel is who gives rain and life: the Lord or Baal. The prophets of Baal have called on their god from morning until evening with no answer (18:26–29). Now Elijah calls the people, “Come closer to me”, and begins by repairing an altar of the Lord that had been thrown down.

Everything about this passage speaks of restoration. The old altar is repaired, the twelve tribes are remembered even though the kingdom is divided into two, and the prayer begins with the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel. Elijah does not claim power for himself: he asks the Lord to “let it be known this day that you are God in Israel”.
str: vv. 30–32: Elijah repairs the altar of the Lord and builds it of twelve stones, with a trench around it.
vv. 33–35: the wood, the bull, and the water poured out three times, so that the trench is filled.
vv. 36–37: Elijah’s prayer: let it be known that you are God, and that you have turned their hearts back.
vv. 38–39: the fire of the Lord falls and consumes everything; the people fall on their faces and confess the Lord.
kw: The prophet’s name is a confession: ’Ēl-i-Yah-u, “my God is Yahweh”. The whole scene on Carmel is the name acted out, and the people’s cry at the end, “The Lord indeed is God”, uses the same words as his name.
The offering that is wholly consumed by fire and rises to God. The Greek word holokauston comes from it. It is a sacrifice of complete giving, in which nothing is kept back.
A double plea in verse 37: “Answer me, O Lord, answer me”. Elijah’s prayer is brief and direct. He asks not for his own honour but for the hearts of the people to be turned back.
vv: Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the Lord came, saying, “Israel shall be your name”

The kingdom was split at the time (1 Kings 12), and ten tribes belonged to the northern kingdom where Elijah lives, but his altar has twelve stones. In the eyes of God, Israel is still one. The verse echoes Genesis 35:10, where Jacob receives the name Israel.
Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood.

The water is poured out three times (verses 33–35), and so the trench is full. In a land of drought, water was precious; it is given up to make the miracle impossible to doubt. No one will say that the fire was a spark that happened to catch.
Answer me, O Lord, answer me, so that this people may know that you, O Lord, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back.
The goal of the miracle is conversion: that the people know the Lord and have their hearts turned back. A sign in the Bible is never for show but for faith.
The Lord indeed is God; the Lord indeed is God.

The people’s answer is a profession of faith. The story shows them first as hesitating (“How long will you go limping with two different opinions?”, 18:21) and then on their faces, confessing. The prophet’s task is to bring them to this point.
ch: The Church reads Elijah as the prophet of prayer and of zeal for the Lord. The Catechism, speaking of the prophets who taught Israel to pray, says that Elijah is the “father of the prophets” and teaches that his prayer on Carmel is the prayer of faith, which asks for the heart of the people to be converted (CCC 2581–2584, in substance). The Gospels show him again at the Transfiguration with Moses, beside Jesus (Matthew 17:3), and Jesus applies the promise of Elijah’s return to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:14). Because of the twelve stones, many readers have seen in this passage a sign of the Twelve whom Jesus chose, on whom the Church’s altar is built.

r.h: Many signs and wonders through the apostles
set: The verses are one of the summaries of the life of the first community in Jerusalem. They come soon after the death of Ananias and Sapphira (5:1–11), who had lied to the Holy Spirit about their gift to the community, and which brought “great fear” on the whole Church. The apostles continue their ministry in the temple, in Solomon’s Portico, a covered walk along the east side of the temple court, where Jesus himself had walked (John 10:23).

Then comes a new open conflict (the apostles had already been arrested once, in 4:1–22): the high priest and the party of the Sadducees, filled with jealousy, arrest the apostles. The text is exact about who acts: it is the high priest and “all who were with him”, and the people continue to hold the apostles in high esteem. The Acts of the Apostles never blames the Jewish people as a whole; the first believers were themselves Jews, and they continued to worship at the temple.
str: vv. 12–13: signs and wonders; the believers gather in Solomon’s Portico; the others hold back, but the people hold them in esteem.
vv. 14–16: more and more believers; the sick carried out so that Peter’s shadow might fall on them; crowds from the towns around; all are cured.
vv. 17–18: the high priest and the Sadducees, filled with jealousy, arrest the apostles.
vv. 19–20: an angel opens the prison at night: “Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life”.
kw: A pair of words from the Greek Old Testament, used of the Exodus (Deuteronomy 34:11). The signs point to something beyond themselves; the wonders astonish. Luke uses them to show that the God of the Exodus is acting again.
A favourite word of Luke’s: the first community was “of one mind” (1:14; 2:46; 4:24; 5:12). It means more than agreement: it is an inner unity of heart given by the Spirit.
The word can mean either, and here it means envy: the leaders saw the apostles’ growing influence and could not bear it. The word shows how good things can be hated when we are jealous of them.
vv: Now many signs and wonders were done among the people through the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico.
The apostles do not work wonders by their own power; the signs are “done” through them. The community meets in a public place, in the temple area. The Church is not hidden.
so that they even carried out the sick into the streets, and laid them on cots and mats, in order that Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he came by.

Luke reports what the people believed and did; he does not say that the shadow healed, but that all were cured (verse 16). The Church understands that God works through the persons and things that he chooses (compare Acts 19:11–12).
Then the high priest took action; he and all who were with him (that is, the sect of the Sadducees), being filled with jealousy

Luke names the group: the high priest and the party of the Sadducees. This is one group inside the Jewish people of the time, and many other Jews, such as the Pharisee Gamaliel in the next verses, take a different view (5:34–39).
Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life.

The angel does not tell them to flee. The released prisoners go back to the same temple, to the same people, to give “the whole message”. The Gospel is not a private matter but a public word. “This life” means the new life that has come through the risen Lord.
ch: The Church has seen in the signs done by the apostles the proof that Christ continues his work in the Church. The Catechism teaches that the apostles’ gifts of healing belong to the life of the Church (CCC 1506–1509, in substance), and that popular devotion, such as reverence for relics, finds a place in this faith (CCC 1674, in substance). The text also shows the pattern of the apostolic Church: they pray and teach together in public, and when they are shut in prison, the Lord sends them out again. The apostles go back into the very place where they were arrested, and the Church sees in this the courage that the Spirit gives.

r.h: Be united in the same mind and the same purpose
set: First Corinthians was written by Paul from Ephesus around the year 55, to a lively and gifted community in a port city, which had also begun to split into parties. After the greeting and thanksgiving (1:1–9) he comes to the first and heaviest matter, which is the quarrels in the community. Verses 9 to 16 introduce his appeal.

In the Corinth of Paul’s day it was usual to attach oneself to a famous teacher. The Christians of Corinth had done the same: some followed Paul, who had founded the community; some Apollos, a learned preacher from Alexandria who had come after him (Acts 18:24–28); some Cephas, that is Peter; and some, perhaps with a sense of being superior, said “I belong to Christ”. Paul answers with three rapid questions that lead to the heart of the matter.
str: v. 9: God is faithful; he has called you into the fellowship of his Son.
v. 10: the appeal: all of you agree, with no divisions, united in mind and purpose.
vv. 11–12: the report from Chloe’s people: four parties, Paul, Apollos, Cephas, Christ.
v. 13: three questions: Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized in Paul’s name?
vv. 14–16: Paul is glad that he baptised few, so that no one can claim baptism in his name.
kw: A rich word for sharing in a common life. Here it is a participation in the Son of God himself, and so it is the root of the unity of the Church. The same word is used of the Eucharist in 10:16.
From a verb meaning to tear. The word is used in Matthew 9:16 for the tear in a garment. Paul’s concern is that the seamless body of Christ be torn.
A verb used of mending nets (Mark 1:19) and, more widely, of putting right what is broken. It is Paul’s word for what unity needs: a repair and a fitting together.
vv: God is faithful; by him you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
Paul begins with God’s faithfulness before he speaks of human failures. The community did not create itself: it was called, and the one who called remains faithful.
that all of you be in agreement and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same purpose

The appeal is made “by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”, the name by which they were baptised. Unity does not mean uniformity: the Corinthians have many gifts (chapters 12 to 14). It means one heart and one mind in the faith.
Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?

The three questions each expect the answer No. Christ is one, and he alone was crucified. The name in which we were baptised is the only name that can unite us. Paul puts himself last in the line of those who might claim the Corinthians.
I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius

Paul does not despise baptism. Verse 17 shows that his emphasis is on preaching, and elsewhere he teaches the greatness of baptism (Romans 6:3–4). His point here is that baptism does not make the baptiser the owner of the baptised.
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its decree on ecumenism with the wound of division, which openly contradicts the will of Christ and gives scandal to the world (Unitatis Redintegratio 1, in substance), and the Catechism teaches that the wounds to unity are healed by repentance and prayer, and that the Church must grow in unity until the end (CCC 817–822, in substance). In her prayer the Church asks for what Paul asks: that we be of one mind. As to baptism, the Council teaches that when anyone baptises, it is Christ himself who baptises (Sacrosanctum Concilium 7). Syro-Malabar Christians pray in the Holy Qurbana for the unity of the Church, and the Catholic Church today speaks with respect and love of the other Churches who share baptism with her.

r.h: Take the lowest place; invite the poor
set: Jesus is at the house of a leading Pharisee on the Sabbath for a meal (14:1). The setting is a banquet in which people are watching one another closely. Jesus has just healed a man with dropsy and asked whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath (14:2–6). Now he notices how the guests choose the places of honour, and speaks first to the guests and then to the host.

The two sayings are a lesson in humility and in generosity, but they are also a picture of the kingdom, to which Luke will turn in the next verse: “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God” (14:15). In the kingdom, the lowly are lifted up, and the table is open to those who cannot pay back. The meal that Jesus describes is the meal he himself will give.
str: v. 7: Jesus sees how the guests choose the places of honour and tells a parable.
vv. 8–10: do not take the place of honour, lest you be shamed; take the lowest place, and the host will say, “Friend, move up higher”.
v. 11: the principle: those who exalt themselves will be humbled; those who humble themselves will be exalted.
vv. 12–14: to the host: do not invite those who can repay you; invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, and you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.
kw: Literally “first couches”. At a banquet guests lay on couches around a table, and the places nearest the host were the most honoured. The word shows how closely the first place was watched.

The verb of Luke’s whole theme. Its noun is Mary’s “lowliness” in the Magnificat (1:48), and the verb is used of Jesus himself in Philippians 2:8. Humility in the Bible is not self-contempt but truth about who we are before God.
A word used for the return of a gift. It appears in verse 12, “you would be repaid”. Jesus asks us to give where no repayment is possible, so that all is God’s gift.
vv: do not sit down at the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited by your host
Jesus first speaks as a practical teacher: it is better not to be shamed. But the practical advice carries a deeper lesson, and the final verse shows that Jesus is speaking of more than manners.
For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.

This saying appears in several places in Luke (18:14) and in Matthew (23:12). It is the law of the kingdom. God raises those who do not grasp, and the one who is raised in the end is the one whom God raises.
do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, in case they may invite you in return

Jesus does not forbid hospitality to friends and family; in the language of the East, the saying says “not only”, and warns against a circle of mutual favours which shuts out the poor. The point is the direction of the gift.
invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind

These are the same people whom the host of the great banquet will invite in the parable that follows (14:21). The poor have a place at the table of the kingdom, and a community that sets a place for them is already living in it.
you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous
The reward is real but is held in God’s hands. Charity is not a transaction, but it is not lost. The resurrection is the horizon of the kingdom.
ch: The Church hears in these verses the humility of Christ himself, who “humbled himself” and took the lowest place (Philippians 2:6–8). The Catechism teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer (CCC 2559, in substance), and that works of mercy toward the poor are a witness to the Gospel and one of the main ways in which we practise charity (CCC 2443–2447, in substance). The Lord’s invitation to the poor has shaped the works of mercy of the Church throughout her history, in the Syro-Malabar Church as everywhere.

qa: Why did Jesus choose twelve apostles?

Twelve is the number of the tribes of Israel. By choosing twelve, Jesus showed that he was gathering and renewing the whole people of God, not starting something unrelated to Israel. The Church is built on the Twelve (Revelation 21:14). After Judas’s death the group was made up again by the choice of Matthias (Acts 1:15–26). Paul and Barnabas are also called apostles in the New Testament (Acts 14:14), though they are not among the Twelve. The Catechism teaches that the Twelve are the foundation of the Church and that the bishops are their successors (CCC 551–553, 880–881, in substance).
Did Peter’s shadow really heal people?

Luke tells us that the people carried out the sick so that Peter’s shadow might fall on them, and that all were cured. The Church does not treat the shadow as a magic charm. In the Catholic understanding, healing is always the work of God, who may use the persons and things that he chooses as signs of his closeness. This is the root of the Church’s respect for holy persons and, in a different way, for relics and sacramentals, always with the understanding that they point to Christ.
Does Jesus say that we should never invite our friends and family to dinner?

No. In the way of speaking used in his time, “do not invite A, but B” often means “not only A, but also B”. Jesus is against a kind of hospitality that is closed, where we give only to those who can give back. He asks us to open the table to those who cannot repay, and so to share what we have as God has shared it with us.
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church begins the season of Kaitha today. The name comes from the Syriac word for summer, and the Church’s year turns from the season of the Apostles, which ends with the feast of Mar Thoma, to the weeks in which the seed sown in the earlier seasons is expected to grow and bear fruit. On this first Sunday the Church honours all the Twelve together, and we remember that, according to tradition, the faith of the Thomas Christians comes from one of them, who is named among the Twelve in every list in the Gospels (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). The Church of the East is proud to call itself “apostolic”, and the Syro-Malabar Church prays in the Holy Qurbana for the one Church built on the foundation of the apostles.
study: Elijah repaired the altar before he prayed. What in my life of prayer or in my family’s faith needs repair?
Paul asks for unity “in the same mind and the same purpose”. What divides my parish, family or community, and what is one thing I could do to heal it?
Jesus asks us to invite those who cannot repay. Whom could I invite to my table, or to my prayer, this month?
Luke says the apostles were sent back to the temple to tell “the whole message”. Which part of the Gospel message do I most prefer to leave out when I speak of it?

lead: Both readings ask whether our worship and our words are matched by our lives. At Corinth the Christians gather for the Lord’s supper, but the rich eat their own meal while the poor go hungry, and Paul tells them that this is not really the Lord’s supper at all. In Matthew, Jesus tells of two sons: one says no and goes, the other says yes and does not. What counts is the will of the Father done, and the Gospel shows who is willing to turn back and do it.

r.h: Is it really the Lord’s supper?
set: At Corinth the Christians met in the houses of the better-off members, and the community meal and the Eucharist were held together. Paul has already spoken of divisions over teachers (1:10–17); now he speaks of a division at the table itself. The wealthier arrived early and ate and drank their own food; the poor, who were often slaves or labourers and could come only after their work, found little left.
Paul’s severity here prepares the way for the account of the institution of the Eucharist (11:23–26), which he hands on exactly because the Corinthians have forgotten what the supper means.
str: v. 17: Paul cannot commend them: their meetings do more harm than good.
vv. 18–19: divisions among them, and the remark that there have to be factions so that the genuine may be shown.
vv. 20–22: what they do is not the Lord’s supper: some go hungry, some are drunk, and the church of God is shamed.
kw: The phrase means a meal that belongs to the Lord (kyrios). It is the earliest name in Paul for the Eucharist as a meal held in the Lord’s name. The word deipnon was the main evening meal.
The word later gave us “heresy”, but here it means a party that divides a community. Paul’s remark is dry: the divisions will show who stands the test, not that divisions are good.
Literally “to think down on”. Paul’s charge is that to shame those who have nothing is to despise the church of God itself.
vv: When you come together, it is not really to eat the Lord’s supper.
They think they are celebrating the Lord’s supper, but what they do does not match its meaning. A meal in his name cannot be a meal at which some are left out.
For when the time comes to eat, each of you goes ahead with your own supper, and one goes hungry and another becomes drunk.
Paul describes the scene without softening it. The table that should show one body shows instead the divisions of rich and poor.
Do you not have homes to eat and drink in? Or do you show contempt for the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?
Paul does not forbid meals at home. He says that when the church gathers, it must act as one body, and the poor must not be humiliated. The Church’s care for the poor is part of its worship.
ch: The Church draws from this passage the link between the Eucharist and love of the poor. The Catechism teaches that to receive in truth the Body and Blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognise Christ in the poorest, his brethren (CCC 1397, in substance). St John Chrysostom in his homilies on this letter insists that we cannot honour Christ at the altar and despise him in the poor (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians 27). The Holy Qurbana, which is the Lord’s supper in our own tradition, is always also the call to share what we have.

r.h: Do the will of the Father
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem, driven the traders out of the temple, and returned to teach there. The chief priests and the elders come to him and ask by what authority he acts (21:23). He answers with a question about John the Baptist, and they will not answer (21:24–27). Then comes this short parable, told to them, followed by two more that press the same point (21:33–46; 22:1–14).

A note on the text: the manuscripts of Matthew differ here in the order of the sons. In the form followed by the NRSV, the first son says no and then goes, and the people answer that he is the one who did the will of his father. The Malayalam Bible follows another old form, in which the son who first says yes is the one who does not go, and the answer is “the second”. The meaning is the same in both: the one who finally does the Father’s will, whatever he said first.
str: vv. 28–30: a father sends two sons to the vineyard: one says no and goes, the other says yes and does not.
v. 31a: Jesus asks: which did the will of his father? They answer correctly.
vv. 31b–32: tax collectors and prostitutes go into the kingdom ahead of you, for they believed John, and you did not even when you saw.
kw: A word that literally means “was concerned afterwards” and so “regretted”, “turned round”. It is used of the son (verse 29), and of the leaders who did not do it (verse 32). It is milder than the great word for conversion (metanoia), but belongs to the same movement.
The word is used of the Father’s will throughout Matthew: in the Our Father (6:10), and for those who enter the kingdom (7:21). The parable is about doing and not only saying.
John came on the path of God’s righteousness; to believe him meant to turn to God and live justly. The tax collectors and sinners did this.
vv: He answered, ‘I will not’; but later he changed his mind and went.
The son’s refusal is not excused; it is rude. But what he does later counts. The door to repentance stays open, even after a hard word.
Which of the two did the will of his father?
Jesus asks a question that the leaders can only answer one way. The parable works because it leads them to speak the truth against themselves.
the tax collectors and the prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God ahead of you

The phrase is a shock to those who thought themselves secure. Jesus does not say that the others are excluded, but that the despised are ahead, because they believed John and repented. The word “ahead” leaves the door open for all to follow.
John came to you in the way of righteousness and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him

This is addressed to the chief priests and elders of the temple. It is not said of the people of Israel as a whole, who, in the same Gospel, flock to John (3:5–6), and the tax collectors and prostitutes were themselves Jews.
ch: The Church hears in the parable the call to turn back at any moment, and the warning that fine words are not the same as obedience. The Catechism teaches that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the kingdom (CCC 545, in substance), and that the call to conversion is a lifelong task for all in the Church, since she is holy and yet always in need of purification (CCC 1427–1428, in substance).

study: Where does my worship at church not match my care for the people around me, especially the poor?
The first son said no and then went. What is a “no” that I have given to God, and what would it take to go now?

lead: Both readings are about gifts given for others and the account that will be asked. In First Corinthians, Paul tells a community gifted with speech and spiritual gifts that they exist to build up the Church, and that when an outsider walks into a gathering which is understood and prophetic, he may bow down and say, “God is really among you”. In Luke, a nobleman leaves his servants a sum of money to trade with while he is away, and the one who was afraid and did nothing is judged by his own fear. On the memorial of St Maria Goretti, a young girl who was faithful in a very small thing and whose forgiveness changed the heart of her killer, the Church asks how we use what the Lord has entrusted to us.

r.h: God is really among you
set: Chapters 12 to 14 of First Corinthians deal with the gifts of the Spirit. Paul has said that gifts are many but the body is one (chapter 12), and that without love they are nothing (chapter 13). In chapter 14 he compares speaking in tongues, a prayer in a language that no one in the assembly understands, with prophecy, which is speaking God’s word in a way that all can understand. His rule is clear: in the assembly, everything must build up (14:26).

Our verses make the point with a surprising picture: the unbeliever who walks into a Christian gathering. What will he find? If it is confusion, he will say that the Christians are out of their minds. If it is the word of God spoken so that it reaches the heart, he will bow down and worship.
str: v. 20: be adults in thinking, but infants in evil.
v. 21: a quotation from the law (Isaiah 28:11–12): God will speak to this people in strange tongues, and still they will not listen.
v. 22: tongues are a sign for unbelievers, prophecy for believers.
vv. 23–25: an outsider entering an assembly of tongues says you are mad; entering an assembly of prophecy, he is convicted, and says “God is really among you”.
kw: A word for the innocence of small children. Paul asks the Corinthians to be like infants in evil, that is, without any experience or taste for it, and adults in thinking.
The gift of speaking in languages not understood by the hearers, which Paul treats as real but of less value in the assembly unless it is interpreted (14:5, 13, 27–28). It is a gift of prayer.
Not only foretelling the future but speaking God’s word to a situation, to “build up, encourage and console” (14:3). In the assembly prophecy has the first place because it can be understood by all.
vv: do not be children in your thinking; rather, be infants in evil, but in thinking be adults.
The Corinthians admired spectacular gifts like children who love a show. Paul asks for a grown-up faith, which tests every gift by whether it serves others.
will they not say that you are out of your mind?
Paul cares how the Church appears to those outside. The liturgy and the life of the community are a witness. Worship that cannot be understood may close a door that could have opened.
that person will bow down before God and worship him, declaring, “God is really among you.”

The final words echo Isaiah 45:14, where the nations say of Israel, “God is with you alone”. The goal of a gathering is that the visitor meets God. When the word is spoken and the community lives in love, the visitor’s own heart is laid open and he recognises the presence of the Lord.
ch: The Church receives the gifts of the Spirit with gratitude and holds that they are all given for the common good. The Catechism teaches that charisms, whether extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Holy Spirit that directly or indirectly benefit the Church and are ordered to her building up (CCC 799–801, in substance), and Vatican II adds that those who lead the Church have the task of discerning them, not of quenching the Spirit (Lumen Gentium 12, in substance). In the liturgy the Church also holds the concern of Paul that worship be intelligible, and that the word be proclaimed so that all may hear.

r.h: Be faithful with what the Lord has entrusted
set: Jesus is near Jerusalem, having just been at the house of Zacchaeus in Jericho (19:1–10). The disciples, and many with them, think that the kingdom of God is about to appear at once. The parable corrects this: the king goes away, and in the meantime the servants have work to do. Jesus is about to enter Jerusalem as king (19:28–40), but his kingship will come through the cross, and the time between his departure and his return is the time of the Church.

The story has a historical echo. When Herod the Great died, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to receive royal power, and a delegation of Jews went after him to oppose it. Jesus’ hearers knew the story, and Luke uses it as a frame. The parable is related to Matthew’s parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30), but the stories differ: Luke has a king, ten servants, and ten small sums, called minas (“pounds”), each about a hundred days’ wages.
str: vv. 11–12: the setting: they supposed the kingdom would appear at once; a nobleman goes to a distant country to receive royal power.
vv. 13–14: ten servants receive ten pounds: “Do business with these until I come back”; the citizens send a delegation: “We do not want this man to rule over us”.
vv. 15–19: the reckoning: the first and the second have gained, and are given charge of cities.
vv. 20–26: the third has hidden his pound out of fear; he is judged by his own words; his pound is given to the one who has ten.
v. 27: the king’s command about his enemies who did not want him to rule.
kw: A Greek sum worth about a hundred days’ wages, so a modest amount. Each servant gets the same, which says that the point is what each does with what has been entrusted.
The command of verse 13, which Jerome rendered in Latin as negotiamini, “do business”. The servants are not told to guard the money but to put it to work.
The word of praise in verse 17. The king rewards faithfulness in a very small thing with much greater responsibility.
vv: Do business with these until I come back.
The time of the king’s absence is the time of work. The Church lives in this time. Waiting for the Lord does not mean standing still.
Because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing, take charge of ten cities.
The reward is not wages but more trust. The servant who was faithful in little is made ready for much. In the Gospel, the greatest rewards are greater responsibilities of love.
I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man

The third servant had a picture of his master as harsh, and fear stopped him from doing anything. The king answers that, even on that picture, he should have done something (verse 23). The parable warns against a fearful faith that does nothing.
to all those who have, more will be given; but from those who have nothing, even what they have will be taken away
This saying is true of every gift of God: what is used grows, and what is buried is lost. It is not a rule of earthly economics but a law of the kingdom.
ch: The Church reads the parable as a call to use the gifts received. The Catechism teaches that God’s plan gives different talents to each, so that those who have particular gifts share the benefit with those in need (CCC 1936–1937, in substance). The parable is not a picture of how Christians should treat their enemies: the harsh last verse belongs to the story’s picture of a king’s court and to the warning of judgment, and Jesus himself, on the cross, prays for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). It is also not a verdict on any people: the “citizens” are those, of any people, who refuse to let Christ be king over their lives.

rite: Maria Goretti was born in 1890 in Corinaldo in Italy, into a poor farming family that later moved to the marshes near Nettuno. After her father’s death she helped her mother with the work of the house and the younger children. On 5 July 1902, when she was eleven, a young neighbour, Alessandro Serenelli, tried to assault her and, when she resisted, stabbed her. She died the next day in hospital, having forgiven him, and she asked that he be with her in heaven. Alessandro, who spent years in prison, repented after a dream in which she appeared to him, and he later asked pardon of her mother. Pope Pius XII canonised Maria in 1950. The Church remembers her as a girl who kept faith and purity in a very small life, and whose forgiveness shows that no one is beyond the reach of God’s mercy.
study: Paul wants worship that helps a stranger say, “God is really among you”. What in my parish’s life, or in my own behaviour at Qurbana, helps or hinders that?
The servant who was afraid did nothing. What gift from God am I burying through fear, and what is one small step to put it to work?

lead: Both readings are about faithful witness and the Lord who keeps those who belong to him. In the First Letter to Timothy, a young minister is told to fight the good fight of faith, holding to the confession he made, as Christ made his own good confession before Pilate. In John, at the winter feast of the Dedication, Jesus is pressed to say plainly whether he is the Messiah, and answers that his works already speak and that his sheep hear his voice. In the first week of Kaitha, the Church turns from the Apostles’ season to the long summer of ordinary discipleship: to hear the Shepherd’s voice, to follow, and to keep the faith to the end.

r.h: Fight the good fight of the faith
set: First Timothy is one of the Pastoral Letters, written to guide a young leader in the care of a church at Ephesus. The Church receives it as Scripture from the apostle Paul’s circle; it is traditionally attributed to Paul, while many scholars think a close disciple wrote it in his name after his death. The teaching is the same in either case.

The passage comes at the end of the letter, after warnings against love of money (6:3–10). “But as for you” turns from those false teachers to Timothy himself, and the letter closes with a solemn charge and a hymn of praise to God.
str: v. 11: flee what is wrong; pursue six virtues.
v. 12: fight the good fight; take hold of eternal life to which you were called.
vv. 13–14: a charge in the presence of God and of Christ, who made the good confession before Pilate: keep the commandment until the Lord appears.
vv. 15–16: praise of God, the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings, dwelling in unapproachable light.
kw: The picture is the athletic contest. Agōn gives our word “agony”; it can mean a race or a struggle. The faith is not only believed but striven for.
Open acknowledgement of faith, here probably made at Timothy’s baptism or ordination. Christ is the model: he also “made the good confession”.
The word the Pastoral Letters use for the coming of Christ, at his first coming and at the end. Timothy keeps the faith with that day in view.
vv: But as for you, man of God, shun all this; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.
“Man of God” was the old title of Moses and the prophets. Timothy is named in their line. Shunning is only half the task; the other half is to pursue what is good.
Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life, to which you were called
Eternal life is both a gift already offered and a prize to be held fast. The Christian runs toward what has already been given.
In the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, I charge you
The name of Pilate is in the Creed because the Passion happened in real history. Christ’s confession before an earthly judge is the pattern for all who must give witness.
