It is he alone who has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see;
The charge ends in worship. The God we serve is beyond all our seeing, and yet he has come near in Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ “bore witness to the truth” before Pilate, and that Christians are not to be ashamed of testifying to the Lord (CCC 2471). The Church has long read Paul’s picture of the good fight as the whole of the Christian life, with Baptism as the beginning of the contest. The hymn in verse 16 is used by the Fathers to teach that God cannot be seen by creatures unaided and is known only as he reveals himself (in substance; compare CCC 1028).

r.h: My sheep hear my voice
set: The festival of the Dedication (Hanukkah) remembered the re-dedication of the altar of the Temple in 164 BC under Judas Maccabeus, after the Temple had been profaned (1 Maccabees 4:52–59). It fell in winter, and John mentions the cold. Jesus walks in the portico of Solomon, a covered colonnade on the east side of the Temple.

This scene follows the Good Shepherd discourse earlier in the chapter (10:1–18). “The Jews” in John’s Gospel here means the leaders gathered round him, not the Jewish people; Jesus and all his first disciples were Jews. Their question is a real one, and he answers it.
str: vv. 22–23: the feast of the Dedication; Jesus in the portico of Solomon.
v. 24: the question: if you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.
vv. 25–26: his works in his Father’s name are his testimony; they do not believe because they are not of his flock.
vv. 27–28: the sheep hear, are known, follow, and receive eternal life; no one will snatch them from his hand.
kw: The festival that gives the passage its place and light. At the feast of the re-consecrated Temple, Jesus appears as the one in whom God truly dwells among his people.
In John, Jesus’ works are signs that reveal who he is and whose Son he is. The question “are you the Messiah?” has been answered by what he does, not only by what he says.
In John, to hear his voice means to listen and obey. The sheep recognise the Shepherd’s voice (10:3–4).
vv: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.”
They ask in the language of their hope. The difficulty is not that Jesus is silent but that his answer is not the kind they wanted: a Messiah who is also the Son of the Father.
Jesus answered, “I have told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name testify to me;
He points to his deeds. The same Jesus who speaks the Father’s words does the Father’s works.
My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
Three things mark the flock: they hear, he knows them, they follow. To be known by Christ comes first; it is his love that makes the following possible.
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand.
A promise of the Shepherd’s strength, not a licence for carelessness. We hold to it by hope and perseverance, listening to his voice each day.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church is the sheepfold whose gate is Christ, and the flock of which God himself is the shepherd (CCC 754). The promise that no one will snatch the sheep from his hand is read by the Church as a ground of hope: Christians hope for the grace of final perseverance, and ask it in prayer (CCC 2016). The Fathers read the works of Christ in this passage as testimony of his divinity: the Son who does the works of the Father is one with the Father, as the next verses say (10:30).

qa: If no one can snatch the sheep from Christ’s hand, can a Christian still be lost?

The promise is a true one: the Shepherd does not let go. The Church also teaches that we keep our own will and can turn from him by grave sin, and so we are called to keep faith and to ask for perseverance (CCC 2016). Hope in Christ’s hand and care for our own walk belong together, as in Timothy’s charge to fight the good fight.
study: Timothy is told to pursue six qualities: righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness. Which one do I most need this week, and what is one step I can take toward it?
Jesus says his sheep hear his voice. In what quiet place or moment of the day do I give him room to speak?

lead: Both readings ask what it means to speak and to be heard. In First Corinthians Paul will not let the gift of tongues stand alone in the assembly: prayer must engage the mind, and the whole community must be able to say its “Amen”. In John, the debate in the Temple over who Jesus is reaches its height: he speaks of Abraham’s joy at his day, and answers the question “Who do you claim to be?” with the divine name: “before Abraham was, I am.” One reading protects the people’s understanding of the prayer of the Church; the other shows who is addressed in that prayer.

r.h: I will pray with the spirit and with the mind also
set: Chapters 12–14 of First Corinthians treat the gifts of the Spirit in the Corinthian assembly. Paul has placed love above all gifts (chapter 13). In chapter 14 he compares prophecy, which is speaking that others understand, with “tongues”, ecstatic prayer in a language no one in the church could follow unless someone interpreted it.
Paul does not despise tongues; he says he speaks in them more than all the Corinthians (14:18). His question is how the gift serves the community: its purpose is “building up” (14:12, 26).
str: v. 13: whoever speaks in a tongue should pray to be able to interpret.
vv. 14–15: prayer in a tongue leaves the mind unproductive; Paul will pray and sing with the spirit and with the mind.
vv. 16–17: if the blessing is not understood, the outsider cannot say “Amen”.
vv. 18–19: Paul’s own gift, and his rule: five words with the mind in church rather than ten thousand in a tongue.
kw: Here it means a prayer-language, a charism given by the Spirit, not a known foreign language. Paul asks that it be interpreted in the assembly.
The reasoning, understanding part of a person. Paul insists that Christian prayer engages the mind as well as the heart and the Spirit.
A Hebrew word meaning “so be it, truly”, by which the community makes a prayer its own. To say it, one must understand what has been prayed.
vv: Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray for the power to interpret.
Even a spiritual gift is meant to reach others. Interpretation turns private ecstasy into common prayer.
I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind also;
Paul does not choose between heart and mind. The Spirit works through both.
how can anyone in the position of an outsider say the “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since the outsider does not know what you are saying?
The “Amen” belongs to the whole people. It is the assembly’s answer, spoken in understanding. This shows how early the Church’s worship was shared: the leader gives thanks, and the people answer.
nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind, in order to instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
Five against ten thousand is a deliberate exaggeration. The measure of the assembly’s prayer is whether others are built up.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the faithful should take part in the liturgy fully, consciously and actively, and that the rites should be within their grasp (Sacrosanctum Concilium 14, 21). The Catechism speaks of the “Amen” by which the people make the prayer their own, in the Creed and in the liturgy (CCC 1061–1065). Paul’s principle, that what is done in church must serve the building up of all, is behind the Church’s care that the prayers of the liturgy be heard and understood by the people.

r.h: Before Abraham was, I am
set: The dispute in John 8 takes place in the Temple during the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 37). Jesus has said “I am the light of the world” (8:12) and has spoken of his Father, of freedom, and of Abraham. The conversation grows sharper; the opponents are the leaders and listeners who will not accept his claim. John’s phrase “the Jews” here means these particular opponents; Jesus himself, Mary, and all the first disciples were Jews, and nothing in the passage can be used against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4).
To call Jesus “a Samaritan” was an insult. Samaritans were despised by many Jews of that time, and the word means something like a heretic or outsider.
str: vv. 48–50: the insult “Samaritan and demon”; Jesus answers that he honours the Father, and the Father seeks his glory.
v. 51: the promise: whoever keeps his word will never see death.
vv. 52–53: the objection: Abraham and the prophets died; who do you claim to be?
vv. 54–56: the Father glorifies him; Abraham rejoiced to see his day.
vv. 57–59: “Before Abraham was, I am”; they take up stones; Jesus hides and leaves the Temple.
kw: To keep is to guard and to obey, in the heart and in life. In John, keeping Jesus’ word is the sign of love (14:23).

Not “I was” and not simply “I exist”. The phrase echoes God’s name given to Moses (Exodus 3:14) and God’s own words in Isaiah (43:10, 13), and in John it is used again and again by Jesus. Here the sense is of timeless being, in contrast to Abraham, who “came to be”.
The penalty for blasphemy was stoning (Leviticus 24:16). The listeners understood that Jesus was claiming to be equal to God.
vv: Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon; but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.
Jesus does not return insult. He points to the one thing his whole life is about: the honour of his Father.
Very truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.
The word of Jesus gives life that bodily death cannot end. The listeners understand “death” only as the death of the body; Jesus speaks of life with God.
Your ancestor Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.
Abraham is not a rival to Jesus but a witness to him. The promise made to him is fulfilled in Christ, and his faith looked ahead to it.
Jesus said to them, “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.”
The verb changes: Abraham “was” (came to be); Jesus simply is. Jesus claims a being that has no beginning.
So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
The Light leaves the Temple; the same will be said at 12:36. The revelation is real, and so is the refusal of some who heard it.
ch: The Catechism lists this saying among the places where Jesus claims divine identity: “Before Abraham was, I am” (CCC 590). It teaches that the name “I AM” revealed to Moses was taken up by Jesus, so that in the New Testament the title “Lord” is given to him (CCC 446; see CCC 211). The Church has always read Jesus’ words about Abraham’s joy as showing that the promises to Abraham are fulfilled in Christ, and that Abraham is the father in faith of all believers (CCC 145–146). With respect for the Jewish people, the Church teaches that what was done in the Passion cannot be blamed on all Jews then or now (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

qa: Why does the Church say Jesus is claiming to be God when he says “I am”?

Because of the way the words are used. In Greek the plain way to say “I am” would not need the word egō; Jesus uses it deliberately, and the Greek of Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10 has the same “I am”. His opponents react as to blasphemy and pick up stones (Leviticus 24:16). John also uses the saying elsewhere, for example “unless you believe that I am he” (8:24). The Church reads it with the whole Gospel, which from its first verse says that the Word was God (John 1:1).
study: Paul would rather speak five words that others understand than ten thousand that they cannot follow. How well do I understand, and join in, the prayers of the Holy Qurbana?
Jesus does not answer insult with insult but speaks of the honour of his Father. When I am wronged, whose honour do I seek?

lead: The four readings of this Friday, the day of martyrs and saints in Kaitha, are one message to a small and threatened people: do not fear. In Isaiah, God speaks to Jacob, a worm of a people, and promises to hold his right hand. In Acts, at Ephesus, God works wonders through Paul, and the name of Jesus proves to be no charm but the power of a living Lord. In the Second Letter to the Corinthians, Paul says that the weapons of the apostles are not human, and that their authority is given to build up. In Luke, Jesus tells his friends not to fear those who kill the body, because the Father counts even the sparrows and the Spirit will teach them what to say. (The calendar also gives the longer forms, Acts 19:8–20, 2 Corinthians 10:3–18 and Luke 12:1–12; the notes below follow the verses printed for the day.) The day keeps the memory of Mar Yakob, James of Nisibis, a bishop on the border of two empires, and the readings are well chosen for his Church.

r.h: Do not fear, for I am with you
set: Isaiah chapters 40–55 are addressed to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC, a people who felt forgotten and small. Many scholars call this part of the book Second Isaiah. It opens with comfort (40:1) and speaks of a coming return.
Chapter 41 sets the Lord’s people against the power of the nations. In this passage God answers Israel’s fear with a series of promises, each beginning with the call “do not fear”.
str: vv. 8–9: Israel is the chosen servant, descendant of Abraham, taken from the ends of the earth.
v. 10: “Do not fear, for I am with you”: three promises, to strengthen, help and uphold.
vv. 11–12: those who fight against Israel will come to nothing.
vv. 13–14: God holds Israel’s right hand; the Holy One of Israel is the Redeemer.
vv. 15–16: Israel will be a threshing sledge, and will rejoice in the Lord.
kw: The call of reassurance God speaks to Abraham (Genesis 15:1), Isaac, Jacob and Moses. It is not a command to feel no fear, but a promise: you are not alone.
In Israel the gō’ēl was the close relative who rescued a family member from slavery or debt (Leviticus 25:47–49). God takes that role for his people.
Israel is God’s servant: not a slave of fear but a chosen one given a task. In this part of Isaiah the word carries honour as well as duty.
vv: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham, my friend;
Abraham is called God’s friend. The people’s hope rests on the friendship of God with their ancestor, and that friendship is not forgotten.
do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand.
The reason not to fear is never our own strength, but the nearness of God: he is with us, and he is our God.
Do not fear, you worm Jacob, you insect Israel! I will help you, says the Lord; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.
God does not flatter. He names the weakness honestly and then holds it. The word “worm” is a name for helplessness, and the answer is the Holy One.
ch: The Church hears in Isaiah’s promise the care of God for his small ones, and prays it in its own time of trial. The Catechism teaches that Israel’s election is a choice made by God’s love, and that the covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked (CCC 218, 839).

r.h: The name of the Lord Jesus was praised
set: Paul stays in Ephesus for more than two years (19:8–10; he later speaks of three years, 20:31), teaching daily. Ephesus was a great port, home to the temple of Artemis, and well known for charms and magical writings. Luke tells how the Gospel meets this world.

Verses 13–14 tell of travelling Jewish exorcists, among them seven sons of a man called Sceva. Luke calls him a Jewish high priest; no high priest of that name is known from other sources, so he may have belonged to a priestly family or used the title himself. What matters is that these men used the name of Jesus as a formula, without belonging to him.
str: vv. 11–12: extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul; cloths touched by him heal the sick.
vv. 13–16: the sons of Sceva try the name of Jesus as a charm and are overpowered.
vv. 17–19: awe in Ephesus; believers confess their practices and burn their magic books.
v. 20: the word of the Lord grows and prevails.
kw: Literally “powers not of the ordinary kind”. Luke wants his readers to see that the power is God’s, working through Paul, not Paul’s own.
Those who believed “confessed”: they said openly what they had done. Conversion is not only a feeling; it includes turning away from the old life, in the open.
The same word is used of a victory. The word of the Lord is not merely spread; it wins ground against the powers that held Ephesus.
vv: God did extraordinary miracles through Paul,
Luke is careful: God does the miracles. Paul is the instrument.
But the evil spirit said to them in reply, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?”
The name of Jesus is not a magic word for anyone to use. It is the name of a person, and only those who belong to him can call on it in faith.
A number of those who practiced magic collected their books and burned them publicly; when the value of these books was calculated, it was found to come to fifty thousand silver coins.
The sum is very large, more than a labourer could earn in a lifetime. The new believers give up what was valuable to them, without being asked, and in the open.
So the word of the Lord grew mightily and prevailed.
Luke ends the scene as he ends several in Acts, with a note of growth. The word is stronger than the old powers.
ch: The Catechism teaches that all forms of divination, magic and sorcery are to be rejected, because they contradict the honour, respect and loving fear owed to God alone (CCC 2116–2117). The Church’s prayer of exorcism and the sacrament of Baptism are not charms: they work by the power of Christ and in faith (CCC 1237, 1673). Acts shows the answer in a city of magic: the open confession of Christ, and the setting aside of every false trust.

r.h: Weapons that are not of this world
set: In chapters 10–13 Paul answers critics at Corinth who say that he is bold only in his letters and weak when present. Many scholars think these chapters come from a separate letter, written before or after chapters 1–9; the Church reads the whole letter as Scripture.

Paul uses the language of war, but he turns it: the battle is not against people but against ideas and pride that stand against God. The aim is obedience to Christ and the building up of the community.
str: vv. 3–4: we live as human beings, but our weapons are not human; they are powerful to destroy strongholds.
vv. 5–6: arguments and pride are destroyed; every thought is taken captive for Christ.
vv. 7–8: “you belong to Christ, and so do we”; authority is given to build up, not tear down.
vv. 9–11: the critics’ charge that Paul’s letters are strong and his presence weak; he is the same present or absent.
kw: The tools of a soldier. For Paul they are truth, righteousness, faith, prayer and the word (see Ephesians 6:11–18).
The aim of all authority in the Church. Paul uses the word also of the Church as a house and of prayer in the assembly (1 Corinthians 14).
The picture is of a prisoner of war brought home. Every thought is brought under the rule of Christ, not to destroy the mind but to set it in order.
vv: for the weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power to destroy strongholds.
The only strength the apostle trusts is God’s. A stronghold here is a way of thinking that shuts out God.
and we take every thought captive to obey Christ.
Faith is meant to shape the whole mind. Christ is Lord of our thinking, not only of our feelings.
Now, even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be ashamed of it.
The test of every authority in the Church, from the bishop to the parent, is whether it builds up.
ch: The Church applies Paul’s words to its ministers: authority in the Church is a service for the sake of building up, and a bishop is to teach, sanctify and govern in the name of Christ and not in his own name (CCC 894–896; Lumen Gentium 27). The Catechism also teaches that faith and reason do not conflict, since the same God gives both, so that taking every thought captive for Christ does not mean silencing the mind (CCC 159).

r.h: Do not fear: you are of more value than many sparrows
set: Jesus is teaching a great crowd (12:1) and begins with a warning to his disciples against hypocrisy. In today’s verses he speaks to his “friends”, a word that is rare and warm in Luke’s Gospel. The reading is about fear, and about the confidence of those who confess him.

The “synagogues, rulers and authorities” of verse 11 mean the places where the first disciples would be tried. The disciples themselves, like Jesus, were Jews, and these words are about the cost of witness, never about blaming a people (Nostra Aetate 4).
str: vv. 4–5: do not fear those who can only kill the body; fear God, who has authority over life beyond death.
vv. 6–7: five sparrows, the hairs of the head: nothing is forgotten by the Father.
vv. 8–9: acknowledge the Son of Man before others, and he will acknowledge you before God’s angels.
v. 10: words against the Son of Man may be forgiven; blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not.
vv. 11–12: do not worry before the authorities; the Holy Spirit will teach you what to say.
kw: Jesus calls his disciples friends (see John 15:15). The one who tells them to be fearless speaks as a friend who is with them.
Two fears are set side by side: the fear of persecutors, which is to be set aside, and the “fear” of God, which is reverent awe and the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10).
To speak publicly for someone as your own. The disciple’s confession of Jesus is answered by his confession of the disciple before God.
vv: I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.
Fear is put in its place. Even the worst that human power can do does not reach the life a person has with God.
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten in God’s sight.
Sparrows were the cheapest food in the market. If not one of them is forgotten, the disciple is certainly not forgotten.
And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before others, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God;
Confession and acknowledgement go together. We speak for Christ, and he speaks for us.
for the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you ought to say.
A promise for the hour of trial, not a reason to neglect learning. The Spirit gives words to those who have first given their lives.
ch: The Catechism says that martyrdom is the supreme witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473), and that the “fear of the Lord” is one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831). On the sparrows, it teaches that Jesus asks for childlike trust in the providence of our heavenly Father, who cares for the smallest needs of his children (CCC 305). The sin against the Holy Spirit, of which verse 10 speaks, is taught by the Church as a deliberate refusal to accept the mercy God offers, remaining in the refusal to the end (CCC 1864). Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed (Apology 50, in substance).

qa: What is the sin against the Holy Spirit that “will not be forgiven”?

The Church teaches that no sin, however grave, is beyond the mercy of God. The sin against the Holy Spirit is the deliberate and final refusal to accept that mercy, and so refusing repentance and forgiveness to the end (CCC 1864). It is not an act of weakness or a moment of anger. Anyone who is worried that they have committed this sin shows by that worry that the door is still open.
Is it wrong to wear a blessed medal or carry a cross, since Acts condemns charms?

The Church distinguishes. Sacramentals such as a cross, a medal or blessed water are signs that prepare us to receive grace and lead us to prayer; they work through the Church’s prayer and our faith, never as a spell (CCC 1667–1670). A charm or amulet trusted to protect on its own is superstition (CCC 2111). The question is always: in whom do I trust?
rite: On the first Friday of Kaitha the Syro-Malabar Church remembers Mar Yakob (Yakob is James, and also the Syriac form of Jacob) of Nisibis, a bishop who died about 338. According to the Syriac tradition he was the first bishop of the city, the teacher of the young Ephrem, and a man of prayer, and he is said to have taken part in the Council of Nicaea. Nisibis stood on the frontier of the Roman and Persian empires, and Ephrem’s later hymns recall the sufferings and the prayer of that city (in substance).

Our Holy Qurbana of Addai and Mari comes from the Church of the East, which grew in this Syriac world. Fridays in Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of that Church. We keep Mar Yakob’s feast with Isaiah’s word to his own namesake: do not fear, I am with you.
study: God says to a “worm Jacob”: do not fear, I will help you. Where do I feel small and afraid, and can I say these words to God in prayer today?
The sons of Sceva used the name of Jesus without belonging to him. What do I trust, besides Christ, when I am afraid, and what could I set aside?
Paul says that authority is given for building up. Where do I have some authority, in a family, a school or a parish, and how can I use it to build up?
Jesus says that not one sparrow is forgotten. How can I remember today those who are persecuted for their faith, and pray for them and for those who wronged them?

lead: Both readings are about the house where God lives and who may come in. In Second Corinthians Paul tells the Christians of Corinth that they are the temple of the living God, and so they must not share in the worship of idols. In Mark, a house in Capernaum is so crowded that four friends tear open the roof to bring a paralysed man to Jesus, and the Lord forgives his sins before he heals his body. The first reading says where God dwells, among his people; the second shows that the Lord who dwells among us is the one who has authority to forgive.

r.h: We are the temple of the living God
set: Corinth was a busy port full of temples, and Christians there were pressed to join in public meals at pagan shrines and feasts (see 1 Corinthians 8 and 10). In this passage Paul asks the community to keep the worship of the one God undivided.

Many scholars notice that this short passage (6:14–7:1) interrupts the flow between 6:13 and 7:2, and that its language has similarities with the writings found at Qumran. Some think Paul took up an earlier text; others think it is his own. The Church receives it as Scripture in either case. Paul is not asking Christians to avoid their neighbours. In another letter he says that to do so they would need to leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10); the demand here is not to share in idol worship.
str: v. 14: do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers: four contrasts, righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness.
v. 15: Christ and Beliar; believer and unbeliever.
v. 16: the temple of God and idols; “we are the temple of the living God”, with a promise from the Old Testament.
vv. 17–18: come out and be separate; God will be a Father to his sons and daughters.
kw: From the yoke of animals of different kinds. The law of Moses did not allow an ox and a donkey to be yoked together (Deuteronomy 22:10). The picture is of a team pulling in two directions.
A form of Belial, a Jewish name for the evil one, used here for the power opposed to Christ.
The inner sanctuary where God dwells. The whole community, not only the building, is God’s dwelling place.
vv: Do not be mismatched with unbelievers. For what partnership is there between righteousness and lawlessness?
Paul’s point is about shared worship and loyalty, not about daily life with neighbours. Christians do not stop being good neighbours; they cannot share in worship that denies the one God.
For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will live in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Paul joins words of Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27. The promise God made to Israel, to dwell among his people, now reaches its fullness: God dwells in the community of believers by his Spirit.
and I will be your father, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”
The last words echo God’s promise to David’s son (2 Samuel 7:14), now extended to “sons and daughters”. Separation is not an end; it is made for the sake of belonging to the Father.
ch: The Catechism teaches that by Baptism the Christian becomes a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265). It warns that idolatry is not only the worship of pagan gods but a constant temptation to the faith, whenever a person puts something in the place of God, such as money, power or pleasure (CCC 2113–2114). The Church also teaches respect for all that is true and holy in other religions and urges Christians to dialogue and cooperation with their followers (Nostra Aetate 2). Both belong together: undivided worship of the one God, and respect and friendship with all.

r.h: Son, your sins are forgiven
set: Jesus has left the synagogue of Capernaum and healed Peter’s mother-in-law and many others (1:21–34), and then healed a leper (1:40–45). He now returns to Capernaum, most probably to the house of Peter (1:29). Houses in Galilee had flat roofs of beams, branches and packed earth, reached by an outside stair, which makes the friends’ action possible.

This is the first of five conflict stories in Mark (2:1–3:6) in which Jesus meets objection from some scribes. The scribes were experts in the Law, and their question is a fair one: only God can forgive sins. Mark invites the reader to see that Jesus is more than they think.
str: vv. 1–2: Jesus at home in Capernaum, speaking the word to a crowd that fills the house and the doorway.
vv. 3–4: four men carry a paralysed man; they open the roof and let him down.
v. 5: Jesus sees their faith and says, “Son, your sins are forgiven.”
vv. 6–9: the scribes question in their hearts; Jesus asks which is easier to say.
vv. 10–12: “the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”; the man rises, takes his mat and goes; all glorify God.
kw: Not only power but the right to act. In Mark the crowds notice Jesus’ authority in teaching, over spirits, over disease, and here over sin (1:22, 27).
The passive form is often used to avoid naming God: God forgives. Jesus speaks and acts in God’s name, and yet in his own person.
The title Jesus uses of himself, from the vision in Daniel 7:13–14 of one like a son of man who receives dominion from God. Here it is used on earth, in a house, over a mat.
vv: And when they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him; and after having dug through it, they let down the mat on which the paralytic lay.
The friends do not give up when the door is closed. Their love is stubborn and costly. Jesus does not scold them for the damage; he praises their faith.
When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.”
Jesus sees the faith of those who carry and forgives first, as if the deepest need were not the legs but the heart. The word “Son” is tender: he is received as a child of God.
“Why does this fellow speak in this way? It is blasphemy! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
The scribes are right in what they say about God. Only God can forgive sins. They do not yet see that God is at work in Jesus.
“I say to you, stand up, take your mat and go to your home.”
The visible healing is a sign of the invisible forgiveness. The man who was carried now carries his own mat.
so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”
The story ends with praise of God. A healing that makes people glorify God is a healing in the way of Jesus.
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins, and that Jesus, as Son of God, says of himself, “The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”, and gives this power to men to exercise in his name (CCC 1441–1442). The Church sees in this story the sacrament of Penance and Reconciliation, in which Christ forgives through his ministers, and also the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, where forgiveness and healing are joined (CCC 1503–1505). The four friends have been read by many as a picture of the Church’s intercession: we are carried by the faith of others, and we carry others (in substance, a common reading of the Fathers).

qa: Why did Jesus forgive sins first, when the man had come to be healed?

In the way Jesus sees, the sickness of the body is not the first need. Forgiveness opens the person to God. At the same time, Jesus does not leave the body untouched: the healing is the sign that the forgiveness is real. The Church keeps this order in the sacraments: grace comes through visible signs for the whole person.
study: Paul asks Christians to keep their worship undivided. What in my life could take the place that belongs to God alone, and how can I keep the door open to my neighbours with kindness?
Four friends carried the paralysed man and broke through a roof. For whom could I do something costly in faith, by prayer, by visiting, by helping?

lead: The four readings of this Sunday tell of a God who first loves, then speaks, and who gives shelter and a place at the table. In Deuteronomy, Moses asks whether any people has ever been loved and chosen like Israel, and gives the reason in one sentence: “because he loved your ancestors”. In Isaiah, after judgment and cleansing, a cloud by day and a flaming fire by night become a canopy and a shelter over Zion. In Second Corinthians, Paul says that the ministry of the Spirit, the new covenant, brings a glory greater than the glory on Moses’ face, and he speaks boldly because of that hope. And in Luke, the parable of the prodigal son shows the Father running down the road to meet a child who has been lost. (The calendar gives the longer forms, Isaiah 3:16–4:6, 2 Corinthians 3:4–18 and Luke 15:4–32; the notes below follow the verses printed for the day.) In Kaitha, when the Church looks at the fruit of the apostles’ sowing, the Sunday asks what fruit the Father most wants: that his children come home.

r.h: Because he loved your ancestors
set: Deuteronomy is Moses’ great farewell address to Israel on the plains of Moab, before the people cross the Jordan. In the first discourse (1:6–4:40) Moses recalls what God has done and warns Israel not to forget it. At Horeb the people heard God’s voice out of the fire but saw no form (4:12, 15). That is why they must not make an image of God.

Verses 32–40 are the climax of this first discourse, and they lead straight into the Ten Commandments (chapter 5) and the Shema (6:4–5). The people are asked to look back across all history and to look at the whole earth, and to ask whether anything like this has ever happened.
str: vv. 32–34: two questions about the voice from the fire and the rescue from Egypt: nothing like it has ever been heard.
vv. 35–36: the purpose: that Israel may know that the Lord is God, and there is no other.
vv. 37–38: the reason: God loved the ancestors and chose their descendants, bringing them out by his presence.
vv. 39–40: the response: know today and take it to heart; keep the commandments, for your good.
kw: The key word of verse 37. Israel’s election is rooted in love, not merit; Moses says the same in 7:7–8 and 9:4–6, where Israel is told that it is not chosen for its own righteousness.
God’s choosing is not a choice against others but a choice for the sake of all. Israel is chosen to be a people through whom the knowledge of God reaches the world.
take it to heart (literally, return it to your heart)
In Hebrew thinking the heart is the place of memory and decision. To “take to heart” is to let a truth shape one’s life.
vv: For ask now about former ages, long before your own, ever since the day that God created human beings on the earth;
Moses invites the people to test his claim against all of history. He is not afraid of the question, because the love of God is a fact of experience.
To you it was shown so that you would acknowledge that the Lord is God; there is no other besides him.
God’s great deeds are not for display but for knowledge. In the Bible, to know God is to trust and to love him.
And because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants after them.
The heart of the reading. The covenant begins not with Israel’s goodness but with God’s love, as a father’s love begins before a child can do anything.
So acknowledge today and take to heart that the Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.
“Today” is an important word in Deuteronomy. Every generation stands at Horeb afresh and is asked to say yes.
Keep his statutes and his commandments, which I am commanding you today for your own well-being and that of your descendants after you,
The commandments are given for good, not as a burden. They follow love as the rules of the house follow the father’s embrace.
ch: The Church reads Deuteronomy’s words about the one God as the root of her own faith, and the Catechism begins its teaching on God with the Shema and the confession that the Lord is one (CCC 200–202). It teaches that God chose Israel out of love and that his covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked (CCC 218, 839; Romans 11:29). The Catechism says that the Ten Commandments are given as a gift of the God who first saved and then gave the law (CCC 2060–2061): the order of Moses’ words, love first and commandments after, is the order of the whole Gospel.

r.h: A canopy over all the glory
set: The verses end a long section of warning in Isaiah 2–4. The prophet has spoken of the pride of Jerusalem and its wealthy women (3:16–4:1), and of a coming judgment that will leave only a remnant. Then comes a sudden turn: “On that day” the Lord will make something new and beautiful grow.

Verses 5–6 recall the Exodus. In the wilderness the Lord led the people by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21–22) and filled the tent of meeting with his glory (Exodus 40:34–38). Isaiah promises the same presence, now over the whole of Mount Zion.
str: v. 2: the branch of the Lord, and the fruit of the land, beautiful and glorious for the survivors.
v. 3: those who remain are called holy, written down for life.
v. 4: the Lord washes away the filth and the bloodstains by a spirit of judgment and burning.
vv. 5–6: cloud by day, fire by night, and a canopy that is shade, refuge and shelter.
kw: A plant springing up. Later prophets use the word for the promised king from David’s line (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8). Here it may mean the fruitfulness of the land; the Church has also heard in it a word about the Messiah.
A register of the living, like the “book” of Exodus 32:32 and Daniel 12:1. Those who remain are held in God’s memory, each by name.
The word used elsewhere for a bridal canopy (Joel 2:16; Psalm 19:5). God’s glory over Zion is like the canopy of a wedding: shelter, joy and belonging.
vv: On that day the branch of the Lord shall be beautiful and glorious,
After judgment, growth. God does not end his story with ruin.
Whoever is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem,
Holiness here is a gift from God, given by being cleansed and counted. It is not first of all an achievement.

Then the Lord will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over its places of assembly a cloud by day and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night. Indeed over all the glory there will be a canopy.
The old presence returns, and “creates”: a verb used elsewhere of God’s creating. The assembly itself, the people gathered to worship, is covered by God’s glory.
It will serve as a pavilion, a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.
A beautiful end: the glory of God is not terrifying here but sheltering. It protects from sun by day and from storm by night.
ch: In the Christian tradition the cloud and fire are signs of the Holy Spirit: the Catechism speaks of the cloud and light as symbols by which God reveals himself and veils himself (CCC 697), and of fire as the symbol of the transforming energy of the Spirit (CCC 696). The Church sees the promise of shelter fulfilled in the Church, where God’s presence rests over those who gather in his name. At Pentecost the Spirit came as fire on those who were gathered (Acts 2:3).

r.h: Ministers of a new covenant
set: Paul is defending his ministry against those who say he needs letters of recommendation or a stronger claim. His answer is the Corinthians themselves, “a letter of Christ” written “not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (3:2–3).

In 3:7–18 he compares his ministry with that of Moses, whose face shone when he came down from Sinai (Exodus 34:29–35) so that he covered it with a veil. Paul does not criticise Moses or the Law; he says that the covenant of Sinai was truly glorious. His point is that the new covenant is more glorious still, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel had promised (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:26–27). The Church has always read this as a fulfilment, not a rejection, of what God gave to Israel.
str: vv. 4–6: our competence is from God, who made us ministers of a new covenant, of Spirit, not letter.
vv. 7–9: if the ministry of the stone tablets came with glory, the ministry of the Spirit and of justification has much more.
vv. 10–11: the earlier glory is surpassed by the greater, as the temporary by the lasting.
v. 12: because of such hope, great boldness.
kw: “Letter” is the written code taken by itself, without the Spirit’s power to keep it. It is not the Law that is bad (Romans 7:12) but the situation of a law that tells what is right and cannot give strength to do it.
The weight and radiance of God’s presence. Paul reasons from the lesser to the greater: if the earlier covenant had glory, the new has far more.
Plain speech and confidence before others and before God. Paul speaks plainly because the hope he proclaims has no veil.
vv: Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God,
The apostle’s confidence is not in himself. Whatever a minister of the Church does well is the work of God.
who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
Paul is not setting the Old Testament against the New. He says that the law without grace shows sin and cannot heal it, and that the Spirit is the gift that makes obedience possible.
For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, much more does the ministry of justification abound in glory!
Paul grants that the earlier ministry was glorious. The new does not deny that glory; it is its fulfilment.
Since, then, we have such a hope, we act with great boldness,
Christian boldness is the child of hope. We can speak plainly and live openly because God’s work is not hidden or passing.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Old Law is a preparation for the Gospel, and that the New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given through faith in Christ and written on the heart (CCC 1964–1966). St Augustine, in his work The Spirit and the Letter, reads Paul’s words to mean that the law, without the help of grace, shows what we should do but cannot give the strength to do it; the Spirit pours love into the heart and so fulfils the law (in substance). The Church also holds, with Paul, that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 121, 839).

r.h: His father saw him and ran
set: Luke 15 opens with a complaint: the Pharisees and the scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them (15:1–2). Jesus answers with three parables: the lost sheep, the lost coin and the two sons. In each, something is lost, then found, and there is joy. The calendar gives the longer form, from 15:4, so that the three belong together.

In the Jewish world of Jesus’ day, asking for one’s inheritance while the father was alive was a grave breach of the family. To keep pigs, animals unclean for Jews, and to long to eat their food showed the lowest point of a Jewish son’s fall. Everything in the parable is meant to make the father’s welcome as surprising as possible.
str: vv. 11–16: the younger son asks for his share, leaves, spends everything and feeds pigs.
vv. 17–19: he comes to himself and decides to return as a hired hand.
vv. 20–24: the father sees him far off, runs, embraces him, orders robe, ring, sandals and a feast.
vv. 25–30: the elder son comes in from the field, hears the music, is angry and refuses to go in.
vv. 31–32: the father’s plea: “you are always with me”; “we had to celebrate”.
kw: Literally “having come into himself”. Repentance begins when a person wakes from the dream of independence and sees the truth about himself.
The verb comes from splanchna, the inner organs, the gut. It is the deepest word of mercy in the Gospels, used of Jesus himself (Luke 7:13).
The same verb used of rising from the dead. The father says that his son was “dead” and “has come to life”, which is more than a return home.
vv: The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me.’ So he divided his property between them.
The father lets the child go. Love does not hold a person by force. The same freedom is what allows return.
But when he came to himself he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired hands have bread enough and to spare, but here I am dying of hunger!
His first motive is hunger, not perfect love. God works with the repentance we have and makes it grow (see CCC 1453).
But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him.
The father has been watching the road. An elder in that culture did not run. He runs, to reach his son before the village can shame him, and he kisses him before the speech is made.
Then he became angry and refused to go in. His father came out and began to plead with him.
The father goes out a second time. He runs to the one who left, and he goes out to the one who stayed. His love is the same for both.
Then the father said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
The elder son has all he wanted, and has not known it. The parable ends without telling us if he comes in. The door is left open for the listener.
ch: The Catechism points to this parable as the great description of conversion and repentance: the son’s misery, his return, and the father’s embrace, a picture of the “gift of reconciliation” in the sacrament of Penance (CCC 1439). St John Paul II, in his encyclical Dives in Misericordia, reflects at length on the parable as a revelation of mercy as love that restores dignity (nn. 5–6). The Church today reads the two sons as pictures of two temptations within every disciple: to leave the Father’s house, and to stay in it without joy. A number of early writers read the elder son as the Jewish people and the younger as the Gentiles; the Church does not lay the elder son’s fault on any people, and Paul says that God’s gifts to Israel are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). The father’s words, “all that is mine is yours”, are spoken to every disciple.

qa: Deuteronomy speaks of driving out nations to give Israel their land. How does the Church read such words?

With care. Moses himself says that Israel did not receive the land for its righteousness (Deuteronomy 9:4–6), and the same book calls for justice to the stranger (10:18–19). The Church teaches that the Old Testament has “imperfect and provisional” elements, and that all of Scripture is read in the light of Christ, who forbids violence and teaches love of enemies (Dei Verbum 15; CCC 122, 129). These verses can never justify force against any people today.
Is “the letter kills” a rejection of the Old Testament or of Jewish law?

No. Paul calls the law “holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12) and says here that it came with glory. “Letter” means the law without the grace to keep it, and the “Spirit” means the new gift of life. The Church holds that the Old Testament remains the Word of God and that God’s covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked (CCC 121, 839).
Why does Jesus leave the end of the parable open?

The parable is addressed to those who grumbled at Jesus for welcoming sinners (15:1–2). The ending asks them, and each of us, what we will do: go in to the feast or stay outside. The father’s plea stands. The Gospel does not say what happened because it is asking the listener to answer.
rite: Kaitha, the Syro-Malabar season in which the Church looks at the fruit of the apostles’ sowing, is also a season of watchfulness. The Father in today’s Gospel, who watches the road, is a good picture of the God for whom we watch. In every Holy Qurbana of the Anaphora of Addai and Mari the Church asks for the pardon of debts and the forgiveness of sins (in substance), and then gathers at the Lord’s table; like the younger son, we come home not as hired hands but as children.

The elder son’s question is one for every parish: do we welcome the one who has come back, with the joy of the Father, or do we stand outside? A family or prayer group might ask: is there someone in our parish or family who needs us to “go out” and plead with them to come in?
study: Moses says: “because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants after them.” How have I experienced God’s love before I could do anything to earn it?
Isaiah promises a canopy of shelter from heat and storm. What is the storm in my life now, and how can I sit under the Lord’s shelter in prayer this week?
Paul says that the Spirit gives life where the letter alone cannot. Where in my life do I know what is right but need the strength of the Spirit to do it?
In the parable, is it easier for me to see myself as the younger son or the elder? What would it look like to go to the Father’s feast today?

lead: Both readings ask what makes a life stand. James says that the one who endures the test will receive the crown of life, and that every good gift, and our very birth by the word of truth, comes from the Father of lights, who never tempts anyone. In Matthew, at the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says that it is not calling him “Lord” but doing the will of the Father that matters, and that the wise person builds on the rock of his words. Together they say: trust God’s goodness, and let his word be done in your life.

r.h: Every perfect gift is from above
set: The Letter of James is addressed to Jewish Christians “in the Dispersion” (1:1) and is full of practical teaching, in the spirit of Israel’s wisdom writings. Tradition names its author as James, “the brother of the Lord”, the leader of the church in Jerusalem; some scholars think it was written later by a disciple in his name. The Church receives it as Scripture.

The passage follows verses on trials as occasions for joy and endurance (1:2–4). The Greek peirasmos can mean either a test from outside or an inner temptation; James uses it in both senses and shows how God stands to each.
str: v. 12: a blessing on one who endures; the crown of life.
vv. 13–15: God does not tempt; temptation comes from our own desire, which leads to sin and death.
vv. 16–17: do not be deceived; every good gift is from the Father of lights, who does not change.
v. 18: by his own will God gave us birth by the word of truth, as first fruits of his creation.
kw: The same word for the testing of faith (1:2–3) and for the pull toward sin (1:14). God allows us to be tested, to strengthen us, but he never tempts us to evil.
The crown here is the wreath of the winner or the guest of honour, not of a king. It is eternal life as a gift promised to those who love God (see Revelation 2:10).
The first part of a harvest offered to God. Believers are the first fruits of a new creation that is to follow.
vv: Blessed is anyone who endures temptation. Such a one has stood the test and will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him.
Endurance is not grim effort alone; it is love of God that holds. The crown is promised, and what is promised is given.
No one, when tempted, should say, “I am being tempted by God”; for God cannot be tempted by evil and he himself tempts no one.
A clear word against blaming God for sin. God is wholly good; evil never comes from his will.
Every generous act of giving, with every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change.
The sun and stars change and cast shadows; the Father who made them does not. His goodness is the one steady light.
In fulfillment of his own purpose he gave us birth by the word of truth, so that we would become a kind of first fruits of his creatures.
Our new birth is the Father’s gift, by the word of truth. It is first of all his work, and we are called to live it.
ch: The Catechism teaches, with this text, that God is not the author of temptation and that in the Our Father we ask the Father not to let us enter into it, and so to keep us from consenting to evil (CCC 2846–2847). The Church’s teaching on the new birth is that Baptism is a gift of God’s grace, before any merit of ours (CCC 1996–1999, 2008). James’s phrase “the Father of lights” is taken by the Fathers as a name for God as the source of all goodness and light, from whom comes every gift, and the Church’s prayer thanks him for these gifts (in substance).

r.h: The wise builder
set: These verses end the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), the first of the five great discourses in Matthew. After the Beatitudes, the teaching on the Law, prayer and trust, Jesus ends with warnings and a parable that call for decision.

The setting is a hill in Galilee. The listeners are the disciples and the crowds (5:1; 7:28). In Palestine a house built on bare sand beside a dry stream bed might stand all summer and be swept away by the first winter flood. A house built on rock remained.
str: v. 21: not saying “Lord, Lord”, but doing the Father’s will, opens the kingdom.
vv. 22–23: many will point to prophecy, exorcism and miracles; Jesus will say, “I never knew you”.
vv. 24–25: the one who hears and acts is like a wise man who built on rock.
vv. 26–27: the one who hears and does not act is like a foolish man who built on sand.
v. 28: the crowds are astounded at his teaching.
kw: Here poieō (“to do”) is the key verb: it occurs again in verses 24 and 26. The Father’s will is not only to be admired but done.
In Hebrew thought to “know” a person is to be in living relationship with him. The tragedy is not a lack of information; the relationship was never real.
A word of amazement. Matthew ends the sermon by saying that Jesus taught “as one having authority” (7:29): his word is not a commentary but a command that creates.
vv: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.
The confession of Jesus as Lord is true and necessary. But it is meant to become a life. Faith that is only on the lips is not yet the faith Jesus asks for.
Then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; go away from me, you evildoers.’
The great deeds of the speakers are not denied here; what is missing is the relationship and the doing of the Father’s will. Gifts and signs belong to God, not to us.
“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
Hearing and doing belong together. The rock is Jesus’ own word, received and lived.
The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on rock.
The wise builder is not spared the storm. The house stands because of its foundation.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in teaching on the Our Father: “Thy will be done” is the prayer that we may do the Father’s will, as Jesus did (CCC 2826). It teaches that our works are done by grace: God first gives us the power to will and do the good, and the merit of our works is due to God’s gift (CCC 2008; Philippians 2:13). So the passage does not set faith against works: it describes living faith, which is, as James says, faith that acts (James 2:17). The Church has long read the rock as Christ’s word and, in Christ, the Church founded on him (Matthew 16:18; CCC 552).

qa: If Jesus says that works of power are not enough, is faith in him not enough?

Faith is necessary and is the foundation (CCC 161). But faith that is real shows itself in obedience and love, as the same Lord teaches (John 14:15). Jesus is not saying that works earn heaven by themselves; he is saying that calling him Lord means asking him to rule our lives. The power to do the Father’s will is itself his gift (CCC 2008).
study: James says that God tempts no one and that every good gift comes from the Father of lights. What gift of the past week do I want to thank God for by name?
Jesus says that the wise person hears and acts. What word of Jesus have I heard recently that I have not yet put into practice, and what is one concrete step this week?

lead: Both readings unmask the wrong kind of wanting. James asks where quarrels come from and answers that they come from cravings at war inside us; he calls his readers back from friendship with the world to humble submission to God. In Luke, Jesus turns the world’s ranking upside down: blessed are the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, and woe to those who have already received their comfort. Together they ask what we really want, and who we are trusting to give it.

r.h: A friend of the world, an enemy of God
set: The Letter of James is addressed to Jewish Christians “in the Dispersion” (1:1) and reads like a sermon full of practical wisdom, much like the Wisdom books of the Old Testament. Tradition ascribes it to James, “the brother of the Lord”, the leader of the Church in Jerusalem; some scholars think it was written by a later disciple in his name. Either way, the Church has received it as Scripture.

Just before today’s verses James has spoken of peace and wisdom from above (3:13–18). Now he asks the hard question: if that wisdom is missing, where do the wars among you come from? His answer looks inside the heart before it looks at any outside enemy.
str: vv. 1–3: quarrels come from cravings; you want, you cannot get, you ask wrongly.
v. 4: divided loyalty: friendship with the world is enmity with God.
vv. 5–6: God’s jealous love for the spirit he has given us, and his greater grace for the humble.
v. 7: the answer in two commands: submit to God; resist the devil.
kw: The word from which we have “hedonism”. James sees these desires as an army encamped inside us, fighting for control. The trouble is not that we want, but that our wants have taken the place of God.

“The world” here is not creation, which God made good, but the order of life that lives without God and measures everything by gain and pride. It is the opposite of the world God so loved (John 3:16). To be its friend is to share its loyalty.
A word of order: to place oneself under another willingly. James uses it for the believer’s relation to God, not for slavery but for trust, the opposite of the proud self-rule that causes quarrels.
vv: You do not have, because you do not ask.
James is not against desire. He is against desire that never turns to God. A prayer that begins with God changes what we ask for.
You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, in order to spend what you get on your pleasures.
A good test of any prayer: whom is it for? A request made to serve our own cravings is not refused out of cruelty; it simply cannot be what a loving Father gives.
God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.
James quotes Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form. The proud close their hands to grace; the humble receive it. The gift comes before our effort and makes it possible.
Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
The command to resist follows the command to submit. We resist the enemy not by our own strength but by standing under God’s.
ch: The Catechism quotes James 4:3 when it explains why some prayers seem unanswered: when we ask wrongly, we do not receive; God wants to bring our desires into harmony with his own (CCC 2737). It also teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer: only when we recognise that we are beggars before God do we receive his gift (CCC 2559). The Church hears in “Submit yourselves therefore to God” the same trust that Mary showed in her “Let it be” (Luke 1:38).

r.h: Blessed are you who are poor
set: This is the start of Luke’s “Sermon on the Plain”, spoken on level ground after Jesus has chosen the Twelve and healed the crowds (6:12–19). Matthew’s longer Sermon on the Mount has eight beatitudes; Luke has four, each followed by a matching “woe”. Jesus speaks to “his disciples” with the crowd listening.

Luke’s Beatitudes are direct and concrete: the poor, the hungry, the weeping, the hated. Matthew adds “in spirit” and “for righteousness” (Matthew 5:3, 6). The two Gospels do not contradict each other; Luke names the people, and Matthew names the heart that Jesus wants to form in them.
str: v. 20: the poor: the kingdom of God is theirs now.
v. 21: the hungry and the weeping: they will be filled and will laugh.
vv. 22–23: the hated for the Son of Man’s sake: rejoice, for the prophets were treated the same way.
vv. 24–26: four woes: the rich, the full, the laughing, the praised.
kw: Not a wish but a declaration: you are blessed, now. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the “happy” of Psalm 1:1 and many other psalms. Jesus tells the poor that God’s favour already rests on them.

A cry of grief more than of anger, as in the prophets. Jesus sorrows over those who have already received their “consolation” (paraklēsis), the comfort they trusted, and so have nothing more to hope for from God.
vv: Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
The kingdom is given in the present tense. The poor are not promised only a future reward; God’s reign has already come near to them in Jesus.
Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, for surely your reward is great in heaven
Joy under persecution is possible because the disciple stands in the line of the prophets. Suffering for the Son of Man is a sign of belonging, not of failure.
Woe to you when all speak well of you
The woe is aimed at those who need everyone’s approval, so that they never say what the truth costs. A prophet and a disciple must sometimes be unpopular.
ch: The Church reads the Beatitudes as the portrait of Christ himself and the call to holiness: they describe the new life of those who follow him (CCC 1716–1717). Because the Lord was poor, the Church has always held that the poor are close to his heart, and her love for them is inspired by the Gospel of the Beatitudes (CCC 2444). The woes are not a curse on wealth itself, but a warning that trust in riches can shut the door against God and against the neighbour at the gate.

qa: Does Jesus say that being poor is good and being rich is bad?

No. Jesus does not praise poverty as such, and he does not hate people for owning things. Poverty can crush, and the Church works to relieve it. He says that God is on the side of those who have nothing to lean on but him, and he warns that wealth, comfort and praise can become so much a person’s whole security that there is no room left for God. The test is where our trust lies, and whether we share what we have.
study: James says we do not receive because we ask wrongly. What do I usually ask for, and how would my prayer change if I began with “Your will be done”?
Which of the four woes in Luke is most dangerous for me: wealth, comfort, laughter that avoids the truth, or the wish to be praised? What one step can I take this week?

lead: Both readings are about a death that bears fruit. Paul says that his body is wasting away while his inner self is renewed day by day, and he looks past what can be seen to a house God has prepared. In John, Jesus says that the hour of his glory is the hour when a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, and he invites the one who serves him to follow where he goes. What looks like loss is the way the Father brings life to many.

r.h: We do not lose heart
set: Paul has just described the apostle’s life as a treasure carried in clay jars (4:7), always being given up to death for Jesus’ sake so that the life of Jesus may show in us (4:10–12). Today’s verses give the reason he does not give up: the one who raised Jesus will raise us.

The passage then moves into chapter 5, where Paul uses the image of a tent and a house. Tents were Paul’s own trade (Acts 18:3), and the tent that is taken down is his body and its earthly life. What follows in 5:1 is not a denial of the body but a hope that God will give a lasting home.
str: vv. 14–15: the ground of hope: God raised Jesus and will raise us; everything is for your sake, for thanksgiving to God’s glory.
v. 16: therefore we do not lose heart: outer nature wasting, inner nature renewed.
vv. 17–18: the slight, passing affliction weighed against eternal glory; looking at what is unseen.
5:1: the earthly tent destroyed; a building from God, eternal in the heavens.
kw: our inner nature (literally, the inner man)

The self that God is making new, as opposed to the outer self that ages and suffers. It is not a part that escapes the body; it is the person whom grace is renewing from within, as Paul says in Romans 12:2.

A temporary dwelling. The word calls up Israel’s tent in the wilderness, a home that moves on, and the Word who “pitched his tent” among us (John 1:14). Our bodily life is a pilgrim’s tent; the end of the journey is God’s house.
Paul sets “weight” against “slight”. In Hebrew “glory” (kābôd) also means heaviness, importance. Our troubles, however real, are light beside the glory that will weigh them down.
vv: because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus
The Resurrection of Jesus is the pledge of ours. Paul’s courage is not optimism about his circumstances, but faith in what God has already done.
So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.

Paul does not say that the outer self does not matter or that it does not hurt. He speaks of two things happening at once: ageing and renewal. Baptism has begun a new life in us that daily prayer and the sacraments feed.
because we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen; for what can be seen is temporary, but what cannot be seen is eternal.
Faith is a way of seeing. The affliction is seen, the glory is not yet seen, but Paul trusts the unseen as more real.
we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
The hope is a home. Paul does not describe it in detail; he is content to say that it comes from God and lasts.
ch: The Church sees in these verses the Christian meaning of death: through Christ, death opens into the house of the Father, and the Church prays for the dead in that hope (CCC 1010). The Catechism also teaches that the renewal of the inner self begins in Baptism and goes on through a life of grace (CCC 1265–1266). The passage is often read at funerals for this reason.

r.h: The grain of wheat
set: In Jerusalem for the Passover, some Greeks asked to see Jesus (12:20–22). Their request is the sign for which he has waited. Throughout the Gospel he has said that his “hour” had not yet come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now he says: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” The glory John speaks of is the glory of the Cross and Resurrection together.

Verses 27–28 are John’s version of Gethsemane. Jesus’ soul is troubled; he faces the prospect of death and chooses the Father’s will. The Father answers with a voice from heaven, as at the baptism (Mark 1:11) and the Transfiguration (Mark 9:7).
str: v. 23: the hour of glory has come.
v. 24: the parable of the grain of wheat.
vv. 25–26: those who give up their life keep it; the servant follows Jesus and is honoured by the Father.
vv. 27–28: the troubled soul; “it is for this reason that I have come”; the Father’s voice.
kw: A single seed. The picture is plain to any farmer: the seed buried in the ground seems to disappear, and from its death comes a harvest. Jesus applies it to himself and to his followers.
The word can mean both biological life and the whole self. To “hate” life “in this world” is a Semitic way of saying: to love it less than God. It is not contempt for life, which is God’s gift.
In John, glory is shown in the lifting up on the Cross (12:32–33). The Father has glorified his name in Jesus’ signs and will glorify it again in the Resurrection.
vv: Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
The seed is not destroyed; it changes. Jesus’ death will not be the end of him but the beginning of a harvest, the Church gathered from every nation, beginning with the Greeks who came.
Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.
Discipleship is following to the place where Jesus goes, which includes the Cross. And the promise is the same: where he is, there the servant will be.
No, it is for this reason that I have come to this hour.
Jesus feels the fear, and he does not hide it. He does not ask to be saved from the hour, because the hour is the reason he came.
ch: The Church has always read the grain of wheat as the Paschal mystery: the death and Resurrection of Christ, from which the Church and the Eucharist come. St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom, wrote (in substance) that he was God’s wheat, to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts to become Christ’s pure bread. The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ death was the voluntary offering of his life out of love for the Father and for us (CCC 606–609), and that his “hour” is the hour of the Cross and Resurrection.

qa: Paul says that “what can be seen is temporary”. Does this mean our life and body in this world do not matter?

No. The Church teaches that the body is good and that it will rise: God made it, Christ took our flesh, and the Resurrection includes the body. Paul’s point is about where we place our final trust. Because the things we see do pass, we should not stake our lives on them alone; and because God has promised a house that lasts, we can care for the body, for the sick and for creation with hope, not with despair.
study: Paul sets “slight” affliction against an “eternal weight of glory”. What burden of mine might look different if I weighed it against that glory?
Jesus says the grain must fall and die to bear fruit. Where is God asking me to let something go so that others may receive life?

lead: Both readings are about faith that holds. James says that trials are a chance for joy, because tested faith grows into endurance, and he tells the one who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives generously, without doubting. In Mark, Jesus teaches his disciples, beside a fruitless fig tree, to have faith in God, to pray with confidence, and to forgive before they pray. Today the Church also keeps the memorial of the martyrs Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, mother and child, whose own readings (Daniel 3, Acts 6, Hebrews 11 and Matthew 10) show faith that stood in the fire; the readings of the day are the two exegeted here.

r.h: Ask in faith, never doubting
set: These are the opening lines of the Letter of James, addressed to the “twelve tribes in the Dispersion” (1:1): Jewish Christians living outside the land. They were under pressure, and James writes to strengthen them. The letter is traditionally ascribed to James, “the brother of the Lord”, though some scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name.
James does not begin with advice about avoiding trials. He begins with joy, a surprising joy that does not deny pain but sees what the trial can do.
str: vv. 2–4: trials, joy, testing of faith, endurance, maturity.
v. 5: the lack of wisdom: ask God, who gives generously.
vv. 6–8: ask in faith; the doubter is double-minded and unstable.
kw: The same word can mean a temptation to sin and a testing of faith; the context decides. Here it is the testing that the believer meets from outside, like gold tried in fire, and James has no fear of it.
Not passive waiting but staying power: remaining under the load and keeping faith. It is the quality that Jesus asks of disciples in the Gospels (Luke 21:19).
Literally “two-souled”: a person divided between God and something else. James uses it again in 4:8. It names the same split that causes quarrels, as in Tuesday’s reading.
vv: because you know that the testing of your faith produces endurance
Joy does not come from the trial itself but from what we know about it: God uses it to build our faith.
ask God, who gives to all generously and ungrudgingly, and it will be given you
Wisdom here is practical: how to live well, how to bear what we cannot change. God is a giver who does not reproach us for asking.
for the doubter, being double-minded and unstable in every way, must not expect to receive anything from the Lord
James is not speaking about the honest struggles of faith but about the person who asks while holding back from trusting God. Even a faltering faith can ask, and the Lord hears it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that prayer is a battle against ourselves and our own doubts, and that the answer to a lack of faith is to ask for it: “I believe; help my unbelief” (CCC 2728, citing Mark 9:24). The Church has always kept the call to endurance beside the call to joy: she honours the martyrs as those whose tested faith bore fruit in endurance to the end.

r.h: Have faith in God
set: Mark places this story in two parts around the cleansing of the Temple (11:15–19), so that each explains the other. Jesus enters Jerusalem on Sunday, and this is Monday and Tuesday of that last week. Jesus is hungry, and he finds a fig tree “in leaf” with no fruit. Mark adds that it was not the season for figs.

In the prophets the fig tree and the vine are signs of Israel’s life with God, and a tree without fruit is a sign of judgement (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). Most commentators therefore read the act as a parable in action: it warns about the Temple’s failure to be what God intended, “a house of prayer for all the nations” (11:17), aimed at its leadership and its use, not at the people of Israel. The Church teaches that the Jewish people remain beloved of God (Romans 11:28–29) and that Jesus’ Passion cannot be blamed on the Jews as a people (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4).
str: vv. 12–14: the hungry Jesus; the fig tree with leaves only; his word to it.
(vv. 15–19, not read today: the cleansing of the Temple.)
vv. 20–21: next morning: the tree withered to its roots; Peter remembers.
vv. 22–24: “Have faith in God”: the mountain; prayer with faith.
vv. 25–26: forgive when you stand praying.
kw: In v. 22 the Greek is echete pistin theou; Jesus literally says “have the faith of God”: some read it as faith in God, others as sharing God’s own faithfulness. Either way, it is trust that rests on who God is, not on our own power.
The word means to let go, to send away, and is the word for the forgiveness of debts in the Our Father. To forgive is to release what we hold against another before we come before God.
vv: he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.
A puzzle on the surface: why curse a tree for being out of season? Mark wants us to see that the story points beyond a tree. It is a sign of a time when God expected fruit and did not find it.
Have faith in God.

Jesus turns the disciples’ amazement into a lesson. The point is not power to destroy but trust in the one who can do what is humanly impossible. “This mountain” may mean the Temple Mount, close at hand; many think so.
Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone

Prayer and forgiveness go together. Faith does not stand apart from the heart that has been healed of its grudges. (Verse 26 is not in the NRSV text, since many ancient manuscripts omit it; it repeats Matthew 6:15, and it appears in the Malayalam Bible.)
ch: The Church hears in the withered fig tree both a warning and a call: God looks for fruit, and the fruit is love of God and neighbour. The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks for a faith that trusts (CCC 2609–2610), and that there can be no prayer to the Father without forgiving our brothers and sisters from the heart (CCC 2842–2845).

qa: Does Jesus promise that whatever we ask for in prayer will be given?

Jesus gives a strong promise, and the Church takes it seriously, but she reads it with the whole of Scripture. Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane, “not what I want, but what you want” (Mark 14:36), and James adds that we can ask wrongly (4:3). Faith asks the Father with trust that he will give what is truly good, and the prayer of faith slowly conforms our wishes to his will (CCC 2737–2741).
rite: On 15 July the Syro-Malabar Church keeps the memorial of St Kuriakose (Cyriacus) and his mother St Julitta, martyrs. According to the traditional account, whose details are not all historically certain, Julitta, a Christian woman, fled with her young child during the persecution under Diocletian and was arrested at Tarsus. When the child confessed Christ before the governor, he was killed, and she was put to death after him. The Church remembers them as a pattern of faith in the family: a mother and her child who stayed faithful together. Daniel 3, with Azariah’s prayer in the furnace, and Matthew 10, “do not fear those who kill the body”, are the readings the Church gives for them.
study: James tells us to consider trials “nothing but joy”. What trial in my life might God use to build endurance, and what help should I ask?
Jesus joins prayer and forgiveness. Is there someone I need to forgive before I pray again, and how can I begin?

lead: Today the Church honours Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and the four readings gather round the mountain of Elijah. On Carmel, Elijah prays seven times with his face to the ground until a small cloud appears and the drought ends. Isaiah promises that the wilderness will bloom with the splendour of Carmel and Sharon, and that the weak will be strengthened. Paul blesses the God of all consolation, who comforts us so that we may comfort others. In Luke, a woman cries out in praise of the mother who bore Jesus, and he answers that those who hear the word of God and keep it are blessed. The Church sees Mary in all of these: the woman of prayer, the garden God makes bloom, the mother who consoles, and the first to hear the word and keep it. (The calendar also names Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, with Isaiah 55:4–11, Acts 4:32–37, 1 Corinthians 15:1–11 and John 20:19–29; this exegesis follows the readings for Our Lady of Mount Carmel.)

r.h: A little cloud rising from the sea
set: The books of Kings tell of the prophet Elijah in the ninth century before Christ, in the reign of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, who promoted the worship of Baal.
