After years of drought, Elijah called the people to Mount Carmel and, in the contest of 18:20–40, the fire of the Lord fell on his offering and the people cried, “The Lord indeed is God.” The verses today follow: the drought ends.

Carmel is a ridge by the Mediterranean in the north of Israel, near the modern city of Haifa. Its name means something like “garden-land” or orchard. Elijah goes up to its top to pray, while King Ahab goes to eat and drink.
str: v. 41: Elijah tells Ahab of the sound of rain.
vv. 42–44: Elijah’s prayer on Carmel; the servant looks seven times; the little cloud.
vv. 45–46: the storm; Ahab rides to Jezreel; the hand of the Lord on Elijah, who runs ahead.
kw: A Hebrew word for a fertile place. Isaiah often names Carmel as the sign of beauty and fruitfulness (Isaiah 35:2); Amos pictures the Lord’s judgement as the top of Carmel drying up (Amos 1:2). The mountain stands for what God makes fruitful, and for what withers when his blessing is withdrawn.

Literally “a cloud, small”, no bigger than the palm of a hand. After three years of drought, a hand-sized cloud is all Elijah needs to hear the rain. Faith can see what is promised before it is large.
A phrase for the Lord’s power at work in a prophet. The same hand that sent the rain gives the prophet strength to outrun Ahab’s chariot.
vv: Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; there he bowed himself down upon the earth and put his face between his knees.
The prophet’s posture is the posture of one who prays with his whole body: bowed to the earth, hidden in himself, waiting. He has just seen fire fall from heaven, and now he asks, humbly, for rain.
Go again seven times.
Seven times, because the answer does not come at once. Persevering prayer is a theme of Elijah’s story; James writes that Elijah “prayed fervently” and that the heavens gave rain (James 5:17–18).
Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea.

The sign is small, yet the whole answer is in it. A later tradition of the Carmelite Order has seen in this small cloud a sign of Mary, from whom the Saviour would come; it is a devotional reading, not the literal meaning of the verse.
But the hand of the Lord was on Elijah
God’s answer in prayer is also God’s strength for the one who prays.
ch: The Catechism calls Elijah the “father of the prophets”, the one who prays for the fire to fall and whose prayer on Carmel is a prayer of faith that the Lord is God (CCC 2582–2584). The Church also reads Scripture in its spiritual senses (CCC 115–117), and in that tradition the Carmelite family has seen the small cloud as a figure of Mary. Whatever one makes of that image, the plain lesson stands: God hears the prayer of those who persevere.

r.h: The splendour of Carmel
set: Isaiah 35 closes the first part of the book with a song of joy. It follows a stern chapter on judgement (34) and looks ahead to the return of God’s people: the desert blooms, the blind see, the lame leap, and a “Holy Way” leads the redeemed to Zion (35:5–10). The verses today are the opening of that promise.

Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon were the fertile, beautiful places of the land: Lebanon for its cedars, Carmel for its orchards and woods, Sharon for the rich coastal plain. The prophet says that even the wilderness will receive their glory.
str: v. 1: the wilderness rejoices and blossoms.
v. 2: it receives the glory of Lebanon and the majesty of Carmel and Sharon; they see the glory of the Lord.
v. 3: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees.
v. 4: the message to the fearful: do not fear, your God comes to save.
kw: From a root meaning weight or heaviness: God’s glory is the weight of his presence. The prophet says that the desert will not only be made green; it will see the Lord’s glory.
fearful of heart (literally, hasty of heart)
The Hebrew describes people who are anxious or in a flutter of fear. God’s word to them is not a scolding but “Be strong, do not fear!”
vv: The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad, the desert shall rejoice and blossom
The prophet imagines the place of death turning into a garden. It is a promise to a people in exile, and it is how the Church speaks of grace: where there was nothing, God makes life.
the majesty of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the Lord, the majesty of our God.
The beauty of the land is a gift to the wilderness, and the greatest sight of all is God’s own glory.
Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees.
The promise comes with a task. Those who have been comforted are to strengthen others.
Be strong, do not fear! Here is your God.
The command to fear not is rooted in a fact: God is coming. In the Church’s hearing, the one who comes is Jesus, born of Mary.
ch: In the Gospels Jesus points to the fulfilment of this promise: the blind see, the lame walk (Matthew 11:5). On this feast the Carmelite family has loved the line about the “majesty of Carmel” as a hymn of Mary, the flower of Carmel, in whom God’s promise to bring a garden out of the desert is seen. The Church also learns from it a mission: to strengthen weak hands.

r.h: The God of all consolation
set: After a short greeting, Paul begins this letter with a blessing, as Jewish prayer does, thanking God for his comfort. He wrote during a troubled time in his relationship with the Corinthians, and he has suffered much (1:8–11 tells of a mortal danger in Asia).

The key word here, parakaleō and its noun paraklēsis, means to console, to encourage, to call alongside. It is related to the title “Paraclete”, which Jesus gives to the Holy Spirit in John’s Gospel. The comfort that Paul receives from God is meant to be passed on.
str: v. 3: blessing: the Father of mercies and God of all consolation.
v. 4: he consoles us so that we can console others.
v. 5: as Christ’s sufferings overflow into us, so does his consolation.
vv. 6–7: our affliction and consolation are for you; our hope for you is unshaken.
kw: More than soft comfort: it means strength given to stand. The “God of all consolation” does not remove all trouble, but stands beside us and gives courage.
Paul says that the Corinthians share both in the sufferings and in the consolation. In the Church, no one suffers or is comforted alone.
vv: the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction
The Father is the source. Everything that follows in the passage flows from his mercy.
so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.
We are comforted in order to comfort. Someone who has been through sorrow and found God there has something that cannot be learned from a book.
For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ.
Christ’s own sufferings overflow into the lives of his people, and so does his consolation. The two cannot be separated.
Our hope for you is unshaken
Paul’s hope is firm because it does not rest on how the Corinthians are doing at this moment, but on God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that by his Passion Christ has given a new meaning to suffering, which can now unite us to his redemptive Passion (CCC 1521). The Church sees Mary as the first to be consoled by her Son in this way, and as a mother who consoles: the Litany of Loreto calls her “Comforter of the afflicted”. Because she stood by the Cross, she is the one who stands by all who suffer.

r.h: Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it
set: This passage comes at the end of a section about Jesus’ casting out a demon and the accusation that he does it by Beelzebul (11:14–23). Jesus warns that a person who has been delivered, if the house is left “swept and put in order” but empty, may fall back into a worse state (11:24–26). Neutral cleanliness is not enough; the house must be filled with God.

Then comes a short scene found only in Luke. A woman in the crowd cries out a blessing on Jesus’ mother. It is a very Jewish way of praising a son: to bless the one who bore him. Jesus’ answer does not reject her words but deepens them.
str: vv. 24–26: the unclean spirit returns to the empty house.
v. 27: a woman’s praise: blessed is the womb that bore you.
v. 28: Jesus: blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it.
kw: The same word as in the Beatitudes and in Elizabeth’s greeting to Mary, “Blessed is she who believed” (Luke 1:45). Luke uses it carefully: Mary is called blessed because of her faith.

This Greek word can mean “rather” (as in the NRSV) or “yes, but even more”. It does not deny the woman’s words; it moves from the womb to the word, from the body to the faith that makes someone a mother of the Lord in the fullest sense.
To hear and to keep, not to hear only. Luke says that Mary “treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (2:19; see also 2:51). She is the perfect example of the one Jesus describes.
vv: Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!
The woman is not wrong. Mary herself says in the Magnificat that “all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). The Church keeps this blessing in the Hail Mary.
Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!

Jesus points out what makes Mary great: she heard the word and kept it, and became the mother of the Word through faith before she conceived him in her womb. And he opens that blessing to everyone who hears and obeys.
the last state of that person is worse than the first
A sober warning: an emptied life, even a cleansed one, needs the word of God to fill it, or the old troubles return.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that Jesus, in extolling a kingdom beyond the bonds of flesh and blood, declared blessed those who hear and keep the word of God, “as she was faithfully doing” (Lumen Gentium 58, citing Luke 2:19, 51). St Augustine says (in substance) that Mary was more blessed in receiving faith in Christ than in conceiving Christ’s flesh. The Catechism teaches that Mary most perfectly embodies the obedience of faith (CCC 148–149), and calls her the perfect “orans”, the one praying, a figure of the Church (CCC 2679).

qa: Does Jesus’ answer to the woman mean that Mary is not so special?

No. Jesus does not say that his mother is not blessed; he explains why she is. She is blessed above all because she heard the word of God and kept it, and the Church holds this up as the way open to every Christian. Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed (Luke 1:45), and Mary herself said that all generations would call her blessed (Luke 1:48). The Church honours her because of what God did in her, and she leads us to her Son, not away from him.
What is the Brown Scapular, and does wearing it save us?

The Brown Scapular is a small garment of the Carmelite Order which many lay people wear as a sign of devotion to Mary and a wish to live under her protection. It has been loved for centuries, and tradition links it with St Simon Stock in the thirteenth century, though the details of that story cannot be proved. The Church does not teach that a piece of cloth saves anyone. It is a sign of belonging to Mary and of a desire to live as she did, hearing the word of God and keeping it. Salvation comes from Christ, by grace, received in faith and a life of love.
Is the little cloud in 1 Kings really Mary?

The literal meaning is a small cloud bringing rain. The Church teaches that Scripture also has deeper senses (CCC 115–117), and from early times Christians have found figures of Mary in the Old Testament, as the Carmelite tradition has with this cloud. It is a devotional image that helps prayer, not something the text itself says.
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church keeps the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel with special joy because the Carmelite family is deep in the history of the Church in Kerala. The Carmelites of Mary Immaculate (CMI), the first indigenous religious congregation of men in India, were founded in 1831 at Mannanam by Kuriakose Elias Chavara and his companions; he was canonised in 2014. Blessed Mother Eliswa founded the first Carmelite congregation for women in India in 1866 (the Teresian Carmelites), and she was beatified in 2025. Many parishes and families in Kerala take the Scapular and the Carmelite devotion. Today’s calendar also remembers Mar Mari, who with Mar Addai is held by tradition to have brought the Gospel to Mesopotamia and the East; the ancient Anaphora of Addai and Mari, one of the three anaphoras of the Holy Qurbana, bears their names.
study: Elijah prays on Carmel seven times, and the answer is only a small cloud. What prayer of mine needs more patience, and what small sign of God’s answer might I be overlooking?
Paul says we are consoled so that we may console others. Whom can I comfort this week with the comfort I have received from God?
Jesus names those who “hear the word of God and obey it” as blessed. What one verse of Scripture will I hear and keep this week, as Mary did?
What does it mean to me to belong to Mary, and how does she lead me to her Son?

lead: Both readings are about who sits at God’s table. James scolds a community that gives the best seat to the person in fine clothes and tells the poor person to stand, when God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith. In Luke, a guest at a dinner exclaims, “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!”, and Jesus answers with a story of a great banquet where those first invited make excuses and the host fills his house with the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame. God’s table is wide, and the question is whether we will come.

r.h: God chose the poor
set: James now turns from trials and prayer to a very concrete example of faith in life: how the assembly treats people. The “assembly” in verse 2 is the Greek word synagōgē, the gathering of the Christian community, a reminder that these first believers were Jewish Christians who still used the language of the synagogue.

James is not describing every rich person. He is describing a situation in the community: a visitor with gold rings and fine clothes is given honour, and a poor visitor is pushed aside. The verses about the rich who “oppress you” and “drag you into court” (2:6) point to the experience of these believers, who in some places had been exploited by wealthy and powerful people. James is not hating the rich, who are called to conversion like everyone else; he is protecting the dignity of the poor.
str: v. 1: the principle: faith in the glorious Lord does not go with favouritism.
vv. 2–4: the scene: the rich man and the poor man; the seat of honour and the place on the floor.
vv. 5–7: God’s choice: the poor, rich in faith, heirs of the kingdom; the community’s own contempt.
v. 8: the royal law: love your neighbour as yourself.
kw: The word is built from “to lift up a face”, to favour someone because of outward appearance. The Bible uses it of what God does not do: “God shows no partiality” (Romans 2:11). The community that shows it contradicts the God it worships.

The law of the King, or the supreme law. James uses it for the command in Leviticus 19:18, which Jesus placed beside the love of God as the heart of the Law (Matthew 22:39). It is “royal” because the Kingdom’s own rule is love.
The poor have no earthly security; so they are open to receive from God. James does not say the poor are automatically holy; he says that God has a special love for them.
vv: do you with your acts of favoritism really believe in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ?
James puts it as a question about belief. Faith in the glorious Lord, who made himself poor, cannot live alongside the judging of people by their wealth.
Has not God chosen the poor in the world to be rich in faith and to be heirs of the kingdom that he has promised to those who love him?

The Church’s “preferential love” for the poor rests on verses like this. God’s choice is not because the poor are better but because they are the ones who most need him and are most likely to trust him.
You do well if you really fulfill the royal law according to the scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
James is fair: the answer to favouritism is not coldness but love. When love is the rule, the seat at the table is for everyone.
ch: The Catechism teaches that all human beings have the same dignity, made in the image of God, and that this equal dignity requires us to work for fairer and more humane conditions (CCC 1934–1935). The Church’s care for the poor, which has always been part of her life, is not an extra but a way of being faithful to the Lord who chose to be poor himself (CCC 2444).

r.h: The great dinner
set: Jesus is at a meal in the house of a leading Pharisee on a Sabbath (14:1). He has just told the guests to invite “the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” rather than those who can repay (14:12–14). One of the guests, hearing this, exclaims a pious blessing about the banquet of the kingdom of God. Jesus answers with a parable.

In the ancient Near East, as many commentators note, a feast often had two invitations: first a notice, then, when the meal was ready, a messenger to call the guests. Those who had accepted the first invitation now make excuses at the second, which was a serious insult to the host.
str: v. 15: the guest’s exclamation: blessed is the one who eats bread in the kingdom.
vv. 16–17: the host invites many; the servant: “Come; for everything is ready now.”
vv. 18–20: three excuses: the field, the oxen, the marriage.
vv. 21–23: the master’s anger; the poor and the crippled; then the roads outside: “there is still room.”
v. 24: the closing word.
kw: to excuse oneself, to beg off
Each guest says the same thing, “please accept my regrets”. The excuses are not wicked: a field, a farm animal, a new marriage. The tragedy is that good things are put ahead of the invitation.

The servant is to press the strangers so that they will not stay outside through shyness, because they feel unworthy to come. It is the urgency of hospitality. The Church has always taught that faith must be a willing answer and cannot be forced (CCC 160).
vv: Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!
The guest is right. Jesus does not correct him but asks whether he and others will actually come.
But they all alike began to make excuses.
The excuses are ordinary. The danger of the kingdom invitation is not that people refuse it with hatred, but that they say, “Not now; I am busy.”
bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.
These are the very people Jesus told his host to invite (14:13). The master’s house is not full of the “right” people but of those who know their need.
Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.
The great generosity of the master: even after the poor of the town are inside, there is still room. God’s house is always larger than we expect.
ch: The Church sees in the banquet an image of the kingdom and also of the Eucharist, the “sacred banquet” in which Christ is received and a pledge of future glory is given to us (CCC 1402). She also hears in the story an invitation to all nations. It must not be read as if God has rejected Israel: Paul writes that God’s gifts and his call are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and the Church teaches that the Jewish people remain beloved of God (Nostra Aetate 4). The parable warns each of us, whoever we are, not to put anything before the invitation.

qa: Does the parable mean that God has turned away from those who were first invited?

No. The parable is told at table to a group of Pharisees, and Jesus says it to warn everyone who is present, including his own disciples, that excuses can keep any of us from the feast. The first invited were people who had the promises; Paul says that God does not take back his call (Romans 11:29). In Luke’s second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, the first believers are Jews who accept the invitation, and then it goes out also to the Gentiles. The parable shows the generosity of God, who keeps widening the table; it does not say that anyone is cast out for what they are.
study: James says that faith and favouritism cannot go together. Whom do I treat as less important because of clothes, money or position, and how will I change that?
The guests in the parable said, “please accept my regrets.” What good thing in my life most often keeps me from the Lord’s invitation, and what is my next step?

lead: The four readings of this Sunday begin with something God has already given, and then ask what grows from it. In Deuteronomy, the Ten Words open with a gift: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”, and only then come the commands. In Isaiah, a friend sings of a vineyard planted with every care, and asks, “What more was there to do?”, when it yielded wild grapes. Paul, writing to the Corinthians who have been hurt by his earlier letter, rejoices that their sorrow led to repentance, not despair. And in John, a man born blind is given sight by Jesus, and with sight comes faith: “Lord, I believe.” Light, grace and love come first; what God hopes for in return is trust, justice and a heart that turns. The Gospel shows that harvest in one person, who goes from darkness to worship.

r.h: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out
set: Deuteronomy is Moses’ great farewell address to Israel on the plains of Moab, before they cross the Jordan. In chapter 5 he calls the people together and repeats the Ten Commandments that were given at Horeb (Sinai), which are also found in Exodus 20. Moses speaks as if the people were all standing at the mountain: “The Lord our God made a covenant with us at Horeb” (5:2). The covenant belongs to every generation.

The Ten Commandments are called in Hebrew the “ten words” (Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4). The reading today covers the first four in the Catholic way of counting (CCC 2066): the worship of the one God and no idols (vv. 6–10), the name of the Lord (v. 11), the Sabbath (vv. 12–15), and honour for father and mother (v. 16). The remaining commandments, on love of neighbour, follow in verses 17–21. Deuteronomy’s form of the Sabbath commandment differs from Exodus 20:11: Exodus gives the Lord’s rest at creation as the reason; Deuteronomy gives the memory of slavery in Egypt.
str: v. 6: the prologue: the Lord who brought Israel out of slavery.
vv. 7–10: no other gods, no idols; the jealous God who shows steadfast love to a thousand generations.
v. 11: do not misuse the Lord’s name.
vv. 12–15: the Sabbath: six days of work, the seventh for the Lord; rest for all, including servants and the resident alien; remember the slavery in Egypt.
v. 16: honour father and mother, that your days may be long in the land.
kw: Egypt is called a “house” of slaves, a place where people were treated as property. The Lord’s first action in the commandments is liberation. The commandments are given to a people who have been released from slavery, to keep them so.

Not the petty jealousy of envy but the exclusive love of a husband or wife who cannot bear to share the beloved. The prophets use the same image of the marriage covenant. It shows the passion of God’s love, and it is why idols betray the relationship.
The Lord’s loyal, covenant love, which does not give up. The verse sets it beside punishment: punishment reaches to the third and fourth generation, but steadfast love reaches to the thousandth.
In Hebrew “remember” means more than recalling; it means to act on the memory. The Sabbath, resting with servants and strangers, is how Israel remembers what the Lord did for them.
vv: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery
Every commandment stands under this sentence. First the Lord says who he is and what he has done; then he says what he asks. Obedience is a response to love already received.
but showing steadfast love to the thousandth generation of those who love me and keep my commandments.

The verse before it speaks of sin’s consequences spreading through families. Here the proportion is stated: grace outruns judgement a thousand times over. The Church reads it with Ezekiel 18, where each person answers for his or her own sin, and with the mercy shown in Christ.
Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm
The Sabbath is a day when no one is a slave: not the child, the servant, the stranger or even the ox. Rest is a sign of liberation, and it is a gift for all.
Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you
The first commandment about people. Family is the first school of faith and the first place where commandments are lived.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Ten Commandments must be understood in light of the Exodus: God first liberates, and then gives the Law (CCC 2056–2057). The Church’s tradition keeps them as the path of love of God and neighbour, and Jesus did not abolish them but fulfilled them (Matthew 5:17). The Sabbath, a day of rest and remembrance, is kept by Christians on Sunday, the Lord’s Day, the day of the Resurrection (CCC 2174–2176), and the Church calls Sunday the day when the Church gathers for the Holy Qurbana.

r.h: The song of the vineyard
set: The prophet Isaiah worked in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ, during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. The “Song of the Vineyard” is placed at the end of the first great section of the book, the opening chapters. It is one of the most famous poems in the Old Testament. Isaiah is a son of the people he addresses, and he sings the song as a love song that turns into a legal case.

Many think the song was first sung at a vintage or harvest festival, where a singer might entertain the crowd with a love song. Isaiah begins, “Let me sing for my beloved” and the crowd is charmed. Only in verse 3 is it clear that the audience is also the accused: “inhabitants of Jerusalem and people of Judah”.
str: vv. 1–2: the love-song: the beloved’s vineyard, the care and the expectation; it yields wild grapes.
vv. 3–4: the appeal to the audience: judge between me and my vineyard.
vv. 5–6: the verdict: the hedge removed, the wall broken, the vineyard made a waste.
v. 7: the explanation: the vineyard is the house of Israel; the Lord expected justice and heard a cry.
kw: A word for a lover. In the poem the singer speaks for his friend, and the friend turns out to be the Lord. The prophet’s own love for his people is part of the song.
Literally “stinking things”, sour or bad-smelling fruit, which have the look of grapes and are useless. The point is the contrast between what was expected and what grew.

A sound-play in Hebrew that cannot be kept in translation: the Lord looked for mishpat, justice, and found mispach, bloodshed; he looked for tsedaqah, righteousness, and heard tse‘aqah, the cry of the oppressed.
vv: Let me sing for my beloved my love-song concerning his vineyard
Prophecy begins with love. God’s dealings with his people are the story of a lover who has given everything.
What more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done in it?
The Lord does not blame the soil or the planter. He has given everything and is saddened, not angry in a cold way. The question invites a real answer: what is wrong with us, when God has done all?
he expected justice, but saw bloodshed; righteousness, but heard a cry!
The “fruit” is not religious feeling but justice among people: the cry of the poor and the wronged. Isaiah’s message to his own nation is the one that the Church hears for itself.
ch: The Church reads the vineyard also as a sign of herself and of every believer, and this is why the Lord says, “I am the vine, you are the branches” (John 15:1–5; CCC 755). Jesus’ own parable of the tenants (Matthew 21:33–43) takes up Isaiah’s song, aimed at the leaders who failed to give the owner the fruit. The Church does not read Isaiah’s song as God’s rejection of the Jewish people: Isaiah himself was a Jewish prophet speaking to his own people out of love, and Paul says clearly that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1, 29; Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The warning is for every generation of those who have been given much, including ourselves.

r.h: Godly grief
set: This passage comes at the emotional turning point of the letter. Paul had sent the Corinthians a severe letter, probably written “out of much distress and anguish of heart and with many tears” (2:4), and he did not know how they would respond. He waited anxiously for Titus; when Titus came with good news, his relief was great.

Verse 1 gathers the promises at the end of chapter 6 (that God will live among his people and be a Father to them) into a call to holiness: “let us cleanse ourselves” (7:1). Then Paul asks the community to open their hearts again to him, and he explains why he is joyful: the letter that hurt them led them to a change of heart. Some scholars think the “severe letter” is lost, or is part of 2 Corinthians 10–13; scholars are divided.
str: v. 1: the promises call us to holiness.
vv. 2–4: “Make room in your hearts for us”; Paul’s love and pride in them.
vv. 5–7: affliction in Macedonia; God consoles through Titus.
vv. 8–9: the painful letter; sorrow that led to repentance.
vv. 10–11: godly grief versus worldly grief; the fruit of repentance.
kw: godly grief (literally, sorrow according to God)

Sorrow that sees sin in God’s light: it is painful but hopeful, and it turns toward him. The other kind, “worldly grief”, looks only at the damage to oneself or to one’s name, and ends in bitterness or despair.
From meta (change) and nous (mind). Repentance is more than feeling sorry; it is turning life around. Paul says it “leads to salvation and brings no regret”.
In verse 11 Paul lists what godly sorrow has produced: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, alarm, longing, zeal. Real repentance is full of energy.
vv: Make room in your hearts for us
Paul asks for a place in their hearts. A relationship damaged by hard words is healed by open hearts on both sides.
But God, who consoles the downcast, consoled us by the arrival of Titus
God’s consolation often comes through a person. The Church sees in this how God uses ordinary friends as his instruments.
Now I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because your grief led to repentance
Paul does not enjoy causing pain. A correction made in love is justified only by the good it brings.
For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret, but worldly grief produces death.
A summary of the Christian way of dealing with sin. Peter’s tears led to restoration; Judas’s remorse ended in despair. The difference is whether sorrow turns toward God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that interior repentance is a radical reorientation of the whole life, a return to God with all our heart (CCC 1431), and that contrition, sorrow of the soul with the resolution not to sin again, is the first step in the sacrament of Penance (CCC 1451). The Church sees in godly grief a gift of grace, since the human heart is hard and God must give a new heart (CCC 1432). It does not paralyse; it opens the door to forgiveness.

r.h: The man born blind
set: John 9 is a single long scene: a healing (vv. 1–7), the neighbours’ questions (vv. 8–12), the inquiry before the Pharisees and the man’s parents (vv. 13–34, not read today), and the meeting with Jesus (vv. 35–41). It takes place on a Sabbath (9:14), and follows the chapters set at the Feast of Tabernacles (7–8), a feast in which light was a central image. Jesus has said in 8:12, “I am the light of the world.”

The reading omits the middle, where those who question the man, “the Pharisees” and “the Jews”, are the religious authorities, and the man’s parents fear being put out of the synagogue (9:22). This reflects tensions in the time of the Gospel’s writing, which many scholars place near the end of the first century, and must never be read as blame on the Jewish people. Jesus, his disciples, the blind man and his parents are all Jews.
str: vv. 1–3: the disciples’ question about sin; Jesus’ answer: God’s works are to be revealed.
vv. 4–5: night is coming; “I am the light of the world.”
vv. 6–7: the mud and the pool of Siloam; the man washes and sees.
vv. 8–12: the neighbours’ disbelief; “I am the man”; “Where is he?” “I do not know.”
(vv. 13–34 are not read: the questioning of the man, the parents and the expulsion.)
vv. 35–38: Jesus finds him; “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”; “Lord, I believe.”
kw: John explains that “Siloam” means Sent. Jesus is the one sent by the Father (9:4), and the man is sent to a pool that bears the same name. The pool of Siloam also appears in Isaiah 8:6 as “the waters of Shiloah that flow gently”.
Light is the main image of the chapter. For John, to see is to come to faith. The healed man sees step by step: first “the man called Jesus”, then “a prophet”, then “from God”, then “Lord”.
The word used for worship of God. In John it appears only here for Jesus, as the man bows before the Son of Man. He has moved from blindness to adoration.
vv: Neither this man nor his parents sinned; he was born blind so that God’s works might be revealed in him.

Jesus refuses to explain every suffering as punishment for sin. He turns the disciples’ attention from blame to what God will do. This does not mean that God sends the blindness for show; it says that God can bring his works out of it.
As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.
The light does not stay far away; it comes close, with mud and water and a command to go and wash.
Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). Then he went and washed and came back able to see.
The man does what he is told, though he cannot yet see why. The first step of faith is obedience before sight.
Do you believe in the Son of Man?
After the man has been put out, Jesus finds him. Those who have been cast out are sought by the Lord.
“Lord, I believe.” And he worshiped him.
The healing ends not with sight but with worship. His physical sight is the sign; his faith is the gift.
ch: From the earliest centuries the Church has read this story as a picture of Baptism, in which the one who washes receives light; for that reason the Catechism notes that Baptism is called “enlightenment” (CCC 1216). St Irenaeus (in substance) saw in the clay a sign that the same hand that formed Adam from the earth was now completing the man’s creation. St Augustine (in substance) taught that the blind man stands for the whole human race, born in the dark, who is lit by Christ. The Catechism also says that Jesus’ healings are signs of the kingdom, though he did not come to abolish every earthly evil (CCC 548–549).

qa: Jesus says the man was born blind “so that God’s works might be revealed”. Did God make him blind in order to show off?

No. The Church teaches that God is never the cause of moral evil, and that he allows suffering only because he can bring a greater good out of it (CCC 311–312). Jesus’ answer is first of all a refusal to blame: the man’s blindness is not a punishment for anyone’s sin. He then turns attention to what God will do. The Church sees in Christ the compassion of God for the sick and the sign of the healing that he brings (CCC 1503–1505).
Does the Sabbath commandment still apply to Christians?

The commandment remains: a day set apart for God, for worship and for rest. Christians keep it on Sunday, the first day of the week, the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, when the community gathers at the Holy Qurbana (CCC 2174–2176). Jesus teaches that the Sabbath is for people and for doing good (Mark 2:27; 3:4), and Deuteronomy already ties it to the memory of liberation and rest for everyone.
Does Isaiah’s song of the vineyard mean that God rejected the Jewish people?

No. Isaiah was a Jew speaking to his own people, as a prophet who loved them. His song was a warning, not a final verdict, and later in the same book there is a new song of the vineyard that promises restoration (Isaiah 27:2–6). The Church teaches that God does not take back his gifts and calling (Romans 11:29), and that the Jewish people remain beloved of God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: The Third Sunday of Kaitha, in the Syro-Malabar calendar, follows the Season of the Apostles. In Kaitha the Church walks Sunday by Sunday through the Lord’s word, and today’s readings give a good frame: the covenant given by grace, the fruit the Lord looks for, repentance, and light. The East Syriac tradition loves the language of light for Baptism. Mar Aprem (in substance) speaks of the baptised as clothed in a robe of glory. The Gospel of the blind man, who washes in a pool and comes back seeing, who then bows down in worship before Jesus, is read in that light. At the Holy Qurbana the Church also bows before the Lord who is truly present, and the people’s confession, “Lord, I believe”, is the Church’s own.
study: The Ten Words begin with “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out.” How does remembering what God has already done for me change the way I keep his commandments?
In Isaiah, God asks “What more was there to do?” What fruit might God be looking for in my life, and what is blocking it?
Paul distinguishes godly grief from worldly grief. When I have failed, which kind do I usually feel, and how can I turn toward God?
The blind man grew in sight: “the man called Jesus”, then a prophet, then “Lord”. Where am I on that road, and what would help me say “Lord, I believe” more fully?

lead: Both readings ask what God sees when he looks at his people. James looks for a faith that has become visible in deeds, as Abraham’s did on the mountain and Rahab’s did at her door. In Matthew, Jesus looks at Jerusalem, the city he loves, and speaks with the grief of a mother hen whose chicks will not come under her wings. Faith that is alive moves toward God and toward neighbour; love that is refused still goes on calling.

r.h: Faith brought to completion
set: James writes to Jewish Christians scattered among the nations (1:1). In 2:14–20 he has asked what good it is to say “I have faith” when there are no deeds, for example when a brother or sister is left hungry and cold. These verses give two examples from Scripture: Abraham, the father of faith, and Rahab, the foreign woman of Jericho.

James is not arguing against Paul. Paul speaks of the works of the law, such as circumcision, as a way to claim a place among God’s people (Galatians 2:16). James speaks of works of love, such as mercy to the poor, which show that faith is real. Both agree that faith in Christ is the root; they look at different dangers.
str: v. 21: Abraham and the offering of Isaac (Genesis 22).
v. 22: faith and works work together, and faith is brought to completion.
v. 23: Genesis 15:6 is fulfilled; Abraham is called the friend of God.
vv. 24–25: the conclusion, and the second example, Rahab (Joshua 2).
v. 26: the picture of the body and the spirit.
kw: In the Greek Old Testament this verb is used for God’s verdict that a person stands rightly before him. James uses it of the verdict that is shown by a life, and Paul of the gift God gives. The one word is used with different emphasis.
In James a work is not a way of earning God’s favour but what faith does when it is alive: welcoming, feeding, risking oneself for others.
The faith was “brought to completion”. Faith is a seed that becomes fruit; the fruit does not replace the seed.
vv: Was not our ancestor Abraham justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?

Abraham’s obedience in Genesis 22 came long after the word of Genesis 15:6. James shows that the trust God first reckoned as righteousness was later proved in the hardest of tests. Abraham is “our ancestor” for Jews and for all who share his faith.
You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was brought to completion by the works.
Faith is the root, works the fruit, and the two belong to one tree. The Church has always read the verse so.
and he was called the friend of God.
The title comes from Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7. A friend is trusted with God’s plans, and Abraham is the friend because he trusted God completely.
Likewise, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by another road?
After the patriarch, a woman of the nations, once outside Israel. She is also named in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5) and among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:31).
For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead.
A faith that never acts is not a sleeping faith but a dead one, as a body without breath. The saying needs no other explanation.
ch: The Catechism teaches that faith is a gift of God and a supernatural virtue, and that this gift remains in one who has not sinned against it, but “faith apart from works is dead” (James 2:26), and without hope and love it does not unite the believer fully to Christ (CCC 1815). The Church teaches that we are justified by grace through faith, not by merits of our own (CCC 1987–1992 and 2010), and that this grace is meant to bear fruit in love. Charity is the “form” of the other virtues (CCC 1827).

r.h: Jerusalem, Jerusalem
set: This is the last public teaching of Jesus in Matthew before the Passion. In Matthew 23 he speaks to the crowds and his disciples about the scribes and Pharisees who “sit on Moses’ seat” (23:2). He first says that their teaching is to be heeded where it is faithful to Moses, then speaks seven woes against hypocrisy, which is a danger for every teacher of religion in every age, and then, in these verses, he turns to lament over the whole city.

Jesus himself is a Jew speaking to Jews, in the manner of the prophets, who often spoke with harsh words to their own people because they loved them. The words are not a judgment on any people as a whole. The Church teaches that what happened in Christ’s passion cannot be blamed on all Jews then living, nor on Jews today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: v. 34: Jesus sends prophets, sages and scribes, and they meet rejection.
vv. 35–36: the line of the righteous slain, from Abel to Zechariah.
v. 37: the lament over Jerusalem, with the image of the hen and her brood.
vv. 38–39: the house left desolate, and the promise of a return with the words of Psalm 118.
kw: The verb of a shepherd gathering the flock, or of exiles being brought home. Jesus wants to gather Jerusalem’s children as God long promised (Isaiah 40:11; Jeremiah 31:10).
Used in the prophets for a house or city that has lost God’s protection (Jeremiah 22:5). It is the opposite of the gathering of verse 37.
blessed is the one who comes
From Psalm 118:26, the pilgrims’ greeting sung at the Temple gates. The crowds sang it at the entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9).
vv: from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

Abel is the first righteous victim in Genesis 4. Zechariah is probably the priest killed in the Temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22, the last book of the Hebrew Scriptures: from the first book to the last. Matthew calls him “son of Barachiah”, while Chronicles calls the priest the son of Jehoiada; scholars explain the difference in several ways, and none is certain.
How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!

One of the tenderest images in the Gospels. The Old Testament often speaks of God’s wings as shelter (Psalm 91:4; Ruth 2:12). Jesus speaks as God speaks, and with God’s longing. “You were not willing” is the sorrow of love that cannot force a reply.
See, your house is left to you, desolate.
Many see here the sign of the Temple’s coming fall (Matthew 24:2). It is a warning spoken in grief, not in triumph.
you will not see me again until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’
The saying ends in hope: a day will come when Jerusalem welcomes him. Paul, too, speaks of the final salvation of Israel (Romans 11:25–32).
ch: The Church has always heard Jesus’ lament as the voice of divine love, never of hatred. At the Second Vatican Council she taught that the Jews remain very dear to God, who does not repent of the gifts he has made nor of the call he has issued (Nostra Aetate 4, citing Romans 11:28–29); Christians must never speak of them as rejected or accursed. The Catechism adds that sinners, not any one people, were the authors and the instruments of Christ’s sufferings (CCC 598). Luke records the same grief when Jesus weeps over the city as he approaches it (Luke 19:41–44).

qa: Do James and Paul contradict each other on justification?

No. Paul argues against the idea that keeping the works of the Mosaic law, such as circumcision, can win a place with God; James argues against the idea that a faith with no deeds of love can save. The Catholic Church holds both: we are justified by God’s grace through faith in Christ, and this faith must work through love (Galatians 5:6; CCC 1814–1815).
study: James says that faith is brought to completion by works. Where in my week does what I believe become something people can see?
Jesus grieves over Jerusalem because love was refused. How do I respond when someone I love will not come back, and what can I do other than pray?

lead: James asks who is truly wise, and answers that wisdom is seen not in clever talk but in a gentle, peaceable, merciful life. In Luke’s Nazareth scene, a congregation that has just admired Jesus turns on him when he reminds them that God’s mercy has always reached beyond the borders they expected. The first reading asks us to examine what is in our hearts; the Gospel shows what happens when the heart is closed to a grace that is larger than its own plans.

r.h: The wisdom from above
set: The letter has just warned teachers about the power of the tongue (3:1–12). Now James asks what real wisdom looks like. In the Jewish tradition a wise person is not simply clever but one who fears the Lord and lives well (Proverbs 1:7; Sirach 1). Two kinds of “wisdom” are set side by side, and the test is the fruit each produces.
str: v. 13: the question and the test: a good life, with gentle works.
vv. 14–16: false wisdom: envy and selfish ambition, which breed disorder.
vv. 17–18: true wisdom, “from above”: seven marks, and a harvest of peace.
kw: The quality of strength under control, like a trained horse. Jesus describes himself as “gentle” (Matthew 11:29). Wisdom does not shout.
The second word was originally used of those who canvass for office for their own gain. Wisdom that serves only its own advantage is “earthly, unspiritual, devilish”.
In the Bible it is not only the absence of conflict but wholeness, right relations with God and neighbour. Those who “make peace” sow it as a farmer sows seed.
vv: Show by your good life that your works are done with gentleness born of wisdom.
Wisdom is proved in daily conduct. A person may know much and still lack it.
For where there is envy and selfish ambition, there will also be disorder and wickedness of every kind.
James looks at the life of a community. Envy and the wish to be first tear a parish, a family or a community apart.
But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, without a trace of partiality or hypocrisy.
A portrait of a wise heart. “First pure”: wisdom begins with a clean heart, and peace follows. The Greek for “willing to yield” means open to persuasion, not stubborn.
And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.
The saying echoes the Beatitude, “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9). Peace is a seed that is sown quietly and bears fruit in time.
ch: The Church sees in this portrait the working of the Holy Spirit, whose gifts include wisdom and understanding (CCC 1831; Isaiah 11:2). The Catechism, speaking of the Beatitude of peacemakers, teaches that earthly peace is the image and fruit of the peace of Christ (CCC 2305). Such peace requires the removal of envy and the other roots of discord (compare CCC 2317).

r.h: No prophet at home
set: Jesus has come to Nazareth, where he grew up, and in the synagogue read from Isaiah 61: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me…” (4:16–21). At first “all spoke well of him” (4:22). Then he says that no prophet is accepted in his hometown (4:24), and gives two examples from Israel’s own Scriptures. These verses are the second half of that conversation.

The anger that follows is the anger of one village at one moment. Luke does not blame a people. Jesus is a Jew teaching in a synagogue, and many Jews believe in him throughout Luke and Acts. The story shows that the Gospel is first heard in Israel’s house and is meant for all.
str: vv. 25–26: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17).
v. 27: Elisha and Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings 5).
vv. 28–29: the rage and the attempt to throw him off the hill.
v. 30: he passes through the midst and goes on.
kw: The congregation “were filled with rage”. The mood changes within minutes from wonder to violence, which shows how quickly a hardened heart can turn.
The word is used elsewhere for driving out demons. Luke may be hinting at a certain irony: the people drive out the one who is able to drive out all evil.
He is not caught. Many readers see here a foreshadowing: at the Passion he will go to Jerusalem willingly, and no one will take his life from him against his will (John 10:18).
vv: there were many widows in Israel in the time of Elijah
Jesus does not say these widows were unworthy. He says God’s choice was not limited by the borders people drew. The famine lasted “three years and six months”, the same period named in James 5:17.
yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon.
Zarephath lay outside Israel, near Sidon. The prophet was sent to a foreign widow, and her jar of flour and jug of oil did not run out (1 Kings 17:8–16).
There were also many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.
Naaman was a commander of an enemy army, yet he was healed when he obeyed the word of the prophet (2 Kings 5:14).
But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.
The scene ends without explanation. The Gospel will not be stopped by one village’s refusal.
ch: Both prophets, Elijah and Elisha, were sent to people beyond Israel; the Church reads this as a sign that God’s saving plan reaches all nations, a plan that Luke will follow in Acts. The Catechism teaches that Elijah is “the father of the prophets” and that his prayer is a model for the people of God (CCC 2582). Jesus is the greater prophet, and like the prophets he meets resistance (Luke 13:33–34); the Church has always taught that he accepted the Passion willingly (CCC 609).

qa: Why did the people of Nazareth become so angry?

Luke does not say in a single sentence, but the reason can be seen in the two examples. Jesus implies that God’s favour is not a right that belongs to one town, and that outsiders, a widow of Sidon and a Syrian commander, responded to God better than many in Israel. This was hard to hear. The passage is a challenge to every community, including the Church, never to treat God’s gifts as its own property.
study: James lists the marks of wisdom from above. Which of them do I most need to grow in this week: purity, peace, gentleness, willingness to yield, mercy?
The people of Nazareth were offended that God’s mercy reaches outsiders. Who are the “outsiders” whose good I find hard to welcome?

lead: Paul describes what has happened in Christ: God was reconciling the world to himself, and the person who belongs to Christ is a new creation. Mark shows how that new creation begins in one ordinary place, a lakeshore, where Jesus calls four fishermen away from their nets. In both readings the first move is God’s. He reconciles; he calls. Our part is to accept the reconciliation and to follow, and then to carry the same invitation to others.

r.h: A new creation
set: Paul is defending his ministry to a community that has doubted him. He says that what drives him is “the love of Christ” (5:14): since one died for all, all have died, and those who live no longer live for themselves. These verses draw out the consequences: a new way of looking at people, a new creation, and a ministry of reconciliation.
str: v. 15: Christ died for all, so that the living might live for him.
v. 16: a new way of seeing people and Christ himself.
v. 17: anyone in Christ is a new creation.
vv. 18–19: God’s work of reconciliation, and the message entrusted to Paul and his companions.
vv. 20–21: the appeal: be reconciled to God; the exchange by which Christ takes our sin and gives us God’s righteousness.
kw: The word comes from the exchange of money and then from restoring friendship after a quarrel. Here God does the reaching out: it is not the offended person who is reconciled by our efforts, but God who reconciles us.
The same phrase is used in Galatians 6:15. It recalls Isaiah’s promise of “new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). In Christ the new age has begun.
An ambassador speaks for a king and carries his authority. Paul does not speak for himself; God is making his appeal through the apostles’ voice.
vv: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
The Greek has no verb in the first clause, which can be read “if anyone is in Christ: new creation!” The Church has long connected the phrase with Baptism, where a person is made new.
in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them
Reconciliation begins in God. He did not wait for the world to make the first step; the initiative is in the cross and Resurrection.
we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
Paul speaks to Christians as well as to the world. Reconciliation is a daily need as well as a first conversion.
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

One of the most compressed lines in Paul. “Made to be sin” does not mean that Christ sinned, for he “knew no sin”. Many translate it as “made a sin offering” (the Greek word can mean both); in either sense Christ took our sin on himself, and we receive God’s own righteousness.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God sent his Son to take away our sins, quoting this very verse: Jesus “knew no sin”, but out of love for us, God made him “to be sin” (CCC 602–603). The ministry of reconciliation, passed by Christ to the apostles, is exercised in the sacrament of Penance (CCC 1442, citing 2 Corinthians 5:18). The Church also sees in the “new creation” the grace of Baptism (CCC 1265).

r.h: Follow me
set: Mark has just reported Jesus’ first words: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news” (1:15). The very next scene is the call of the first disciples. Jesus does not first collect a following and then teach; he first calls a few people to be with him, so that the good news will spread through them.

Capernaum and the north shore of the Sea of Galilee were busy with fishing, an honest trade that required teamwork. Simon and Andrew cast the net; James and John mend their nets. Zebedee has hired men, which suggests a family business with some means.
str: vv. 16–18: Simon and Andrew are called while casting their net, and follow at once.
vv. 19–20: James and John are called while mending their nets, and leave their father and the boat.
kw: Literally “come behind me”. A disciple is one who walks behind a teacher. The word suggests not an idea but a person, and a road.
Jeremiah 16:16 uses the picture of fishers sent by God. Here the image is not of capture for harm but of gathering people into the net of the kingdom.
A favourite word of Mark’s, used dozens of times. It gives his Gospel its urgency: the kingdom is near, and the answer must not be put off.
vv: Follow me and I will make you fish for people.
Jesus promises to make them what they are not yet. The call is also a gift: he will form them.
And immediately they left their nets and followed him.
The response is prompt. They leave the tools of their trade, though Mark tells us a little later that Simon still had a home in Capernaum (Mark 1:29).
they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, and followed him.
A real cost: leaving a father and a family business. Jesus does not despise the family; he asks that the call be put first.
ch: The Catechism teaches that from the beginning Jesus associated his disciples with his own life, revealed the mystery of the kingdom to them, and gave them a share in his mission (CCC 787). St John Chrysostom, commenting on the calling of the fishermen, remarks that Christ chose simple, unlettered men so that the power of the Gospel would be seen to be God’s and not human eloquence (in substance, Homilies on Matthew).

qa: Does “made him to be sin” mean that Christ became a sinner?

No. Paul says in the same sentence that Christ “knew no sin”. The Church’s faith is that Christ was sinless (Hebrews 4:15). The sentence means that he took on himself the burden of our sin, entering fully into our condition so as to heal it, as the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 bore the sins of many. Many scholars also hear a sacrificial sense: God made him a sin offering.
study: “Everything old has passed away.” What is one old habit or grudge that I am being invited to leave behind through Christ’s reconciliation?
The four fishermen left their nets. What is the “net” that I find hardest to put down when Christ calls?

lead: Today the readings for St Mary Magdalene come first. Paul asks who can separate us from the love of Christ, and answers that nothing in all creation can. John shows that love at work: Mary Magdalene stays at the tomb when the others go home, hears her name spoken by the risen Lord, and is sent to tell the disciples. The weekday readings of the Third Thursday are also appointed: James 5:13–20, on the prayer of faith for the sick and the anointing of the elders, and Matthew 10:5–15, the sending of the Twelve. Mary’s own sending is a fitting companion to both.

r.h: More than conquerors
set: This is the end of Romans 8, the great chapter on life in the Spirit. Paul has just said that God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (8:32), so that no accusation can stand against God’s chosen (8:33–34). Now he asks whether any power can undo what God has done, and lists the worst things he and the Roman Christians can imagine.
str: v. 35: the question, with seven trials: hardship, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword.
v. 36: a quotation from Psalm 44:22: the faithful suffering for God’s sake.
v. 37: the answer: in all these things we are more than conquerors.
vv. 38–39: a sweeping list of powers, and the conviction that none can separate us from God’s love.
kw: to be more than a conqueror
A strong compound found only here in the New Testament. The believer does not merely survive: the victory is already won by Christ, and the believer shares in it.
The word is a gift that begins in God. Paul’s sentence is not about our love for God, which may waver, but about “the love of Christ” and “the love of God in Christ Jesus”, which does not.
Perfect tense: Paul has been persuaded and stays persuaded. It is the settled conviction of one who has already suffered much (2 Corinthians 11:23–28).
vv: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will hardship, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
Paul does not ignore suffering. He lists it plainly, as one who has known it. The Christian life is not promised to be painless, but it is promised to be never apart from Christ.
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
“In all these things”, not after them: the victory is within the trial. “Through him who loved us”: the strength is Christ’s.
neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers
Pairs of opposites cover everything: death and life, present and future. “Angels” and “rulers” may mean the spiritual powers that people feared in the ancient world.
will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
The chapter ends where it began, in Christ Jesus (8:1). The love of God is not a feeling that comes and goes but is rooted in Christ himself.
ch: The Church reads these verses at the feasts of martyrs and saints, because they show where the saints found their strength. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, says that Paul feared nothing so much as being cut off from the love of Christ (in substance, Homilies on Romans). The Catechism reminds us that we are able to turn away from God by mortal sin (CCC 1861), and that we may hope for the grace of final perseverance (CCC 2016). So the verse is a promise of God’s faithfulness and also a call to hold on to him.

r.h: Mary, and the garden
set: The scene follows John’s account of the burial in a garden near Golgotha (19:41–42). Jesus was laid in a new tomb, and the Sabbath has passed. Now, on “the first day of the week”, an expression that recalls the first day of creation, a new beginning is about to happen.

Mary Magdalene comes from Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Luke says that seven demons had gone out of her (Luke 8:2) and that she, with other women, supported Jesus out of their means. She is named at the tomb in all four Gospels. She is not the sinful woman of Luke 7, and she is not Mary of Bethany; the Gospels do not say so, and the Church does not teach it.
str: vv. 1–2: Mary finds the stone moved and runs to tell Peter and the other disciple.
vv. 3–10: the two disciples race to the tomb, see the cloths, and the beloved disciple “saw and believed”.
vv. 11–13: Mary stays, weeping, and sees two angels.
vv. 14–17: Jesus speaks, she knows him when he says her name, and he sends her.
v. 18: Mary announces: “I have seen the Lord.”
kw: An Aramaic word, a more personal form of “rabbi”. John calls it “Hebrew”, which for him means the Aramaic spoken by the Jews of that time. Mary uses the word of love and respect she used before the Passion.
do not hold on to me

The Greek present imperative means “stop clinging”, rather than “do not touch”. Jesus is not rejecting her. The old way of being with him is ending: he is about to ascend, and a new, deeper presence will begin.
Mary takes him for the gardener. The garden, the new day and the woman with the Lord echo the garden of Genesis; many readers see Jesus as the new Adam in a restored garden.
In John 20:18 Mary comes “announcing” (the verb gives us the word “angel” and shares a root with “gospel”). She is the first to proclaim the Resurrection.
vv: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.
“While it was still dark”: the darkness is real, but she comes anyway. Love goes to the tomb when there seems to be nothing left to hope for.
But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb.
The two disciples have gone home (20:10). Mary stays. Her tears are not a lack of faith but a sign of how much she loved.
Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?”
Jesus’ first words are two questions. They echo his first words in this Gospel: “What are you looking for?” (1:38). Mary does not yet recognise him.
Jesus said to her, “Mary!” She turned and said to him in Hebrew, “Rabbouni!” (which means Teacher).
The turning point. She knows him by his voice, as the Good Shepherd’s sheep do (John 10:3–4). One word, her name, is enough.
But go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’
Jesus calls his disciples “my brothers” for the first time. Through his Resurrection they share his relation to the Father.
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”
The first witness to the Resurrection is a woman, sent by Jesus himself. Her announcement is the beginning of the apostolic preaching.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Mary Magdalene and the holy women were the first to encounter the Risen One, and so women were the first messengers of the Resurrection to the apostles themselves (CCC 641). Early writers, among them Hippolytus of Rome (in substance, Commentary on the Song of Songs), described the women as apostles to the apostles, and St Thomas Aquinas later called Mary Magdalene “the apostle of the apostles”. In 2016 the Roman Church raised her memorial to a feast, with the same rank as the feasts of the apostles. The Church honours her as a model of persistent love, of those who remain when others leave, and of those sent to proclaim the Lord.

qa: Is Mary Magdalene the sinful woman who anointed Jesus’ feet in Luke 7?

No. The Gospels never identify them. Luke 8:2 introduces Mary Magdalene as a woman from whom seven demons had gone out, and says nothing of any sin of the kind later legend imagined. The idea that she was the woman of Luke 7 grew in the West from the sixth century, and the Roman liturgy today no longer treats her so. She is also distinct from Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus.
study: Mary stayed at the tomb when the others went home. When has staying faithful, even without answers, opened something new for me?
Jesus called her by name, and she knew him. Where do I hear the Lord calling me by name, in prayer, in Scripture, in the Holy Qurbana, in a person in need?

lead: Both readings are about seeing. Paul bends his knees and prays that his readers may be given strength to take in the breadth and length and height and depth of Christ’s love, a love beyond all knowing. In Mark, a blind man is healed in two stages, and slowly sees everything clearly. The Church has long seen in this a picture of the way faith grows: not all at once, but through the patient touch of Christ, until we see clearly and are filled with the fullness of God.

r.h: Rooted and grounded in love
set: The letter has described the mystery hidden for ages, that Gentiles are fellow heirs with the Jews in Christ (3:1–13). Now the writer breaks into prayer. The passage is the second great prayer of Ephesians (the first is in 1:15–23), and it is a single long sentence in Greek, with a prayer for strength (vv. 16–17a), for love and understanding (vv. 17b–19), and a doxology (vv. 20–21).

Ephesians presents itself as a letter of Paul. Many scholars think it was written in his name by a close disciple, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture and as the apostolic teaching of Paul.
str: vv. 14–15: Paul bends his knees before the Father, from whom every family takes its name.
vv. 16–17a: the prayer for strength by the Spirit, and for Christ to dwell in hearts through faith.
vv. 17b–19: rooted and grounded in love, to grasp the dimensions of Christ’s love and be filled with the fullness of God.
vv. 20–21: the doxology: glory to the God who can do more than we ask or imagine.
kw: The Greek word is a play on patēr, father. Every group of people that descends from one father, on earth or in heaven, owes its name and existence to the Father of all.
Two images joined: a plant with roots, a building with foundations. Love is both the soil and the ground on which the Christian stands.
The completeness of God’s own life. The prayer asks that believers be filled with it, which is nothing less than a share in God’s own life.
vv: I pray that, according to the riches of his glory, he may grant that you may be strengthened in your inner being with power through his Spirit
The strength is not human willpower. It comes from the Spirit, and it works in the “inner being”, where a person is most truly himself or herself.
and that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love.
Christ makes his home in the heart as in a house. The dwelling is through faith, and the soil is love.
what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge

Paul does not say what the four dimensions measure. St Augustine and others saw in them the shape of the cross; some read them as the whole of God’s plan. All agree that love of Christ is greater than any measure, and that it can still be known, though not fully grasped. “To know what surpasses knowledge” is a deliberate paradox.
Now to him who by the power at work within us is able to accomplish abundantly far more than all we can ask or imagine
The prayer ends in praise. God’s generosity is greater than our prayers, and his power already at work in the Church.
ch: The Catechism, quoting the opening verses, teaches that no one is father as God is Father, and that every human fatherhood and family takes its name from him (CCC 239, citing Ephesians 3:14–15). The passage is trinitarian in shape: the Father who grants, the Spirit who strengthens, Christ who dwells in the heart. St Augustine reads the “breadth and length and height and depth” as the cross of Christ, whose arms embrace the world and whose root goes deep into the earth (in substance, Letter 140).

r.h: He saw everything clearly
set: This miracle is found only in Mark. It comes at a turning point of the Gospel. Just before it, Jesus has asked his disciples whether their hearts are hardened, and whether, having eyes, they fail to see (8:17–18). Just after it comes Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi (8:27–30). The healing of a blind man stands between a question about the disciples’ blindness and the first moment they begin to see who Jesus is.

Bethsaida lay on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, a fishing town known to the Gospels as the home of Philip, Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). Its people had already seen Jesus’ deeds (Matthew 11:21).
str: v. 22: friends bring a blind man and beg Jesus to touch him.
vv. 23–24: Jesus takes him outside the village, puts saliva on his eyes, lays hands on him; the man sees, but not clearly.
v. 25: a second laying on of hands, and he sees everything clearly.
v. 26: Jesus sends him home and asks him not to enter the village.
kw: After the second touch the man “looked intently”. The verb suggests looking through, seeing clearly. It is the beginning of true sight.
Used of restoring health and, in Mark 9:12, of the restoring of all things. The cure is a sign of the restoration that Christ brings.
Jesus leads the man out of the village (v. 23) and sends him away from it (v. 26). The healing is private, and it does not seek publicity, a theme of Mark’s Gospel.
vv: He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village
Jesus does not heal from afar. He takes the man by the hand: the healing begins with closeness. The man’s journey with Jesus is already a journey from darkness.
when he had put saliva on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, “Can you see anything?”
Jesus uses touch and saliva, as he does with the deaf man in Mark 7:33. He also asks a question: the man is invited to take part, to tell what he sees.
I can see people, but they look like trees, walking.
An honest answer. The man does not claim more than he sees. Partial sight is real sight, but it is not yet clear.
Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he looked intently and his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly.

The only healing in the Gospels given in two stages. Many interpreters see here a picture of the disciples, who have begun to see (the confession of Peter) but do not yet see clearly (Peter will soon reject the Cross, 8:32–33).
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus often asks the sick to believe, and uses signs such as spittle, the laying on of hands, mud and washing (CCC 1504). The Church has long read this gradual healing as a picture of the growth of faith and of Christian life: faith is a light that grows, not an instant possession. The gift of sight is always Christ’s doing, and he takes the person by the hand, as he does in Baptism, which the early Church called “illumination” (CCC 1216).

qa: Why did Jesus need two attempts to heal the man?

The Gospel does not say Jesus lacked power; it shows a gradual healing as a sign. Jesus is never limited. Most commentators understand that Mark placed the story here to illustrate how the disciples were slowly coming to see. There is also a kindness in the method: Jesus lets the man’s sight grow in the way he can bear, and asks him what he sees.
study: Paul prays that Christ may dwell in our hearts “through faith”. What would it look like for Christ to be truly at home in my heart this week?
The blind man saw “people like trees” before he saw clearly. In which part of my faith do I still see only dimly, and what would let Christ touch it again?

lead: Both readings correct a kind of pride. James tells the confident planners, who say they will go to this town and make this profit, that life is a mist and that every plan should be made under the words “If the Lord wishes”. In Luke, the disciples want to stop a man who is casting out demons in Jesus’ name because he is not one of their group, and later want fire to fall on a village that will not receive Jesus. Jesus answers both times with a correction and a wider heart. God is the Lord of our plans, and his grace is not confined by our boundaries.

r.h: If the Lord wishes
set: James has just spoken against judging a neighbour (4:11–12). Now he turns to a different arrogance: the traveling merchant who plans a year of business as if the future were his own. The merchants of the Mediterranean world moved from city to city, and James knows the type. He does not condemn business or planning; he condemns planning that leaves God out.
str: v. 13: the planners: “today or tomorrow we will go…”.
v. 14: the reply: you do not know what tomorrow will bring; life is a mist.
v. 15: the right attitude: “If the Lord wishes…”.
vv. 16–17: boasting is evil; and the sin of knowing the good and not doing it.
kw: The word is used of smoke or of breath on a cold morning. Life is brief and cannot be held, a theme of Psalm 39:5–6 and Psalm 144:4.
A word for a show-off who claims more than he has. James calls it “evil”, not because it is loud but because it takes God’s place.
Verse 17 defines sin as failing to do the good one knows: sin of omission as well as of commission.
vv: Yet you do not even know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.
A sober reminder. James is not gloomy; he wants us to live wisely, aware that each day is a gift.
Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wishes, we will live and do this or that.”
Not a mere formula to be recited, but a way of living: the plan is made, and held open to God’s will. Paul uses the same phrase (1 Corinthians 4:19; Acts 18:21).
As it is, you boast in your arrogance; all such boasting is evil.
Self-reliance that forgets God is not a small fault. James names it for what it is.
Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, commits sin.
A searching verse for the conscience: it is not enough to avoid doing wrong; we are also answerable for the good we leave undone.
ch: The Church teaches that God’s providence guides all things, and that Jesus asks us to abandon ourselves with childlike trust to the providence of the heavenly Father, who cares for the smallest needs of his children (CCC 305). The Catechism also teaches that sin may be committed by omission as well as by commission (CCC 1853). The words “If the Lord wishes” are not an excuse for idleness: they are the other side of the Our Father, “Your will be done”.

r.h: Whoever is not against you
set: Luke 9 is the turning point of the Gospel. After Peter’s confession and the Transfiguration, “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51), and the long journey narrative begins, lasting to Luke 19:28. The two stories in today’s reading show how the disciples must learn on the road: John’s concern about an outside exorcist, and James and John’s anger at a Samaritan village.

Jews and Samaritans had been long divided, and many Jews travelling between Galilee and Jerusalem avoided Samaritan territory. The Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim, so a party on its way to the Temple at Jerusalem touched an old disagreement. Luke will later make a Samaritan the model of neighbourly love (10:30–37; 17:11–19).
str: vv. 49–50: John reports an exorcist who does not follow with them; Jesus: “Do not stop him”.
v. 51: Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem, the days of his being “taken up” drawing near.
vv. 52–53: messengers to a Samaritan village; the village does not receive him.
vv. 54–56: James and John want fire from heaven; Jesus rebukes them; they go on.
kw: The word in v. 51 points beyond the Cross to the Ascension. Luke sees Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem as a journey to glory through death.
The same word appears for the exorcist (“casting out demons”) in v. 49. The unnamed man is doing the work Jesus himself does, in Jesus’ name.
Jesus uses the same word of rebuking evil spirits and storms. He rebukes his own disciples’ wish for vengeance as something to be driven out.
vv: we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.
The disciples’ reason: he does not belong to our group. They do not deny that the work is genuine.
Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you.

Jesus refuses to draw the circle narrowly. Compare Mark 9:38–41. Elsewhere he says that whoever is not with him is against him (Luke 11:23): the two sayings together warn against both indifference and narrowness.
When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.
“Set his face” echoes Isaiah 50:7, the servant who sets his face like flint. He goes toward Jerusalem knowing what awaits him.
Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?

The echo is of Elijah and the fire in 2 Kings 1:10–12. Some later manuscripts add “as Elijah did”, and, after v. 55, the words “You do not know what spirit you are of, for the Son of Man has not come to destroy the lives of people but to save them”. These additions are probably not original, but they express the sense of the story well.
But he turned and rebuked them.
Jesus turns and faces them. The prophet Elijah called down fire; the Son of Man refuses. His way is not destruction.
ch: The Church has seen in Jesus’ answer to John a call to recognise good wherever it is found: the Second Vatican Council teaches that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the visible structure of the Catholic Church, and that these, as gifts belonging to Christ’s Church, impel toward Catholic unity (Lumen Gentium 8; Unitatis Redintegratio 3). The refusal of fire teaches that the Gospel is never to be spread by force: no one is to be compelled to embrace the faith (Dignitatis Humanae 10).

qa: Does “whoever is not against you is for you” mean that all religions and Churches are the same?

No. Jesus is speaking about a man who casts out demons in his own name, and he teaches his disciples not to be jealous of good done in his name by someone outside their circle.
