The Church teaches that Christ founded one Church and that the fullness of the means of salvation subsists in the Catholic Church, while she rejoices in the grace and truth found in other Churches and treats others with respect (Lumen Gentium 8, 15; Nostra Aetate 2). Jealousy and violence are never the Church’s way.
study: James reminds us that we do not know what tomorrow will bring. What plan of mine do I need to hold more openly, saying “If the Lord wishes”?

The disciples wanted to stop someone who was not “one of us”, and to punish those who would not welcome Jesus. Where am I tempted to limit God’s work to my own group, or to answer rejection with anger?

lead: All four readings ask what really honours God: words and customs, or a heart that listens. In Deuteronomy, Moses recalls the day at Horeb when God spoke the commandments out of the fire, among them the command to honour father and mother. In Isaiah, a people struck by God’s correction will not turn back to him, and the whole society consumes itself. Paul, writing to the Corinthians, refuses to boast of what he has not done and gives the rule for every Christian: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” In Mark, Jesus is asked why his disciples do not follow the tradition of the elders about washing, and he answers with a question of his own: how can a custom be used to set aside a commandment of God, above all the commandment to honour one’s parents? The lesson is not that tradition is bad, but that nothing, however venerable, may take the place of God’s word and of love for the neighbour closest to us.

r.h: The commandments spoken out of the fire
set: Deuteronomy presents itself as the farewell addresses of Moses on the plains of Moab, before Israel crosses the Jordan. In chapter 5 he gathers the people and recalls what happened at Horeb, the name Deuteronomy uses for Sinai: God himself spoke the ten words to the whole assembly. Today’s reading begins in the middle of the Decalogue, with the fourth commandment and the commandments about the neighbour, and goes on to the people’s fear at the voice of God.

This version of the Decalogue differs a little from the one in Exodus 20. The fourth commandment adds “as the Lord your God commanded you” and “that it may go well with you”, and the commandment on coveting uses a different word for the neighbour’s house than for his wife. Deuteronomy is preaching the law to a new generation: the words are not only history but a living address to “you”.
str: v. 16: honour father and mother, with the promise of long life and good in the land.
vv. 17–21: the commandments about the neighbour: do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet.
v. 22: the Lord spoke these words from the fire, cloud and darkness, added no more, and wrote them on two tablets.
vv. 23–24: the leaders of the tribes come to Moses, astonished that they have heard God’s voice and still live.
kw: From a root meaning “to be heavy”. To honour is to give weight to someone, to treat them as important. The word is also used of honouring God (Proverbs 3:9), so the fourth commandment stands on the border between our duty to God and our duty to people.
The Hebrew name for the Decalogue (Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4). They are “words” before they are “laws”: a voice that addresses a people with whom God has made a covenant.

In verse 24 the people say that God has shown them his “glory and greatness”. Glory is the weighty, radiant presence of God. The same root as “honour” appears here: God is honoured because he is truly weighty.
vv: Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the Lord your God is giving you.
The commandment is the only one of the ten that carries a promise. Families that hand on respect and care from one generation to the next are the roots of a lasting society.
These words the Lord spoke with a loud voice to your whole assembly at the mountain, out of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, and he added no more.
“And he added no more” means that these ten words stand apart as the heart of the covenant. All other laws are explanations of them.
He wrote them on two stone tablets, and gave them to me.
The words are written down so that they may be kept, taught and passed on. Written Scripture begins here with God’s own hand.
Today we have seen that God may speak to someone and the person may still live.
Israel had feared that to hear God would be fatal. The surprise is that God’s voice gives life. This is already a sign of the Gospel, where the Word becomes flesh and lives among us.
ch: The Catechism follows the fourth commandment through Deuteronomy’s wording. It teaches that the commandment is addressed first to children, but also speaks of the duties of parents, of grown children towards aged parents, and of citizens towards those in authority (CCC 2196–2200, 2214–2220). The promise of verse 16 is read as a sign that observing this commandment bears fruit in peace and in the common good (CCC 2200). The same Catechism teaches that the Ten Commandments are the words of God to his people, spoken before they are written, and that they are not set aside but fulfilled in Christ (CCC 2056–2063, 2074). Christians also hear verse 24 in the light of the Gospel: God speaks to us not out of fire and darkness, but through his Son, in whom the Word became flesh (Hebrews 1:1–2).

r.h: They did not turn to the one who struck them
set: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ. The northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim, was in crisis. Its kings had fought each other and had made and broken alliances with Syria and Assyria, and in 722 Samaria fell to the Assyrians. This section (9:8–10:4) is a poem in four stanzas, each ending with the same refrain: “For all this his anger has not turned away; his hand is stretched out still.” Today’s reading gives the second and third stanzas.

The point is not cruel punishment but a refusal to change. God had warned Israel through hardship, but the people did not turn to him. The poem shows how a society that will not turn to God begins to turn on itself.
str: vv. 13–15: the people do not turn; the Lord cuts off head and tail, the elders and the lying prophets.
v. 16: those who lead the people lead them astray.
v. 17: no pity for the young, the orphans and the widows, since all are godless; the refrain.
vv. 18–19: wickedness burns like a fire through the land; no one spares another.
vv. 20–21: hunger that is never satisfied; Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; the refrain again.
kw: The Hebrew verb for repentance, a turning around. The whole poem hangs on a refusal to “turn”. Isaiah’s own son was called Shear-jashub, “a remnant shall return” (7:3).
The refrain. It can mean a hand raised in judgment, but also a hand still held out, a sign that God has not yet withdrawn. The words are sad rather than final.

A common Hebrew picture for the whole of society, from the highest to the lowest. Verse 15 explains it: the head is the elders and dignitaries, the tail the prophets who teach lies. (The NRSV notes that verse 15 may be a later explanation, as it interrupts the flow of the poem.)
vv: The people did not turn to him who struck them, or seek the Lord of hosts.
Suffering that does not lead to prayer only hardens. The prophet’s complaint is not that God punished but that the people did not hear him in it.
for those who led this people led them astray, and those who were led by them were left in confusion.
The leaders are held to account first. The Church has always taught that those with authority will answer to God for those entrusted to them.
for everyone was godless and an evildoer, and every mouth spoke folly.
When no one is left to speak truth, the poor and defenceless suffer most: the orphans and widows of the same verse.
no one spared another.
The fire is the people’s own wickedness spreading. Sin does not stay private; it burns through a community.
Manasseh devoured Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh, and together they were against Judah.
The two tribes descended from Joseph’s sons turn on each other. Division within the people of God is both a consequence and a cause of turning away from God.
ch: Christian tradition has read this poem as a warning about the effects of unrepented sin on whole societies. The Catechism describes “structures of sin”: social situations and institutions that result from and encourage personal sins (CCC 1869). It teaches that sin is never only private, because it wounds the unity of the Church and of the human family (CCC 1440, 1869). But the refrain also speaks of patience. Lines that sound only like judgment are read in the Church as a call to conversion, for the Lord does not desire the death of the wicked but that they turn and live (Ezekiel 18:23; CCC 1428–1429). The Church prays for her leaders, and for all who suffer because of the failures of others, and for those who caused them to suffer.

r.h: Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord
set: Paul wrote this letter, probably from Macedonia, around AD 55–56, to a Church in conflict with him. Newcomers had arrived in Corinth who praised themselves, carried letters of recommendation, and measured themselves against each other. Paul calls them, with some irony, “super-apostles” (11:5; 12:11). Many scholars think that chapters 10–13 come from a sharper letter written at a different time from chapters 1–9; the Church receives the letter as one inspired text.

Paul has to defend his ministry, and he does so reluctantly. His answer is not to put forward his own achievements but to speak of the limits that God has given him: he is the one who first brought the Gospel to Corinth, and he looks forward to going on to places where Christ has not yet been proclaimed.
str: v. 12: Paul will not classify himself among those who commend themselves and compare themselves with one another.
vv. 13–14: his boasting stays within the field God has assigned to him, which includes Corinth.
vv. 15–16: he will not boast in the labours of others; he hopes that as faith grows, his work may go beyond Corinth.
vv. 17–18: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord”; it is not self-commendation but the Lord’s that counts.
kw: The key word of 2 Corinthians, used some twenty times. It can mean sinful self-praise or glad pride in what God has done. The difference is where the boast is placed: in oneself, or in the Lord.
Originally a measuring rod, then the sphere of work assigned to someone. From it comes our word “canon”. Paul lives within a measure given by God, not one he draws for himself.
To recommend someone, to put in a good light. Paul’s opponents commend themselves; he asks only for the commendation that comes from God.
vv: But when they measure themselves by one another, and compare themselves with one another, they do not show good sense.
Comparing ourselves with others is a rule that always misleads: we find someone worse to feel better, or someone better to feel worse.
We, however, will not boast beyond limits, but will keep within the field that God has assigned to us
Each person has a vocation. Humility is not thinking little of oneself but knowing the task given by God.
“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
Paul quotes Jeremiah 9:23–24, which he also quotes in 1 Corinthians 1:31. The Lord is the proper object of boasting, because every good work is his gift.
For it is not those who commend themselves that are approved, but those whom the Lord commends.
The final judgment on a life belongs to God. We are asked to be faithful, not to be praised.
ch: The Church applies verse 17 to the teaching on merit. The Catechism teaches that the merit of a person before God arises from the fact that God has chosen to associate him with the work of his grace, so that our good works are first of all God’s gifts to us (CCC 2006–2011). St Augustine put it in a saying that has become classic: when God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts (in substance). The same verse sets the pattern for apostolic work: the Second Vatican Council teaches that the mission of the Church is carried on in obedience to Christ, who sends and gives the increase (Ad Gentes 2–5; 1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Paul’s plan to go on to “lands beyond you” has been read by the Church as the missionary instinct that never rests while there are people who have not heard the Gospel.

r.h: You make void the word of God through your tradition
set: Jesus is in Galilee. A group of Pharisees and scribes has come from Jerusalem, probably to examine him, and they notice that some of his disciples eat without first washing their hands. Mark adds an explanatory note for readers who are not Jewish (vv. 3–4): the Pharisees “and all the Jews” follow the tradition of the elders about washing. This is a generalisation for outsiders, not a statement about every Jew, and many Jews of that time did not observe these customs in the same way. Washing before eating was a pious practice, not a law of Moses for everyone; the Law asks for ritual washing mainly of the priests (Exodus 30:17–21). The Pharisees were sincere teachers who wished to extend the holiness of the Temple into daily life.

Jesus does not condemn the custom of washing or the elders as such. His reply goes to the heart of the matter: he accuses of hypocrisy any religion that honours God with the lips while the heart is far away, and he gives a concrete example in which a human custom has been used to excuse people from a commandment of God.
str: vv. 1–5: the Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem ask why Jesus’ disciples do not follow the tradition of the elders.
vv. 6–8: Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13: lips honour, hearts far away; human precepts taught as doctrines; you abandon the commandment of God for human tradition.
vv. 9–13: the example of Corban: Moses commands honour for father and mother, yet a vow dedicating goods to God is used to avoid supporting them; the word of God is made void.
¶ The passage continues (vv. 14–23) with Jesus’ teaching to the crowd and the disciples on what truly defiles a person.
kw: In Greek, a stage actor, one who plays a part. Jesus uses it for a religion of appearances, not for a whole people. The word aims at the gap between lips and heart that every believer must examine in himself.

Literally “what is handed over”. It is a neutral word: Paul also uses it of the faith he hands on (1 Corinthians 11:2, 23; 15:3). The question is what is handed on, and whether it serves the word of God or replaces it.

An Aramaic form of the Hebrew word for an offering brought to God (Leviticus 1:2). Mark explains it as “an offering to God”. The word has the same root as the Syriac qurbānā, the name of our Holy Qurbana.
vv: This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me
Jesus quotes Isaiah in the Greek (Septuagint) form. The Hebrew text speaks of a worship learned by rote. Either way, the fault is worship that does not come from the heart.
You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.
Jesus names what is at stake: not tradition as such but the choice to put a human rule in the place of the divine commandment.
For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must surely die.’

He quotes the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16) together with the law in Exodus 21:17. Honour is serious: to curse a parent was a grave crime. The first reading of today stands behind this verse.
thus making void the word of God through your tradition that you have handed on.
“Making void” is strong: a human rule can empty the word of God of its force. Jesus does not oppose the word to tradition, but warns that tradition must serve the word.
ch: The Church has always asked how to hold together Jesus’ criticism of “human tradition” and her own reverence for Tradition. The answer given by the Second Vatican Council is that Sacred Tradition, which comes from the apostles, is the word of God handed on by the Holy Spirit and is inseparable from Scripture (Dei Verbum 9–10; CCC 80–82). The Catechism distinguishes this one Tradition from the “theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions” of local Churches, which can change and which must always serve it (CCC 83). The fourth commandment that Jesus defends is taught in the Catechism as a duty that continues into adult life: grown children owe their parents material and moral support in old age, illness, loneliness and distress (CCC 2218). Jesus’ words about the Corban vow show that no religious gift, however pious, may be used to avoid this duty. Early Christian writers also applied this Gospel against the plea of “custom”: St Cyprian, quoting an earlier writer, said that custom without truth is only the antiquity of error (in substance, Letter 74).

qa: Did Jesus condemn the Pharisees or the Jewish people for washing their hands?

No. Jesus himself came as a Jew who kept the Law, and Mark’s note about “all the Jews” is an outsider’s generalisation, not a statement about every Jew. Washing was a sincere pious custom of some groups, and Jesus does not forbid it. He criticises the use of any custom to excuse oneself from a commandment of God. The Church teaches that the Jewish people remain beloved by God (Romans 11:28–29; Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839), and that no blame may be laid on the Jews as a people (CCC 597–598). The warnings of this Gospel belong to every believer’s heart, and to Christians no less than to anyone.
If Jesus criticised tradition, why does the Catholic Church keep Tradition?

Jesus criticised a human rule that cancelled God’s commandment. The Church’s Sacred Tradition is something else: the word of God that Christ gave to the apostles and that the Holy Spirit keeps alive in the Church. It never contradicts Scripture and is always measured by it (Dei Verbum 9–10). Customs of local Churches, such as devotions and some rules, are kept or changed with the same test Jesus gives: do they help people to love God and neighbour, or do they empty the commandment?
What if it is hard to honour a parent who has been unkind or unjust?

To honour is not the same as to obey every command. A child is never bound to obey a command to sin (Acts 5:29), and in cases of abuse the Church encourages seeking safety and help. But honour includes gratitude for the gift of life, respect, prayer and, where needed, practical care in old age. Many people find that to forgive and to pray for a difficult parent is itself a way of honouring the commandment, and the Church asks pastors to accompany such families with patience.
rite: In the Season of Kaitha, the summer season of the Syro-Malabar calendar, the Church turns after the Apostles’ season to a long stretch of teaching on how to live the Gospel in ordinary time, and today’s readings give a clear rule of life. The Syro-Malabar Church has received a rich inheritance from the Thomas Christians: family prayer, reverence for elders and for the priest, and the blessing of parents on children. This is a living tradition of the kind Jesus does not reject, and it is worth cherishing, together with the call to examine whether the heart is in it. Many Kerala families today are separated by distance, with sons and daughters working far away from ageing parents. The fourth commandment asks that care for them be more than a money transfer, and that visits, calls and prayer be part of it.

The word “Corban” in the Gospel is the same root as qurbānā, the offering we make at the altar. In the Holy Qurbana we offer ourselves with the gifts of bread and wine; the Gospel today asks that no offering to God be a way of closing our hand to the neighbour, beginning with our own father and mother.
study: Moses reminds the people that they heard the voice of God and lived. How do I hear God’s word in the Holy Qurbana, and what do I do with it afterwards?
The poem in Isaiah ends in people turning on each other. What divisions in my family, parish or community need the prophet’s call to turn back?
Paul measures himself by the “field” God gave him, and not by comparison with others. In what way do I compare myself with others, and how could I boast in the Lord instead?
Jesus accuses people of honouring God with the lips while the heart is far away. What custom of mine, however good, could be keeping me from a commandment of God, especially honour to my parents?

lead: The weekday readings speak about wealth. James warns the rich who have kept back the wages of their workers: their riches are rotting, and the cry of the labourers has reached the Lord of hosts. In Luke, Jesus says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God, and when the disciples ask who then can be saved, he answers that what is impossible for people is possible for God. Today the Church also remembers Saints Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Virgin Mary according to tradition, and offers readings for them about God who gives life to the barren: Hannah’s song, Isaiah’s “Sing, O barren one”, Abraham and Sarah in the Letter to the Hebrews, and the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew. The two sets meet in one truth: what people cannot do, God can, and he lifts up the poor and the lowly.

r.h: The cry of the labourers
set: The Letter of James is addressed to Jewish Christians “in the Dispersion” (1:1). Its writer is James, whom tradition identifies with the “brother of the Lord”, the leader of the Church in Jerusalem; some scholars think it was written in his name a little later. The letter is full of concern for the poor. Here, in the manner of the prophets, James turns to the rich landowners and speaks of judgment. He is not condemning wealth in itself but wealth gained by fraud and kept at the cost of others.
str: vv. 1–3: the rich must weep and wail; their riches rot, their gold rusts, and the rust will bear witness against them.
v. 4: the wages kept back by fraud cry out; the cry of the harvesters has reached the Lord of hosts.
vv. 5–6: lives of luxury; hearts fattened for a day of slaughter; the righteous one condemned and killed.
kw: The word of the prophets for the cry of anguish at coming judgment (for example Isaiah 13:6). James speaks like Amos and Isaiah.
The pay of labourers. The Law commanded that a hired worker be paid on the same day (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15), because he is poor and depends on it.
Used in the New Testament only here and in Romans 9:29. It recalls the Lord who commands heaven’s armies and takes the side of the oppressed.
vv: Your riches have rotted, and your clothes are moth-eaten.
In the ancient world wealth was stored as grain, garments and metal. James says these treasures are already perishing, and what is hoarded is lost.
Listen! The wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out
The wages themselves cry out, as Abel’s blood cried from the ground (Genesis 4:10). God hears what no judge heard.
You have condemned and murdered the righteous one, who does not resist you.
It may mean the poor and innocent, who cannot defend themselves in court. Christians have also heard in it an echo of the Righteous One, Christ (Acts 3:14; 7:52).
ch: The Catechism teaches that a just wage is the legitimate fruit of work, and that to refuse or withhold it can be a grave injustice (CCC 2434, citing this letter and Leviticus 19:13, Deuteronomy 24:14–15, James 5:4). It lists the injustice done to wage earners among the sins that cry to heaven (CCC 1867). Passages such as this one are among the roots of the Church’s social teaching on the dignity of work.

r.h: What is impossible for mortals is possible for God
set: The passage follows the story of a rich ruler who asked what he must do to inherit eternal life and went away sad when Jesus asked him to sell his possessions and give to the poor (18:18–24). Jesus looks at him and says how hard it is for the wealthy to enter the kingdom. The camel and the needle’s eye is a deliberate exaggeration, a picture of what is humanly impossible. The idea that “the Needle’s Eye” was a low gate in Jerusalem is a later story with no support in the ancient texts.
str: v. 25: a camel through the eye of a needle is easier than a rich person entering the kingdom.
vv. 26–27: “Then who can be saved?” “What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.”
vv. 28–30: Peter: “Look, we have left our homes and followed you.” Jesus promises much more in this age and eternal life in the age to come.
kw: The answer turns on these two words. Salvation is not earned by human strength, whether rich or poor, but given by God’s power.
The question of the crowd is the question of every hearer. For Luke, salvation is already present in Jesus, and the poor and sinners are among the first to receive it.
Luke’s word for what is received in return. Mark has “a hundredfold” and adds “with persecutions” (10:30). What the disciple receives is not riches but a larger family, the community of believers.
vv: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
The danger is not money as such but the heart that clings to it. Riches can fill the heart so that there is no room for God and neighbour.
What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.
This is the Gospel in one line. The rich person can be saved, as can the poor, because grace can open what human effort cannot.

there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not get back very much more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life.
The reward is promised both now and then. Those who give up their own security for the Gospel find a family of faith and the joy of belonging to Christ.
ch: St Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole treatise on this passage, Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved? He taught in substance that what Jesus asks us to renounce is the passion for riches, not the possession of goods, and that a rich person can be saved by using wealth to help others. The Catechism teaches that poverty of heart is a requirement of the Gospel: the Lord asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544–2547), while those called to the evangelical counsels give up everything to follow him (CCC 915–916). It also teaches love for the poor as the sign of authentic discipleship (CCC 2443–2446).

r.h: Hannah’s prayer
set: Hannah, wife of Elkanah, was barren and prayed at the sanctuary of Shiloh for a child. God gave her Samuel, and she brought him to serve the Lord (1:1–2:11). This song is her thanksgiving. Its themes are the reversal of fortunes: the strong are broken, the weak are raised, the poor are seated with princes. The name Anne is the Greek form of Hannah, which means “favour, grace”.
str: vv. 1–2: joy in the Lord, the Holy One and Rock.
vv. 3–8: the proud are brought down; the barren bears seven; the Lord raises the poor from the dust.
vv. 9–10: the Lord guards the faithful; the Lord judges the ends of the earth and exalts his anointed.
kw: A name for God as the unshakable refuge of his people (compare Deuteronomy 32:4).
The last word of the song. In its first sense it is the king of Israel; the Church also hears the Messiah, whom Mary’s own song, the Magnificat, will recall.
vv: The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble gird on strength.
God’s way overturns human strength. The weak are not helpless because the Lord is their strength.
He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap
This is the verse behind many psalms and the Magnificat: Mary says he has “lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:52).
ch: The Church has always seen Hannah’s prayer as the model for Mary’s Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55); the two songs share the same movement of praise for a God who raises the lowly (CCC 2619). Today Saint Anne, who tradition says was granted a child after long waiting, is honoured as a woman of the same faith.

r.h: Sing, O barren one
set: These verses come from the second part of Isaiah, addressed to the exiles in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. Jerusalem, left desolate, is pictured as a barren woman and a forsaken wife. God now calls her to sing and to enlarge her tent, for her children will be more than ever. The “Maker” who is her husband has not abandoned her for good.
str: vv. 1–3: sing, enlarge your tent; your descendants will fill the nations.
vv. 4–6: do not fear; your Maker is your husband; the Lord calls you back like a wife forsaken.
vv. 7–8: for a brief moment I abandoned you; with everlasting love I will have compassion on you.
kw: The close relative who rescues a family member from slavery or debt (Ruth 4). God takes on that role for his people.
Raḥămîm comes from the word for womb: the mother’s tenderness. The same Lord who seems silent for a moment loves with a love that does not end.
vv: Enlarge the site of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out
Faith prepares room before the gift arrives. Hope enlarges the heart.
For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great compassion I will gather you.
The shadows are real but brief. God’s final word is not abandonment but the gathering of his people.
ch: The Church applies verse 1 to the barren who become mothers by God’s grace: Sarah, Hannah, Elizabeth, and Saint Anne. Saint Paul applies the same verse to the Jerusalem above, our mother (Galatians 4:26–27). The Catechism teaches that God’s power is shown in the weakness and lowly estate of those he chooses (CCC 64, 489, on the holy women of the Old Testament who prepared for Mary).

r.h: By faith Abraham and Sarah
set: The Letter to the Hebrews, written to Jewish Christians who were tempted to lose heart, presents a long list of people of faith in chapter 11. Abraham and Sarah stand at the head: they trusted the promise of a land and a child when both seemed impossible. The reading is chosen for Joachim and Anne because they too, according to tradition, waited long for a child.
str: vv. 8–10: Abraham obeys the call, lives in tents as a stranger, and looks for the city whose builder is God.
vv. 11–12: by faith Abraham, too old and with Sarah barren, received power of procreation; from one man, as good as dead, came descendants like the stars.
kw: In Hebrews, faith is trust that holds fast to what is promised though it is not yet seen (11:1).
The two words for the maker of the city. Abraham looks for a city that human hands did not found.
vv: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out, not knowing where he was going.
Faith moves before the road is clear. Abraham is the pattern of obedient trust.
because he considered him faithful who had promised.
The reason for hope is not our strength but the faithfulness of God who promises.
ch: The Catechism points to Abraham as the model of faith in his obedience to the call (CCC 144–147) and to Sarah, whose child Isaac was born by God’s promise (CCC 706). The Church holds up these ancestors in faith to the families who wait on God. Saints Joachim and Anne are remembered in the Church as a couple of the same patient trust.

r.h: The genealogy of Jesus the Messiah
set: Matthew opens his Gospel with the family tree of Jesus, arranged in three sets of fourteen generations (v. 17), from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, and from the exile to the Messiah. In Hebrew letters the name David adds up to fourteen, a clue to the pattern. Jesus is presented as son of Abraham, the father of the people, and son of David, the king.

Unusually for a Jewish genealogy, four women are named: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and “the wife of Uriah” (Bathsheba). The list ends with a break in the pattern: Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born”. It is Mary, not Joseph, through whom Jesus is born, and Matthew goes on to tell of his conception by the Holy Spirit (1:18–25). The names of Joachim and Anne do not appear in Scripture; they come from the second-century Protoevangelium of James, an early writing the Church does not receive as Scripture, and tradition has kept the names.
str: v. 1: the title: the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.
vv. 2–6: from Abraham to David, including Tamar, Rahab and Ruth.
vv. 7–11: from Solomon to the exile in Babylon.
vv. 12–16: from the exile to Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born.
kw: The same words as the opening of Genesis in the Greek Bible (Genesis 2:4; 5:1). Matthew begins a new genesis, a new creation, in Christ.
The Greek for “anointed”. The first verse names Jesus as the Messiah, son of David.
vv: An account of the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
In one line, Matthew places Jesus in the whole story of Israel. The promise to Abraham and the promise to David meet in him.
and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.
The pattern “father of” breaks here. Joseph is not named as Jesus’ father but as Mary’s husband: Jesus is born of Mary.
ch: The Church reads the genealogy as proof that God’s promises are kept through history, including through sinners and foreigners. The Catechism teaches that Mary, the daughter of Zion, is the one in whom the long preparation of the Old Covenant reaches its goal (CCC 489). The Church honours the parents of the Virgin Mary in this tradition of those who handed on faith, and Mary’s own descent from David has been the common teaching of Christians from early times.

qa: Who were Saints Joachim and Anne?

The Gospels do not name the parents of the Virgin Mary. The names Joachim and Anne come from the Protoevangelium of James, written in the second century. The Church does not treat this book as Scripture or as a reliable historical source for its details, but the names have been honoured in the East from early centuries and in the West from the Middle Ages, and 26 July is kept for them. They are remembered as the grandparents of Jesus according to tradition, and as an example of faithful parents who handed on the faith.
Does the Gospel say the rich cannot be saved?

No. Jesus says it is hard, not that it is impossible, and he says that all things are possible for God. Zacchaeus, a rich man, was saved when he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid those he had cheated (Luke 19:1–10). The danger is the heart that clings to riches and forgets God and neighbour.
rite: Saints Joachim and Anne remind the Syro-Malabar family of the part grandparents play in handing on the faith. In many Kerala homes it is the grandmother who teaches the first prayers and the grandfather who leads the evening prayer, and these are among the things the parish and the eparchy are glad to protect. The readings of the day also ask how a family uses its goods: the wages owed to workers, the generosity of the home, and the trust in God’s power that is greater than our plans.
study: James says the wages held back “cry out” to the Lord. Do I pay a fair wage and a fair price, and do I listen to the workers whose labour I use?
Jesus says that what is impossible for people is possible for God. What do I think is impossible in my life, and can I place it in his hands?
Hannah, Sarah and Anne waited long for a child. What am I waiting for, and how do I wait in faith?

lead: Both readings are about waiting for the Lord’s coming. James tells his readers to be patient like a farmer who waits for the early and late rains, to stop grumbling at one another, and to take the prophets and Job as examples of endurance. In Mark, Jesus describes the day when the Son of Man will come in clouds with power and glory and gather his chosen ones from the four winds, and he tells the disciples to learn from the fig tree and to trust that his words will never pass away. The Church’s waiting is neither fear nor calculation but patient, watchful hope.

r.h: Be patient until the coming of the Lord
set: James has just warned the rich who oppress the poor (5:1–6). Now he turns to the poor and suffering believers, who may be tempted to take matters into their own hands or to complain against each other. His word to them is patience. The farmer’s picture suits the land of Israel: the early rains come in autumn and the late rains in spring, and the crop depends on both (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24).
str: vv. 7–8: be patient like the farmer until the coming of the Lord, which is near.
v. 9: do not grumble against one another; the Judge stands at the door.
vv. 10–11: the prophets and Job as examples of endurance; the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
v. 12: do not swear oaths; let your “Yes” be yes and your “No” be no.
kw: Literally to be “long of spirit”, slow to anger and slow to give up. The word is used of God’s own patience with sinners.
A steady holding on under pressure. Job is the model: he did not curse God even in his sorrow.
The word for the arrival of a king or the coming of Christ in glory. The early Christians prayed Maranatha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22).
vv: The farmer waits for the precious crop from the earth, being patient with it until it receives the early and the late rains.
The farmer works, but he cannot make the rain fall. A Christian also does what he can and leaves the harvest to God.
Beloved, do not grumble against one another, so that you may not be judged.
Complaining against each other is the first fruit of impatience. The Judge is already near, so there is no need to judge one another.
You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
The story of Job ends in God’s mercy, not in his silence. The words “compassionate and merciful” echo the name God gave himself in Exodus 34:6.
let your “Yes” be yes and your “No” be no
James echoes the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:34–37). A person of integrity needs no oath to be believed.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church awaits the Lord’s glorious return, which is certain though its day and hour are unknown (CCC 673–677). It also teaches that the Lord’s words about oaths do not forbid solemn oaths for grave and right reasons, as in a court of law, but call all Christians to truthfulness in ordinary speech (CCC 2150–2155). The Church has long held up Job’s endurance as a model for the sick and sorrowing, and the great commentary of St Gregory the Great, the Moralia on Job, shows how seriously the Fathers took the book.

r.h: The Son of Man coming in clouds
set: Jesus is on the Mount of Olives, looking across at the Temple, in the last days of his earthly life. Four disciples have asked him when the Temple will fall and what the sign will be (13:1–4). The whole chapter is an apocalyptic discourse: it speaks of wars, persecution and the destruction of Jerusalem, and then of the end of the age. The language of sun, moon and stars comes from the prophets (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10) and the scene of the Son of Man comes from Daniel 7:13–14. Such language is not a weather report but a way of saying that the order of the old world gives way to the reign of God.
Mark does not give a timetable. He gives a call to watch: the disciples are to read the signs as one reads the fig tree, with attention and without panic.
str: vv. 24–25: after the distress, the sun and moon are darkened and the powers of heaven are shaken.
v. 26: the Son of Man comes in clouds with great power and glory.
v. 27: he sends the angels to gather his elect from the four winds.
vv. 28–29: the lesson of the fig tree: when you see these things, know that he is near.
vv. 30–31: this generation will not pass away before all this happens; heaven and earth will pass, but my words will not.
kw: Those whom God has called and gathered, the whole people of God. The gathering from the “four winds” recalls God’s promise to bring home his scattered people (Deuteronomy 30:4; Zechariah 2:6).
Used of summer, and of the Lord. The Lord is near “at the very gates”. Nearness here is as much a matter of readiness as of time.
Can mean the people living at one time, or a kind of people. Verse 30 is one of the hardest in the Gospels (see below).
vv: Then they will see ‘the Son of Man coming in clouds’ with great power and glory.
Daniel’s vision of one like a son of man receiving the kingdom is now fulfilled in Jesus. The one who is about to be judged is the one who will come as Judge and King.
Then he will send out the angels, and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
The picture is not of terror but of gathering. The end is the final coming together of God’s scattered people.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have taken place.

Interpreters have understood this in different ways. Many hold that it refers to the generation that would see the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus describes as the first great sign of the end; others take “generation” as the whole people of faith, or take “all these things” as the signs that are the beginning. All agree that Jesus gives no date, as the next verse says (13:32).
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
The sure ground of hope is not the calendar but the word of Christ. Everything else may change; his promise will not.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s glorious return awaits the end of history and that the Church’s task is to watch and pray, for “about that day or hour no one knows” (CCC 668–677; Mark 13:32). It teaches that the Last Judgment will come when Christ returns in glory, and that God alone knows the hour (CCC 1040). The Church rejects any attempt to calculate the date. St Augustine, in a letter to Bishop Hesychius, wrote that Christians should not try to determine the time of the Lord’s coming but should live always ready for it (in substance, Letter 199).

qa: Does Jesus say the world will end in the lifetime of those who heard him?

Not in that sense. Mark’s Jesus says in the very next verse that nobody knows the day or hour, not even the Son (13:32). Verse 30 is explained by the Church in different ways, most often as a reference to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus speaks of as an early sign, or to the whole generation of those who see the signs begin. What is clear is that Christ calls his disciples to be ready every day.
study: James says the farmer waits for the early and the late rains. Where in my life must I wait patiently, doing what I can and leaving the rest to God?
Jesus says that his words will not pass away. Which of his words do I most need to hold on to this week?

lead: Today the Church of the Syro-Malabar rite keeps the memory of St Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, a Franciscan Clarist sister of Kerala who died on this day in 1946, and gives her four readings alongside the readings of the weekday. The weekday readings already prepare the theme: Paul, defending his ministry, says that Christ “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God”, and that we share in that weakness and in that life; Jesus, moved with pity for the crowds like sheep without a shepherd, asks his disciples to pray for labourers for the harvest and then sends them out. The saint’s readings read as a single story. Deuteronomy tells of the blessing God promises to a people who keep his covenant. Isaiah describes the Servant who pours himself out for the many, and who, through that offering, sees his offspring and the will of the Lord prospers in his hand. Paul says what that means for the believer: “I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.” And in John, Jesus tells the Greeks who wish to see him that the grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit. Alphonsa lived this word. Her life was hidden, brief and marked by long suffering, and it has borne fruit in the hearts of many.

r.h: Crucified in weakness, alive by the power of God
set: These are among the last words of the letter. Paul announces his third visit to Corinth and warns that he will not be lenient with those who have sinned and not repented. The principle “any charge must be sustained by the evidence of two or three witnesses” is quoted from Deuteronomy 19:15, the same rule Jesus gives for the Church (Matthew 18:16). Some in Corinth have asked for proof that Christ speaks in Paul. He answers by pointing to the Cross: Christ himself seemed weak, and yet he lives by God’s power.
str: vv. 1–2: third visit; the law of two or three witnesses; a warning to those who have sinned.
v. 3: you ask for proof that Christ speaks in me; he is not weak toward you but powerful in you.
v. 4: he was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God; we are weak in him and will live with him.
kw: The word runs through 2 Corinthians (11:30; 12:9–10). For Paul weakness is not shameful: it is the place where God’s power appears.
The power that raised Jesus from the dead. It is the same power at work in the apostle and in the Church.
vv: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God.
The Cross and the Resurrection are not opposites. The weakness of Good Friday and the life of Easter are one act of God’s love.
For we are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
The disciple shares both. Paul’s own frailty does not cancel his authority; it is the form in which Christ’s power is exercised.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Cross is the sign of God’s power: Christ died “for our sins”, and God raised him, so that the weakness of the Passion leads to the glory of the Resurrection (CCC 648). The Church teaches that Christians, by baptism, are united to the death and Resurrection of Christ and called to carry that mystery in their own lives (CCC 1227, 1521). This reading prepares the way for the readings on St Alphonsa, who lived out in her body the “weakness” Paul speaks of.

r.h: The harvest is plentiful
set: Matthew has told of a series of Jesus’ healings (chapters 8–9). Now he sums up his work: teaching in the synagogues, proclaiming the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease. The sight of the crowds, “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd”, moves him to compassion, and he calls on the disciples to pray. In the next breath, he gives the Twelve authority to continue his work (10:1). The disciples who are told to pray for labourers become the first labourers.
str: v. 35: Jesus goes through the cities and villages teaching, proclaiming and healing.
v. 36: moved with compassion for the crowds, like sheep without a shepherd.
vv. 37–38: the harvest is plentiful and the labourers are few; ask the Lord of the harvest.
10:1: he summons the Twelve and gives them authority over unclean spirits and every sickness.
kw: From splanchna, the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. Jesus is moved in his very being, as the Lord is in Hosea 11:8.
In the prophets, the harvest is a picture of the gathering of the nations or of the final judgment (Joel 3:13). Here it is the gathering of people into the kingdom.
vv: When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
The picture comes from Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34. The people need a shepherd, and Jesus, the Good Shepherd, comes to be that for them.
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
The work belongs to the Lord of the harvest, and the first task of the Church is to pray. Those who pray find that they are themselves sent.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the whole Church is missionary by her nature and that every baptised person shares in this mission (CCC 849–856). The Second Vatican Council quotes this passage when it calls for prayer for vocations and for workers for the harvest (Ad Gentes 23, 39; Optatam Totius 2). Jesus’ compassion for the crowds is the model of every pastoral work, as the Church’s documents on priestly life remind us.

r.h: The Lord will command the blessing
set: Deuteronomy ends its long legal address with blessings and curses (chapters 27–30): Israel is shown two ways, the way of life and the way of death, and urged to choose life (30:19). Chapter 28 begins with a series of blessings for those who listen to the voice of the Lord and keep his commandments. Today’s verses come from the middle of this list. The blessings are those of a farming people: full barns, fruitful land, seasonal rain, children and cattle. Behind them stands the covenant bond: God makes Israel “his holy people”, and the nations will see that Israel is “called by the name of the Lord”.

These promises were made to Israel as a people, and as a people they depend on faithfulness to the covenant. They are not a guarantee that every faithful person will become wealthy. The Book of Job and the Psalms, and above all the Cross, show that suffering is not a sign of God’s anger and that the righteous often suffer. The deeper blessing is the one named in verse 9: to be God’s own, and to carry his name.
str: v. 8: the Lord commands blessing on barns and on all undertakings in the land.
v. 9: the Lord will establish Israel as his holy people, if they keep his commandments and walk in his ways.
v. 10: all peoples will see that Israel is called by the name of the Lord.
vv. 11–12: abundance in children, cattle and crops; the heavens opened to give rain in season; Israel will lend to many nations.
kw: In the Bible, a blessing is God’s life-giving power at work in people and creation. To be blessed is first of all to be in the presence of God.
“Holy” means set apart for God. Israel is holy not because of its own goodness but because the Lord has chosen and claimed it (Exodus 19:5–6).
God swore an oath to the ancestors (Genesis 22:16–18). The blessing rests on a promise that cannot fail, even when the people do.
vv: The Lord will establish you as his holy people, as he has sworn to you, if you keep the commandments of the Lord your God and walk in his ways.
The covenant has a gift and a response. God first chooses and then asks for a life that fits the choice.
All the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the Lord
The holiness of God’s people is meant to be seen. A holy life is a witness to those who do not yet know the Lord.
The Lord will open for you his rich storehouse, the heavens, to give the rain of your land in its season and to bless all your undertakings.
Rain is not earned but given from above. God’s generosity is the source of everything that grows.
ch: The Church reads the blessings of Deuteronomy in the light of Christ. The Catechism teaches that God’s blessing is his gift of life and that Christ is the fulfilment of all the blessings, in whom the Father “has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3; CCC 1077–1083). The Church also teaches that the holiness of God’s people is God’s own work in them: the Church is holy because Christ, the Holy One, gives himself to her, and the holiness of the saints shows it (CCC 823–829). The saints, among them Alphonsa, are those on whom this blessing has most clearly come: those who carry the name of the Lord and whose lives make others see him.

r.h: He shall see his offspring
set: This is the end of the fourth Servant Song (52:13–53:12) in the second part of Isaiah, addressed to Israel in exile in the sixth century before Christ. A mysterious servant of the Lord suffers, is despised and put to death, and yet through his suffering many are made righteous. In the Jewish tradition the Servant has often been read as Israel itself, or as the faithful remnant, or as a prophet. Christians have read the poem as a prophecy fulfilled in Jesus: the New Testament applies it to him (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25; Mark 10:45), and he himself speaks of his death with its words (Luke 22:37).
Today’s verses are the conclusion. After the suffering, the Lord’s purpose prospers: the Servant sees light, sees his offspring, and shares in the triumph. His suffering is not the end.
str: v. 10: it was the will of the Lord to crush him; his life is an offering for sin; he will see his offspring and prolong his days.
v. 11: out of anguish he sees light; the righteous servant makes many righteous and bears their iniquities.
v. 12: therefore he has a portion with the great; he poured out himself to death, was numbered with sinners, bore the sin of many, and interceded for the transgressors.
kw: The guilt offering of Leviticus 5–7, an offering that makes amends for a wrong. The Servant offers his own life in place of the sacrifice of an animal.
Literally “he will make many to be in the right”. The Servant’s offering restores people to a right relation with God.
From the root for “meeting, interposing”. The Servant steps between sinners and the judgment they deserve.
vv: When you make his life an offering for sin, he shall see his offspring, and shall prolong his days
A paradox: the one offered becomes fruitful. His suffering does not end in loss but in a family, a people born from his offering.
The righteous one, my servant, shall make many righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.
The Servant is not only an example but a source. He bears what others cannot bear and gives them a share in his righteousness.
because he poured out himself to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
Jesus quotes the phrase “numbered with the transgressors” on the night of his arrest (Luke 22:37). Even on the Cross he prays for those who crucify him (Luke 23:34).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s death fulfils the prophecy of the Suffering Servant: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures” (CCC 601), and that by his obedience unto death Jesus fulfilled the substitution of the Servant who “shall make many righteous” (CCC 615). The Church also teaches that Christ’s passion gives new meaning to human suffering: it can be united to his redemptive passion (CCC 1505, 1521; Colossians 1:24). This is the teaching in which the Church sees the life of St Alphonsa. She did not value suffering for its own sake; but when it came, she placed it in the hands of Christ, trusting that nothing offered in love is lost.

r.h: Crucified with Christ
set: Paul has just told how he opposed Peter at Antioch when Peter drew back from table fellowship with Gentile believers (2:11–14). He explains why: no one is justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ (2:16). Today’s verses are the heart of the argument, and one of the most personal passages in his letters. “Through the law I died to the law” does not mean the law is evil (3:19–25; Romans 7:12) but that the believer has been freed through Christ from the law’s power to condemn, and now lives to God.
The central sentence is a confession of love: the Son of God “loved me and gave himself for me”. For Paul, the Gospel is not first an idea but a person who loves each one.
str: v. 19: through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
v. 20: I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live but Christ who lives in me; I live by faith in the Son of God who loved me and gave himself for me.
v. 21: I do not nullify the grace of God; if justification came through the law, Christ died for nothing.
kw: A Greek verb in the perfect tense: it happened once and its effect remains. The believer’s old self was nailed to the Cross with Christ in Baptism (Romans 6:6).
Here not mere belief but trusting surrender to the person who loved and gave himself. Faith is the way Christ’s life becomes the believer’s life.
The undeserved gift of God’s love. Paul says that to seek justification by law alone would make the Cross pointless.
vv: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.
This is the goal of Christian life: not to copy Christ from outside, but for Christ to live in us.
And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
The Cross is personal: “for me”. Paul can say this because the love that gave itself was addressed to him by name.
I do not nullify the grace of God
Grace is not set aside by a religion of effort. The Cross is the proof that no one can save himself.
ch: The Catechism quotes “who loved me and gave himself for me” when it speaks of the love of the Heart of Jesus for each person (CCC 478), and teaches that the Cross is the unique sacrifice of Christ, in which each believer is invited to share (CCC 618). It teaches that our justification comes from the grace of God and that, since grace is God’s gift, our own good works are his gifts in us (CCC 1996–2001, 2006–2011). In Baptism we are united to the death of Christ so that we may walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3–4; CCC 1227). A saint is a person in whom this has become visible: someone of whom it can truly be said that Christ lives in her.

r.h: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies
set: It is the last public scene of Jesus’ ministry in John, in Jerusalem during Passover week. The crowds have just welcomed him on Palm Sunday (12:12–19). Some Greeks, probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, ask Philip to see Jesus. Philip, whose name is Greek and who comes from Bethsaida, tells Andrew, and together they tell Jesus. Jesus does not simply receive them. He declares that “the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”: the coming of the Gentiles is a sign that his hour has arrived, the hour of the Cross and Resurrection through which he will draw all people to himself (12:32).
He then explains in a parable what the hour will mean: the grain must die to bear fruit. The same law holds for his followers.
str: vv. 20–22: some Greeks wish to see Jesus; Philip and Andrew bring them.
v. 23: the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.
v. 24: the grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit.
v. 25: those who love their life lose it; those who hate their life in this world keep it for eternal life.
v. 26: whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am my servant will be; the Father will honour him.
kw: In John, the “hour” is the time of Jesus’ Passion, death and glorification. Until now it “had not yet come” (2:4; 7:30); now it has.
For John, Jesus’ glory is revealed in the Cross. He is lifted up on the Cross, and lifted up in glory.
A Semitic way of speaking that means to love less, to put second (compare Luke 14:26). It does not mean contempt for life, but that the life given to God is worth more than clinging to it.
vv: Sir, we wish to see Jesus.
The whole Gospel is answered in this request. Everyone who comes to the Church is asking to see Jesus. The Church’s task is to show him.
Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Death is not the end of the grain but the beginning of the harvest. The image holds for Christ, for his martyrs and for every life given in love.
Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.
The disciple follows into the same place: the Cross, and then the glory. Being with Christ is the reward of service.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this chapter, saw in the grain Christ himself, who died and then rose in many members, so that the Church is the harvest sown by his death (in substance, Tractates on John 51). The Catechism teaches that Christ’s sacrifice makes it possible for his disciples to be associated with his Passion (CCC 618), and that the way to holiness passes by the Cross, for there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle (CCC 2015). It also teaches that those who unite their own suffering and death to Christ’s receive a share in his fruitfulness (CCC 1521). The martyrs and saints bear witness to this: their hidden lives become a source of life for others.

qa: Who was St Alphonsa?

Alphonsa was born on 19 August 1910 at Kudamaloor in Kerala and was baptised Anna (called Annakutty). Her mother died soon after her birth, and she was brought up by relatives. When a marriage was being arranged for her, her biographers tell us, she stepped into a pit of burning chaff so as to be unfit for marriage, and she carried the injury to her feet for life. She joined the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam in 1927, received the habit and the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception in 1928, and made her first vows in 1931 and her final vows in 1936. She lived a quiet life of prayer, work and patient suffering from illness, and died on 28 July 1946 at the age of thirty-five. Blessed Alphonsa was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1986, and Pope Benedict XVI canonised her in Rome on 12 October 2008. She is the first woman of India raised to the altars of the Church, and her tomb at Bharananganam is a place of pilgrimage for many people.
Does God want people to suffer?

No. God does not will suffering for its own sake, and the Church asks us to ease suffering and to seek healing wherever we can. But suffering that cannot be removed can be offered, in union with Christ, and can become a place of love and fruitfulness. This is the meaning of today’s readings: the Servant offers himself and bears fruit; the grain dies and bears much fruit. St Alphonsa did not value suffering for its own sake; she offered what came to her with trust in God, and it became a gift to others. The Church honours her for her love, not for the pain itself.
Do the blessings promised in Deuteronomy mean that good people will always be prosperous?

No. Deuteronomy speaks to Israel as a people in covenant with God, and the blessing is the life of a community that lives by God’s law. The Bible itself also shows that the righteous often suffer (the Book of Job, many Psalms, the Servant of Isaiah 53), and the Cross is the fullest sign of this. The deepest blessing is to belong to God and to carry his name. Material gifts, where they come, are to be received with thanks and shared with others.
rite: St Alphonsa belongs to the Syro-Malabar Church, and her feast is kept in our rite on the day of her death, 28 July. Born in Kerala, formed in a Christian family and in the life of the Church, she gave her whole life to Christ in the quiet service of a convent. Each year pilgrims come to her tomb at Bharananganam, including many who are sick or burdened. The Church teaches us to honour the saints by imitation as well as by prayer: Alphonsa’s life asks us not to look for extraordinary things but to do small, hidden things with great love, and to place our sufferings in the hands of the Lord. In the Holy Qurbana, we too bring our lives as an offering together with Christ, the grain that died and rose. The readings of the day are a good moment for the family to pray for the sick and for all who suffer in many lands, and for those who have wronged them.
study: Paul says that Christ “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God.” Where do I experience weakness, and can I believe that God’s power is at work there?
Deuteronomy says the people of God are to be “called by the name of the Lord” so that all nations see it. What does my life say about the One whose name I carry?
Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.” What would it mean this week to let Christ live in my work, my family and my suffering?
Jesus says the grain must fall into the earth and die. What small hidden act of love could I offer today, like St Alphonsa, for someone who will never know?

lead: The weekday readings call for a decision. James gives a string of short commands to those who try to serve God and the world at once: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, humble yourselves, and stop judging your neighbour. In Luke, Jesus says he has come to cast fire on the earth, longs for his “baptism”, the Passion, to be fulfilled, and warns that he brings division, because to follow him cuts through even the closest ties. Today the Church also remembers St Martha of Bethany, the sister of Mary and Lazarus, and gives two readings for her: the first letter of John, “God is love”, and the Gospel in which Martha, grieving for her brother, hears Jesus say, “I am the resurrection and the life”, and answers with a confession of faith. The day’s message is that love and faith ask for a whole heart, and that the one who asks for it is himself the resurrection and the life.

r.h: Submit yourselves to God
set: James has just spoken sharply about quarrels and cravings among Christians (4:1–6) and said that friendship with the world is enmity with God. Now he gives ten short commands, in the style of the prophets’ call to repentance. They describe one movement: turn from the devil and double-mindedness, draw near to God, and live humbly with others. The reading ends with a warning against slander and judging, which he treats as a sin against the law of love.
str: v. 7: submit to God; resist the devil and he will flee.
vv. 8–9: draw near to God; cleanse your hands and purify your hearts; lament and mourn.
v. 10: humble yourselves before the Lord and he will exalt you.
vv. 11–12: do not speak evil against one another; there is one lawgiver and judge; who are you to judge your neighbour?
kw: A military and social word for placing oneself in order under another. Before God it means a willing act of trust, not fear.
Literally “two-souled”: people who try to belong both to God and to the world. James uses the word of the one who doubts in 1:8.
In the Old Testament, priests “drew near” to God in the Temple (Exodus 19:22; Leviticus 10:3). James tells every believer to draw near, with clean hands and a pure heart, as the Psalm says (24:4).
vv: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Resistance is possible because it begins with obedience to God. The devil flees not from our strength but from our belonging to the Lord.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.
God’s nearness answers ours. The first step is a human one, yet God has long been seeking us.
Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
It is the same promise as the Lord’s in the Gospel (Luke 14:11) and of Mary’s song (Luke 1:52). God raises the lowly.
So who, then, are you to judge your neighbor?
Only God knows hearts. When we judge, we take a place that is not ours.
ch: The Catechism teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer (CCC 2559), and that we should not judge others rashly, speak evil of them, or run down their good name (CCC 2477–2479). The Church sees in James’s call to “draw near” the movement of conversion and penance, which begins with God’s own first love for us (CCC 1427–1429). The letter’s call to resist the devil is part of the Church’s teaching that Christians are in a spiritual battle in which they can count on God’s grace (CCC 409, 2846–2849).

r.h: I came to bring fire to the earth
set: Jesus is on the way to Jerusalem (9:51), teaching his disciples and the crowds about readiness for the coming of the Son of Man (12:35–48). Then his tone turns to himself. Three short sayings speak of fire, of a baptism, and of division. They are among the hardest sayings in the Gospel because they seem to contradict the angels’ song of peace at his birth (2:14).

The fire is generally understood to mean the Holy Spirit, who will come at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), and also the purifying judgment that his coming brings. The “baptism” is his Passion (compare Mark 10:38). The “division” is the result of the choice his coming forces on each person and each household. Verse 53 echoes Micah 7:6, a prophecy of division within families before the day of the Lord.
str: v. 49: I have come to cast fire on the earth, and I wish it were already kindled.
v. 50: I have a baptism to receive, and I am under stress until it is completed.
vv. 51–53: not peace but division; households are divided, father against son, mother against daughter.
kw: In the Bible, fire is a sign of God’s presence (Exodus 3:2), of purification (Malachi 3:2–3) and of the Spirit (Acts 2:3). It does not only destroy; it refines.
From a verb meaning “to immerse”. Here it means being plunged into death, the Passion, from which Jesus will rise.
The verb means to be pressed from all sides, held in tension. It shows that Jesus approaches his Passion not with indifference but with a deep longing to complete the Father’s will.
vv: I came to bring fire to the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!
The fire is lit by Christ’s Passion and kindled at Pentecost. He desires that it burn in every heart.
I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and what stress I am under until it is completed!
Jesus is not merely a teacher of wisdom; he goes to meet his Passion as the work for which he came.
Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division!
The peace he brings is real, but it is not the peace of avoiding every choice. Christ’s call asks a decision, and where people decide differently, division can come, even in homes.
ch: The Catechism teaches that fire is a symbol of the transforming energy of the Holy Spirit, and quotes this verse in speaking of the Spirit (CCC 696). It teaches that Christ’s whole life leads to his “baptism”, the Passion, which is the Father’s plan (CCC 536, 607–609). On division in families, the Catechism says that family ties are important but not absolute: a person’s vocation comes from God, and loyalty to Christ may bring misunderstanding and, at times, pain (CCC 2232–2233). The Church does not read this passage as a licence for hostility, since the same Lord commands his followers to love their enemies and to seek peace with all (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:18). Christians are asked to remain faithful to Christ with gentleness, and to pray for those who oppose them.

r.h: God is love
set: The First Letter of John was written for a community troubled by a split in its own ranks, around the end of the first century. Its writer insists that knowing God cannot be separated from loving the brothers and sisters, and that the heart of faith is the love of God shown in the sending of his Son. This reading is given for St Martha because she is the woman of Bethany who loved the Lord and served him in her home (Luke 10:38; John 12:2).
str: vv. 7–8: love one another, for love is from God; the one who does not love does not know God, for God is love.
vv. 9–10: God’s love was shown in sending his Son; love is not that we loved God but that he loved us first.
vv. 11–12: since God has loved us, we ought to love one another; no one has seen God, but if we love, God abides in us.
vv. 13–16: the Spirit is the sign of this abiding; to confess that Jesus is the Son of God is to abide in God; God is love.
kw: The word John uses of God’s own love, without selfishness, poured out on others. To say that “God is love” is to say that God is a communion who gives himself.
The offering that removes sin and restores friendship with God. It echoes the Day of Atonement and is fulfilled in the Cross.
A favourite word in John for staying in lasting communion. God abides in us, and we in him.
vv: Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.
This is one of the shortest and deepest sentences in the Bible. All that we say of God must be said in the light of love.
In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
The initiative is always God’s. We love because we have first been loved.
No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God lives in us, and his love is perfected in us.
God is invisible, but the love of Christians for one another makes him visible. Love is the Church’s chief witness.
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on the Trinity and on God with these words: God is love, and the whole life of God is a gift of himself (CCC 214, 220, 221, 257). It teaches that the Cross is the revelation of this love (CCC 604) and that the love of God and neighbour is the sum of the commandments (CCC 2055, 2196). The saints, including Martha in her service, show that loving is not a feeling but a way of life.

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, has died, and Jesus arrives four days later. In the Gospel, Bethany is about two miles from Jerusalem, so many from the city have come to console the sisters. John says “the Jews” here simply of these neighbours and mourners who had come to comfort the family (11:19, 31, 45). Jesus comes to a house in grief. Martha, the active sister, goes out to meet him, while Mary stays at home (compare Luke 10:38–42).

Martha’s words are a mixture of grief and faith: “If you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Yet she adds, “even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask.” Jesus answers with promise, and then with one of the great “I am” sayings of John’s Gospel. Martha’s confession that follows (11:27) is, in John, one of the clearest professions of faith: “You are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.”
str: vv. 17–20: Lazarus has been in the tomb four days; Martha goes out to meet Jesus; Mary stays at home.
vv. 21–22: Martha: if you had been here my brother would not have died; even now God will give you what you ask.
vv. 23–24: Jesus: your brother will rise again; Martha: I know he will rise at the resurrection on the last day.
vv. 25–26: Jesus: I am the resurrection and the life; those who believe in me, even though they die, will live; do you believe this?
kw: The “rising again” of the dead. Martha shares the faith of many pious Jews of the time, based on Daniel 12:2, that the dead will rise on the last day.
Jesus’ solemn way of speaking in John, echoing the divine name (Exodus 3:14). The “resurrection” is not only a future event; it is a person standing before her.
In John, not an opinion but the entrusting of oneself to Christ. “Do you believe this?” is the question to every reader.
vv: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask of him.
Martha’s prayer is honest. She says her pain, and she says her hope, in the same breath.
I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live
Jesus does not only promise a resurrection; he is the resurrection. Life is to be found in union with him.
Do you believe this?
A question addressed to Martha and to every Christian at a graveside. Faith is the answer of the whole person to the One who speaks.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus ties faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the Resurrection and the life” (CCC 994). It teaches that death is the end of earthly pilgrimage, yet for those who die in Christ it is a passage to life (CCC 1006, 1010–1014). St Augustine, preaching on the raising of Lazarus, heard in the story a call to rise from the death of sin as well as from the tomb (in substance, Tractates on John 49). The Church sees in Martha both the faithful servant and the believer who confesses Christ in the hour of loss.

qa: Who was St Martha, and is she the same as Mary Magdalene?

Martha was the sister of Mary and Lazarus, who lived at Bethany near Jerusalem and were friends of Jesus. Luke tells how she welcomed Jesus into her home and was busy with serving, and how the Lord told her gently that only one thing is needed (10:38–42). In John she confesses her faith when Lazarus dies (11:20–27), and she serves again at the supper six days before the Passover (12:2). Mary of Bethany, her sister, is not the same person as Mary Magdalene, who is a different woman from Magdala in Galilee. Martha is honoured as a model of hospitality, service and faith, and the readings of the day show that the two sides belong together: service grows from love, and love is confessed in faith.
Does Jesus really want to bring division?

Jesus does not want hatred or quarrels. He is called the Prince of Peace and gives his peace to his disciples (John 14:27). But the Gospel calls for a decision, and people in the same family may answer differently. When that happens, the Church asks believers to remain loyal to Christ with patience, love and prayer, and not to look for conflict.
study: James tells us to “draw near to God.” What is one concrete step I can take today to draw near, in prayer or in forgiveness?
Jesus says, “I came to bring fire.” Where do I feel the fire of the Spirit in my life, and where am I trying to keep it small?
Martha says her grief and her hope together to Jesus. What do I need to say to him honestly today?

lead: Both readings turn the world’s values upside down in order to teach what lasts. James says that the lowly believer should boast in being raised up, and the rich in being brought low, because wealth passes like the flower of the grass. In Matthew, when a lawyer asks which commandment in the law is the greatest, Jesus answers with two: love God with all one’s heart, soul and mind, and love one’s neighbour as oneself. The two readings are close: what lasts is not what we own but whom we love.

r.h: The lowly and the rich
set: James begins his letter with a section on trials (1:2–18), in which he says that tests produce endurance and that God gives wisdom generously to those who ask. In today’s verses he applies this to rich and poor in the community. The person of low standing is told to be proud of the high position God has given him, and the person of wealth to be proud of being brought low. Scholars discuss whether the “rich” here is a rich Christian, who is called to humility, or a rich outsider, as in 5:1–6. Either way, the logic is the same: wealth is not a lasting foundation.
The picture of the flower in the field comes from Isaiah 40:6–8 and Psalm 103:15–16, where human life is like grass that withers in the scorching wind, while the word of God stands for ever.
str: v. 9: the lowly believer should boast in being raised up.
v. 10: the rich in being brought low, because the rich will disappear like a flower in the field.
v. 11: the sun rises with scorching heat, the grass withers, the flower falls; so the rich wither in the midst of a busy life.
kw: In the Bible the word often means those who are poor and without power, whom God favours (Luke 1:52). It also means the humble in heart.
The same word as in 2 Corinthians 10:17. The only boast worth having is in what God gives, which includes dignity as his child.
vv: Let the believer who is lowly boast in being raised up, and the rich in being brought low
The ranks of the world are reversed in God’s eyes. The poor believer is raised by God’s adoption; the rich believer learns that wealth cannot save.
For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the field; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes.
A vivid picture of how quickly beauty and wealth fade. It teaches that our lasting treasure is not on earth.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God has a special love for the poor and that poverty of heart is a condition for entering the kingdom (CCC 2443–2446, 2544–2546). The Church’s teaching has always been that riches in themselves are not evil, but that attachment to them can close the heart to God and neighbour.
